When risen, gently deflate, divide into 6 to 8 equal pieces, round each into a ball, and rest them covered for another 15 minutes so the gluten relaxes and the dough rolls out without fighting back.

Set a heavy cast-iron skillet or tawa over high heat for a full 5 minutes until it is smoking-hot — this is your stand-in for the tandoor. Meanwhile, on a lightly floured surface, roll or stretch each ball into a teardrop or oval about 5 to 6 inches long and a generous 3 to 4 millimetres thick, leaving it slightly thicker than a tortilla. Don't roll it paper-thin; naan needs body to puff. Brush the top lightly with water just before it hits the pan — the moisture helps it grip and steam.

Lay the naan wet-side-down onto the dry, smoking pan. Within a minute it will balloon up with steam and the underside will char in dark spots — cover with a lid for 30 seconds to trap heat and encourage the puff. When the top is bubbling and the bottom is blistered black-and-gold, flip and cook the second side 30 to 60 seconds until spotted too. For an even more tandoor-like char, hold the puffed naan with tongs directly over an open gas flame for a few seconds. Keep finished breads wrapped in a towel to stay soft.

Warm the ghee or melted butter with the minced garlic just until fragrant — don't brown the garlic. The moment each naan comes off the heat, brush it generously with the garlic-ghee so it soaks into the hot, open crumb, then scatter with chopped coriander. Serve immediately, stacked and wrapped in a clean towel to hold their softness and steam.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nam Jim Seafood Sauce
description: Thailand's electrifying raw dipping sauce for grilled seafood — pounded garlic, fresh chili, and coriander root let loose in a sharply sour, intensely herbaceous fish-sauce-and-lime mix.

ingredients.text: 3 parts Bird's eye chilies (prik kii nuu), stems removed
1 parts Coriander roots, scraped clean (or stems)
1 parts Palm sugar or white sugar

instructions: In a granite mortar, combine the garlic cloves, bird's eye chilies, and coriander roots. Begin by pounding the garlic first — it takes the most force. Once the garlic is a rough, juicy smear, add the coriander roots and pound again. Finally add the chilies. Work them all together with a circular grinding motion, alternating between pounding down and scraping the sides inward with a spoon. The goal is a coarse, wet paste — not a smooth puree. You want visible threads of coriander root, small flecks of chili skin, and a slightly chunky garlic base. The oils released by pounding are fundamentally different from those released by cutting: they are brighter, more volatile, and more intensely fragrant.

Add the palm sugar directly to the mortar and pound briefly to break it into the paste — it needs to fully dissolve, not just sit as lumps. Then pour in the lime juice and fish sauce. Stir with a spoon to combine everything, tasting as you go. The sequence of flavors in a properly balanced nam jim seafood should be: sour first and loudest, then salty, then sweet as a background that keeps the acid from being harsh, then a building heat that arrives last and lingers. Adjust lime for more sour, fish sauce for more salt, sugar to soften harshness. This sauce should be bold to the point of almost-too-much — it is meeting grilled seafood that can take it.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nam Prik Pao
description: Thai roasted chili paste — each ingredient char-roasted individually before being ground together into a dark, smoky, sweet-savoury jam that smells of campfire and caramelised shallot. The backbone of tom yum, the secret in pad thai, and remarkable on plain rice by itself.

ingredients.text: 2 parts Dried long red chilies, stemmed and seeded
0.5 parts Palm sugar or brown sugar

instructions: Roast each ingredient separately in a dry wok or skillet over medium-high heat, turning occasionally. Chilies: 3–4 minutes until fragrant and slightly puffed, not burnt. Shallots (unpeeled): 8–10 minutes until the outer skins are charred black and the interior is soft. Garlic (unpeeled): 6–8 minutes until the skins are blackened and the cloves soft. Cool, then peel shallots and garlic — the charred outer skins are discarded but their flavour has penetrated the flesh.

Peel the roasted shallots and garlic. Place in a mortar with the roasted chilies and dried shrimp. Pound firmly, working the dried shrimp in first (they take the longest), then the garlic, then shallots, then chilies. Pound until a rough, fragrant paste forms — some texture is correct for this style. Alternatively pulse in a food processor to a chunky consistency.

Heat oil in a wok or saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 8–10 minutes until the paste darkens, the moisture evaporates, and the oil begins to visibly separate from the solids. Add fish sauce and palm sugar. Stir and continue frying for 3–4 more minutes until the sugar caramelises and the paste smells complex, sweet, and deeply smoky. Cool and store in a jar — the flavour improves over 24 hours.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nashville Hot Sauce
description: The incendiary cayenne-and-lard basting sauce that is brushed over freshly fried chicken at Prince's Hot Chicken and its descendants — a deep-red, glossy paste of cayenne, brown sugar, and spices that soaks into the crust and builds a slow, rolling heat that earns its city's reputation. The lard is non-negotiable; it is what makes the sauce cling.

ingredients.text: 4 parts Lard or neutral frying oil (from the fried chicken fryer, strained)
2 parts Cayenne pepper (ground, freshly opened jar)

instructions: Gently heat the lard or frying oil in a small saucepan over medium heat until it reaches approximately 150–160 C (300–320 F) — just beginning to shimmer and move in the pan when swirled. This temperature is hot enough to bloom the spices and dissolve the sugar without scorching. If using strained fryer oil from freshly fried chicken, it is likely already at the right temperature.

Remove the pan from heat. Add the cayenne, brown sugar, smoked paprika, garlic powder, and salt to the hot fat all at once. Whisk vigorously and continuously for 30–45 seconds. The residual heat will bloom the spices, dissolve the sugar, and toast the powders in the fat, deepening their flavor dramatically. The mixture will foam and sizzle briefly and turn a vivid, deep brick-red.

Allow the bloomed spice-fat mixture to cool slightly for 2 minutes — to approximately 80 C (176 F). Add the apple cider vinegar and whisk immediately to emulsify. The sauce will thin slightly and brighten from the acid. Taste carefully (it is very hot): it should be fiery, slightly sweet from the brown sugar, with a sharp acidic back end from the vinegar. Use immediately to brush generously over freshly fried chicken, or store in a jar at room temperature for up to 2 weeks.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nasi Goreng Paste
description: A dark, intensely savoury paste of charred shallots, garlic, and fermented shrimp paste ground into a fragrant black-red roux — the aromatic engine that transforms day-old rice into something smoky, funky, and deeply satisfying the moment it hits a screaming-hot wok.

ingredients.text: 1 parts Dried red chilies (5–8), soaked in hot water 10 min
0.25 parts Bird's eye chilies (2–3, optional for extra heat)

instructions: Wrap the terasi in a small square of aluminium foil and press it flat. Toast directly over a gas flame or in a dry pan for 30–45 seconds per side until it smells cooked and deeply savoury — the raw, ammonia-like sharpness of the raw paste should give way to a roasted, fermented complexity. Do not skip this step: raw terasi has an aggressive, harsh smell that cooking tames into something extraordinary. The foil prevents the paste from sticking and the flame from charring it unevenly.

Drain the soaked dried chilies — they should be soft and pliable. Combine shallots, garlic, soaked dried chilies, fresh bird's eye chilies (if using), and toasted terasi in a large mortar. Pound methodically starting with the hardest items (shallots, garlic) before adding the chilies and terasi. Work in a circular pounding motion, turning the pestle and occasionally scraping down the sides. The goal is a smooth, uniformly coloured, deep brick-red paste with no visible chunks. A blender works but produces a slightly more watery paste — add a tablespoon less water.

Heat the oil in a wok or heavy frying pan over medium heat until shimmering. Add the spice paste all at once — it will spit and hiss loudly. Stand back. Fry, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, for 6–8 minutes. The paste will progress through three visible stages: first it steams and sputters (water evaporating); then it fries and darkens from bright red to a deeper brick-brown; finally the oil separates around the paste (minyak pecah) and the paste smells sweet, toasted, and complex rather than raw. This cooked paste base is the foundation of all nasi goreng flavour.

Add kecap manis and a pinch of salt to the cooked paste and stir over low heat for 1 minute until incorporated. The kecap manis adds sweetness and a deeper colour — the paste will darken further to a glossy, very dark brown. Taste: it should be savoury and complex with a distinct fermented depth. It will be intensely flavoured — this is a concentrated paste meant to season 2 cups (400 g cooked) of rice per this recipe amount. Store cooled paste in a sealed jar in the refrigerator for up to 1 week. To use: add 2 tablespoons of oil to a hot wok, add paste and stir-fry 30 seconds, then add day-old rice and toss.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nasi Goreng
description: Indonesia's national fried rice — day-old rice stir-fried in a screaming-hot wok with shrimp paste, kecap manis, and sambal, scrambled with egg until each grain is coated in the dark, sweet-savory glaze and the wok edges smoke.

ingredients.text: 600 g Day-old cooked jasmine rice, cold and separated
15 ml Regular soy sauce or kecap asin
20 g Sambal oelek or fresh red chili, sliced
30 g Fried shallots, cucumber slices, spring onion, and/or fried egg for serving

instructions: Break up the cold day-old rice with your fingers or a fork until no clumps remain — every grain should be individual and dry. Cold, separated grains fry; fresh warm rice steams and turns to paste. If using solid terasi (shrimp paste), break off the required amount and toast it briefly: wrap in foil and hold over a low gas flame for 1 minute per side, or dry-fry in a small pan until fragrant and slightly crumbly. The toasting kills any fishy rawness and converts the paste into a powerfully savory, nutty compound. Crumble the toasted terasi into a small dish. Have all other ingredients measured and within arm's reach — nasi goreng moves fast.

Heat a wok or large cast-iron skillet over the highest flame you have until a drop of water vaporizes instantly on contact — this takes 2–3 minutes. Add the oil; it should ripple and shimmer immediately. Add the sliced shallots and stir-fry for 60 seconds until translucent and beginning to colour. Add the minced garlic and crumbled terasi, pressing the terasi against the hot wok with the spatula to break it up. Stir-fry for 30 seconds — the kitchen will fill with a powerful, savory, slightly funky aroma that quickly becomes complex and toasted. Add the sambal and toss for 15 seconds. The wok should be smoking lightly.

Push the aromatics to one side of the wok. Crack both eggs into the empty space. Leave them to set for 10–15 seconds without touching — the yolk should just begin to set at the edges. Then scramble them roughly with the spatula, breaking up into large, irregular curds. Before the egg is fully set and while it still looks slightly wet and shiny, push the aromatics back over the eggs and fold everything together. Partially-set egg integrates into the rice better than fully-cooked scrambled egg, which clumps separately.

Add the separated rice to the wok in two additions, tossing vigorously after each — use a spatula and a rapid scooping-and-flipping motion. Pour in the kecap manis and regular soy sauce over the rice (not the aromatics directly, which can burn) and toss continuously for 2–3 minutes. Every grain should be coated in the dark, mahogany-brown glaze. The rice may crackle and pop as individual grains toast against the wok surface — this is the wok hei you want. Taste and adjust with soy or kecap manis. Plate immediately.

Plate the nasi goreng immediately — it does not wait well. Top with a fried egg (sunny-side up, the yolk runny), crispy fried shallots scattered over the top, sliced cucumber alongside, and spring onion. The fried egg's yolk, broken at the table, acts as a sauce for the rice. The fried shallots add a final crunch and sweetness that the recipe sorely needs after all that heat. A few slices of cucumber cut through the richness. Serve with extra sambal on the side for those who want more heat.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nasi Lemak
description: Malaysia's national morning: jasmine rice cooked in coconut milk with pandan leaf until each grain is individually rich and perfumed, served with a deep, caramelised sambal, crunchy fried anchovies, and roasted peanuts — an architecture of contrasts in a single bowl.

ingredients.text: 0.5 parts Dried red chilies, soaked and blended

instructions: Combine rinsed rice, coconut milk, pandan leaves, and salt in a heavy saucepan. Add enough water so the total liquid sits exactly 1.5 cm above the rice surface. Bring to a boil over medium heat, stir once, then immediately reduce to the lowest possible heat, cover tightly, and cook for 12 minutes. Remove from heat and steam, undisturbed, for 10 more minutes. Remove pandan before serving.

Heat oil in a wok until shimmering (about 175 C). Add dried anchovies in a single layer and fry, stirring constantly, for 3–5 minutes until deep golden and crunchy throughout. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper. They will continue to crisp as they cool. In the same oil, fry peanuts for 2 minutes until golden. Drain separately.

In the same wok (add oil if needed), fry blended shallots and chili paste over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 12–15 minutes. The paste will sputter, darken, and shrink dramatically. Add palm sugar and continue to cook, scraping the bottom, for 5 more minutes until the sambal is very dark brick-red, glossy, and the oil has separated back to the surface. Season with salt and a small squeeze of tamarind if available.

Mound coconut rice in the centre of a banana leaf or plate. Add a generous spoonful of sambal alongside. Scatter fried anchovies and roasted peanuts over and around. Classic accompaniments include half a hard-boiled egg and sliced cucumber. Serve immediately — the contrast of hot rice, room-temperature sambal, and crunchy toppings is the point.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nasu Dengaku
description: Halved Japanese eggplant roasted until molten, then glazed with sweet white miso and caramelized under the broiler to a lacquered, bittersweet finish.
instructions: Preheat oven to 200°C (400°F). Halve the eggplants lengthwise. Using a sharp knife, score the cut flesh in a deep crosshatch pattern — cuts about 1.5 cm apart and 1 cm deep — without piercing the skin. Brush the scored flesh generously with sesame oil. Place cut-side down on a lined baking tray and roast for 15–18 minutes until the flesh is completely soft and the skin has begun to wrinkle.

Whisk together the white miso, mirin, sake, and sugar in a small bowl until completely smooth and glossy. The glaze should be thick enough to mound on a spoon — if it seems too stiff, add a teaspoon of mirin. If it runs freely, the miso may be very wet; a brief stir over low heat will tighten it.

Flip the roasted eggplant halves cut-side up. Using a spoon or pastry brush, spread the dengaku glaze generously and evenly across each cut surface, covering the entire flesh and working it into the scored crosshatch. Place under a hot broiler (or return to top rack at 230°C) for 3–5 minutes, watching closely, until the glaze darkens to a deep mahogany brown and bubbles vigorously at the edges. Garnish immediately with sesame seeds and scallion.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nduja Butter
description: Unsalted butter whipped with fiery Calabrian nduja until the two meld into a silky, pork-scented compound that spreads like luxury and burns with a slow, building heat.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
10 parts Fresh chives, very finely minced

instructions: The butter must be genuinely soft — not cold and hard, and not starting to melt. Leave it at room temperature for at least 45–60 minutes before beginning, or until it dents easily under gentle finger pressure. Beat the softened butter in a bowl with a wooden spoon or hand mixer on medium speed for 2–3 minutes until it turns pale ivory, increases in volume, and becomes noticeably lighter and fluffier in texture. This step aerates the butter and creates the foundation for a silky compound that melts smoothly rather than breaking into greasy pools.

Add the nduja to the whipped butter. At room temperature, nduja is soft and spreadable — it will cream into the butter easily. Beat on medium speed until the nduja is completely incorporated and no red-orange streaks remain. The nduja's fat and spice oils will dye the butter a warm terracotta-orange color throughout. The mixture will smell intensely of pork fat, fermented meat, and Calabrian chili — a very direct, animal aroma. This step should take no more than 90 seconds of active beating.

Add the chives, lemon zest, black pepper, and salt to the nduja butter base. Fold in gently with a rubber spatula — do not beat, which would bruise the chives and turn them dark. Three or four broad folds are enough to distribute them evenly. Lay a large sheet of plastic wrap on the counter. Spoon the butter along one edge and use the wrap to roll it into a compact log about 5 cm in diameter. Twist the ends firmly to compress and shape the log. Refrigerate for at least 45 minutes until very firm, or freeze for up to 2 months. Slice into rounds directly from the refrigerator.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nduja Tomato Sauce
description: Calabria's fiery, spreadable salami — all pork fat, Calabrian chili, and cured intensity — melted into a simple tomato sauce until it disappears into a glossy, brick-red emulsion that stains everything it touches with heat and pigment. Thirty minutes from start to table, and more complex than anything that quick has a right to be.

ingredients.text: 400 g Canned San Marzano whole tomatoes
100 g Burrata or fresh mozzarella to serve (optional)

instructions: Heat olive oil in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium heat. Add garlic and cook for 90 seconds until pale golden. Add nduja in one piece. Using a wooden spoon, press and break it up as it heats — within 2–3 minutes it will melt into the oil completely, releasing vivid orange-red fat and transforming the olive oil into a blazing, chili-scented emulsion.

Add canned tomatoes to the pan, crushing them with your hand as you pour. Stir to incorporate the nduja emulsion into the tomatoes — the sauce will instantly turn a deep, vivid red-orange. Season lightly with salt (remember nduja is already salty). Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally and crushing any remaining tomato chunks. The sauce should reduce and thicken visibly.

Remove from heat. Tear basil leaves and stir through the sauce. Taste and adjust salt. Toss immediately with cooked rigatoni, paccheri, or calamarata (tube pastas that trap the spicy sauce inside). Add a spoonful of pasta water if needed to emulsify. Serve with torn burrata draped over the top, which cools the heat and adds rich contrast.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Neapolitan Pizza Dough
description: A 60% hydration lean dough leavened slowly with commercial yeast. The structure relies on long autolyse and gluten development through folds, not kneading.
instructions: Stir yeast into cool water (18–20 °C / 65–68 °F) until no granules float on the surface.
Add flour to the slurry. Stir with a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains.
Cover and let the dough rest 20–30 minutes at room temperature. The flour will fully hydrate and gluten will begin organizing on its own.
Sprinkle salt across the surface. Pinch and fold until it disappears into the dough.

Perform stretch-and-folds at 30-minute intervals: lift one side, stretch up, fold over. Rotate. Repeat across four rounds (about 2 hours total), then let the dough relax 15–20 minutes before the bulk rise.
Cover. Let rise at cool room temperature (18–20 °C / 65–68 °F) for 8–12 hours — or 4–6 hours at a warm 24–26 °C / 75–79 °F — until the dough has roughly doubled and is jiggly when nudged.

Divide into equal portions (about 250–280 g each for a 30 cm pizza). Tuck each into a tight ball under cupped hands, sealing the seam underneath, then cover and proof 4–6 hours at room temperature (or cold-proof in the fridge 24–48 hours, returning the balls to room temperature about 2 hours before stretching) until puffy and relaxed.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: New England Clam Chowder
description: A bowl of ivory cream thickened with tender potatoes and salt pork, shot through with briny, sweet clam liquor — every spoonful carries the cold Atlantic inside it.

ingredients.text: 30 parts Chopped clams, canned or fresh (with liquor reserved)
8 parts Salt pork or thick-cut bacon, diced
25 parts Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and diced 1cm
2 parts Kosher salt, white pepper, and fresh thyme

instructions: Place the diced salt pork in a cold, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven and set over medium-low heat. Cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the fat has fully rendered and the pork bits are golden and crispy. Starting cold ensures maximum fat extraction. Remove the crispy pork bits with a slotted spoon and reserve.

Add the diced onion to the rendered fat over medium heat and cook, stirring occasionally, for 5–7 minutes until soft and translucent but not browned. Sprinkle the flour over the onions and stir continuously for 1–2 minutes, coating every piece of onion. This blonde roux is the chowder's body — it must cook enough to lose its raw flour taste but must not take on any color.

Pour the reserved clam liquor plus enough water or clam juice to cover the potatoes by 2cm into the pot while whisking to prevent lumps. Add the diced potatoes. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 12–15 minutes until the potatoes are tender but still holding their shape. Do not boil vigorously — aggressive boiling will cause the potatoes to break apart and make the chowder muddy.

Reduce heat to low. Stir in the heavy cream and the chopped clams. Heat gently for 3–5 minutes until warmed through. Do not boil after adding the cream — it will break and curdle. The clams only need to be warmed, never cooked; if they were raw they would toughen severely at this stage. Taste and adjust salt and white pepper.

Ladle the chowder into warm bowls. Top with the reserved crispy pork bits and a crack of black pepper. Optionally drizzle with a few drops of heavy cream in a spiral. Serve with oyster crackers or crusty bread on the side. The chowder thickens considerably as it cools — serve while hot.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: New York Bagels
description: Dense, chewy, irreducibly satisfying — the NY bagel's singular texture comes from a high-gluten dough, an overnight cold retard, and a malt-spiked boil before baking, producing a crust that snaps under the knife and a crumb that resists all impostors.

ingredients.text: 30 g per liter Barley malt syrup (boil water)
20 g Everything bagel seasoning or sesame/poppy seeds

instructions: Combine flour, salt, yeast, and malt syrup. Add cold water (cold water slows fermentation and improves texture). Mix until a very stiff, dry-looking dough forms — bagel dough is noticeably stiffer than any other bread dough, with only 55% hydration. Knead vigorously for 12–15 minutes by hand (or 10 minutes on medium in a stand mixer) until the dough is satiny smooth and extremely tight. Divide into 8 portions (about 110 g each).

Shape each portion into a tight ball, then use the thumb-through method: press both thumbs through the center of the ball and stretch the ring to 8–9 cm diameter with a 3 cm hole (the hole shrinks during proofing and baking). Alternatively, roll each ball into a 25 cm rope and join the ends with a 3 cm overlap, pressing firmly and rolling the seam against the work surface to seal. Place on parchment-lined trays dusted with cornmeal or semolina. Refrigerate uncovered overnight (12–16 hours).

Remove bagels from refrigerator. Float test: drop one bagel in cold water — it should float within 10 seconds. If it sinks, let the batch proof at room temperature for 30 more minutes. Bring a wide pot of water to a rolling boil. Add barley malt syrup. Boil bagels 2–3 at a time for 60 seconds per side (softer) or 90 seconds per side (chewier, more authentic). Remove with a spider or slotted spoon, drain, then immediately press the wet top into seeds or seasoning.

Bake on a parchment-lined tray (or preheated baking stone) at 230 C (450 F) for 18–22 minutes until deeply golden-brown with no pale patches. Rotate the tray at 10 minutes. The bagels will darken significantly in the final 3 minutes. Cool on a wire rack for at least 15 minutes before cutting — the crumb is still setting.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: New York Cheesecake
description: A dense, ivory-white round of cream cheese, eggs, and sour cream baked low and slow until it trembles, then cooled for hours until it slices into clean, silken wedges with a biscuit crust that crumbles at the touch of a fork.

ingredients.text: 15 parts Graham crackers, crushed to fine crumbs
100 parts Full-fat cream cheese, room temperature
15 parts Full-fat sour cream, room temperature
1 parts Vanilla extract and fine salt

instructions: Combine the graham cracker crumbs and melted butter in a bowl and mix until the crumbs are evenly moistened — they should look like wet sand and hold together when squeezed. Press firmly into the bottom of a 23cm springform pan using the flat bottom of a measuring cup. Press firmly and evenly — including 2–3cm up the sides. Bake at 175°C for 8–10 minutes until just set. Cool completely before filling.

All ingredients must be at room temperature — cold cream cheese will not beat smooth and will leave lumps that never fully incorporate. Beat the cream cheese with a stand mixer paddle (not whisk) on medium speed until completely smooth and creamy, about 2 minutes. Scrape the bowl and beater thoroughly. Add the sugar and beat for 2 more minutes. Scrape again. Beat in the vanilla and salt. The goal is smooth — not airy. High-speed beating incorporates air that causes cracking.

With the mixer on low speed, add the eggs one at a time, beating only until each is just incorporated before adding the next — no more. Overmixing after adding eggs develops the batter and adds air. Finally, add the sour cream and mix on low just until combined. Scrape the bowl one final time and fold gently by hand with a spatula. The finished batter should be smooth, thick, and flow slowly.

Preheat oven to 160°C. Wrap the outside of the springform pan tightly in two layers of heavy foil (to prevent water ingress). Pour the batter into the cooled crust. Set the pan in a larger roasting pan and pour boiling water into the roasting pan to come halfway up the sides of the springform. Bake for 60–70 minutes until the edges are set and the center 10cm jiggles as a single mass. Turn off oven, crack door 5cm, and leave for 1 hour.

Remove from the water bath after the oven rest. Run a thin knife around the inside edge of the springform to release the cheesecake (this prevents cracking as it shrinks). Cool at room temperature for 2 hours. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight. Remove the springform ring only when the cheesecake is fully cold. Slice with a hot, dry knife for clean cuts.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Niban Dashi
description: The second extraction from spent kombu and katsuobushi — less refined than ichiban dashi but richer and more complex, carrying the fermented depth of exhausted bonito into braises, simmered vegetables, and noodle broths.
instructions: Place the spent kombu and katsuobushi from your ichiban dashi into a pot with fresh cold water. Bring slowly to 140°F (60°C) over medium-low heat — this is below simmering, and you should see gentle movement in the water but no bubbles. Niban dashi is extracted at a lower temperature than the initial steep because the depleted ingredients release their remaining glutamates and inosinates more slowly and at lower temperatures. Hold at this temperature for 15 minutes.

If adding fresh katsuobushi for a flavor boost, add it now and simmer (not boil) for 8–10 minutes. Simmering niban dashi slightly harder than ichiban is acceptable — the goal is richer, more assertive umami rather than delicacy. Bring to a very gentle simmer (barely perceptible movement), not a rolling boil. Turn off the heat and let steep 5 minutes undisturbed.

Line a fine-mesh strainer with a sheet of cheesecloth or a coffee filter. Pour the dashi through slowly without pressing the solids — pressing extracts bitter tannins. Discard the kombu and katsuobushi. The strained dashi should be clear or nearly so, with a warm amber color. Allow to settle 5 minutes; any remaining fine particles will sink. Use immediately or cool rapidly and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for 1 month.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nibitashi
description: A Kyoto vegetable preparation of quiet, meditative restraint — blanched greens briefly simmered in a delicate dashi seasoning liquid, then left to absorb the broth as they cool. The greens drink in the umami of the dashi and emerge deeply flavored yet vibrant, a study in subtraction.

ingredients.text: 300 g Spinach or watercress, roots trimmed

instructions: Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a rolling boil. Submerge the spinach stems first for 15 seconds, then push the leaves under and blanch for 30–45 seconds total. The water must be at a full rolling boil throughout — a weak boil steams instead of blanches and the color suffers. Transfer immediately to a bowl of ice water and leave for 1 full minute.

Combine dashi, soy sauce, and mirin in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Taste — the broth should taste pleasantly salty and lightly sweet, slightly more assertive than you want the finished dish to be, because the greens will dilute it. Simmer for 2 minutes to cook off the raw mirin alcohol.

Add the squeezed blanched greens to the simmering broth. Gently submerge them and simmer for just 60 seconds — this opens the cell walls slightly to allow the broth to enter. Remove from heat and let the greens steep in the broth, off the heat, for 15 minutes as the liquid cools. Lift the greens out, squeeze gently again to remove excess broth, and cut into 4 cm lengths. Arrange in small mounds in serving bowls. Spoon a small amount of the steeping liquid over each portion and top with bonito flakes.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Niter Kibbeh
description: Ethiopia's clarified spiced butter — whole butter slowly infused with onion, garlic, ginger, fenugreek, turmeric, cardamom, and korarima until deeply golden and fragrant, then strained clear into a golden cooking fat of extraordinary complexity.

ingredients.text: 20 g Fresh ginger, peeled and sliced
4 g Korarima (Ethiopian cardamom) or black cardamom pods, seeds only
2 g Dried basil or Ethiopian besobela (sacred basil)

instructions: Place the butter in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over low heat. Let it melt gently without stirring. As it melts, a white foam will rise to the surface — this is the milk proteins beginning to separate from the butterfat. Continue heating on very low heat, never stirring, until all the butter is fully liquid and a steady, gentle bubble appears. The goal at this stage is gentle melting, not browning. Do not rush with high heat — the milk solids need time to separate cleanly from the fat.

Add the onion, garlic, ginger, fenugreek seeds, turmeric, korarima, cinnamon, nutmeg, and dried basil directly to the melted butter. The addition of the aromatics will dramatically increase bubbling — the water in the fresh ingredients will begin evaporating. Maintain very low heat and let the mixture gently bubble and infuse for 30–40 minutes. Stir once or twice but otherwise leave undisturbed. Over this time, the onion and garlic will slowly soften, wilt, and begin to turn golden at the edges, while the fat turns a deep, saturated golden-yellow from the turmeric and the infused spices.

Set a fine-mesh sieve lined with a double layer of cheesecloth or a clean muslin cloth over a heatproof bowl or jar. Add salt to the pan and stir once. Pour the infused butter slowly through the lined sieve, letting gravity do the work — do not press on the solids. The strained fat should run through clear and golden. Discard the solids: all the flavour they had to give is now in the fat. Let the strained niter kibbeh cool slightly before tasting.

Pour the strained niter kibbeh into a clean glass jar. Let cool at room temperature, uncovered, until it drops to 40 C or below, then seal and refrigerate. Refrigerated niter kibbeh will solidify to a firm, deep golden paste — this is correct and expected. Use a clean, dry spoon each time to prevent contamination. It keeps in the refrigerator for 3 months and in the freezer for 6 months. Use it anywhere you would use butter or oil: it is transformative in Ethiopian stews, but equally good sautéing eggs, finishing rice, or basting roasted chicken.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Vietnamese Quick-Pickled Vegetables
description: Ribbons of daikon and carrot pickled in sweetened rice vinegar brine — crunchy, bright, tangy, and essential alongside banh mi, pho, or any grilled protein.

ingredients.text: 60 parts Daikon radish, peeled and julienned (matchstick cut)
40 parts Carrot, peeled and julienned (matchstick cut)
5 parts Fresh red bird's eye chili, thinly sliced

instructions: Toss the julienned daikon and carrot with 1 teaspoon of the fine salt in a large bowl. Toss well and let stand for 10 minutes. This draws out excess water from the vegetables through osmosis, which concentrates their flavor, improves their texture, and allows the pickle brine to penetrate more evenly.

Gather the salted vegetables in your hands and squeeze firmly over the sink, expelling as much water as possible. Rinse briefly under cold water, then squeeze again. This step removes excess salt and the bitter, sulfurous compounds released from the daikon during salting. Taste a strand — it should taste faintly salty, not aggressively so.

Combine the rice vinegar, remaining salt, sugar, and warm water in a bowl or small saucepan. Stir until the sugar and salt dissolve completely — no heat is strictly necessary since warm water (not boiling) does the job. The brine should taste assertively sweet-sour-salty in a 3:4:2 balance: punchy but not painful.

Pack the squeezed daikon and carrot into a clean jar, tucking the sliced chili throughout. Pour the brine over until the vegetables are fully submerged. Gently press down any floating strands. Seal the jar loosely and allow to sit at room temperature for 30 minutes minimum.

After 30 minutes at room temperature, refrigerate the jar for at least 30 more minutes — ideally 1 hour total from when the brine was poured. The cold accelerates the penetration of the brine into the vegetable cells. Pickles are best used within 2 weeks and keep well refrigerated for up to 3 weeks.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Nuoc Cham
description: Vietnam's essential dipping sauce — a balance of fish sauce, lime, sugar, garlic, and chiles that is simultaneously salty, sour, sweet, and pungent, the condiment that appears at nearly every Vietnamese table.

ingredients.text: 2 cloves Garlic cloves, minced to a fine paste
2 chiles Bird's eye chiles, thinly sliced

instructions: Combine the warm water and sugar in a bowl or mortar. Stir vigorously for 1-2 minutes until every granule of sugar has dissolved and the water is completely clear. The water should be warm — around 50-60°C — not hot, which would drive off aroma, and not cold, which leaves the sugar undissolved and the sauce grainy.

Add the fish sauce, then the lime juice to the sugar water. Stir gently to combine. Taste immediately and assess the balance using the classic Vietnamese ratio: equal parts salt, sour, and sweet on the palate, in that order of arrival, finishing clean. The fish sauce should not smell raw or aggressive — it should be oceanic, savory, and rounded. Adjust at this stage: more fish sauce for salt and umami, more lime for acidity, more sugar syrup for sweetness.

Mince the garlic to a very fine paste — almost a puree — by rocking the knife across the cloves and then using the flat of the blade to crush and smear them against the cutting board with salt. For the chiles, slice them into thin rounds; leave the seeds in for full heat. If you prefer less heat, slice the chiles lengthwise first and scrape out the seeds before slicing into rounds.

Stir the garlic paste and chile rounds directly into the base sauce. Let the mixture sit for at least 5 minutes before tasting again — the garlic needs time to lose its sharpest raw edge and infuse its sweetness into the liquid. Do not skip this rest; raw garlic immediately added and immediately tasted will seem too aggressive and cause you to under-garlic the sauce.

Add the julienned carrot to the sauce if using — this is the do chua version common in central Vietnam, and it adds crunch and color, not just garnish. The carrot should be cut into threads no thicker than a matchstick. Serve immediately or chill up to 3 days (the carrot will soften over time; add fresh carrot to order if serving multiple days). Makes about 200ml of finished sauce.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Okonomiyaki
description: A thick, golden-edged Osaka savory pancake — cabbage-heavy, bound with egg and dashi batter, studded with pork belly — cooked until the outside has a lacquered, slightly caramelized crust and the interior remains soft and custardy, then finished with zigzagging lines of sweet okonomiyaki sauce, Kewpie mayo, bonito flakes that wave like sea anemones, and a snowfall of aonori.

ingredients.text: 300 g Napa cabbage (roughly shredded, 5 mm strips)
120 g Dashi (or water with 1 tsp MSG)
30 g Okonomiyaki sauce (or Worcestershire sauce + ketchup 2:1)
25 g Kewpie mayonnaise + aonori (green seaweed flakes) + katsuobushi for topping

instructions: Whisk the flour, dashi, eggs, and soy sauce together in a large bowl until smooth and no lumps remain — this base batter should have the consistency of thin pancake batter. Unlike tempura, here we want a cohesive, developed batter that will hold the cabbage together through a long cook. Whisk for about 1 minute. The batter should pour freely from a ladle but coat it in a thin film. Taste it — it should be lightly seasoned and taste faintly of the ocean from the dashi.

Add all the shredded cabbage and the bonito flakes for the batter into the batter. Fold together with a spatula until every strand of cabbage is coated and the mixture looks more cabbage than batter — this is correct. The very high cabbage-to-batter ratio is what makes Osaka-style okonomiyaki distinct from the Hiroshima layered style. The mixture should look far too loose and cabbage-heavy at this stage; do not add more batter. If using beni shoga (pickled ginger) or tenkasu (tempura scraps), fold them in now.

Heat a wide, flat skillet or griddle (teppan) over medium heat. Add the oil and swirl. Lay the pork belly slices in a single layer and cook for 1 minute to render some fat. Mound the entire cabbage batter on top of the pork belly, shaping it into a round disc about 2 cm thick. Press gently with the back of a spatula to compact into an even round, about 20 cm across. Cook undisturbed for 4 to 5 minutes until the edges begin to look set and the bottom has developed a crust — you can check by carefully lifting one edge with a spatula. Flip confidently in one motion: slide the spatula fully under the okonomiyaki and flip away from you. Cook for a further 4 to 5 minutes on the second side. The pancake should feel firm and spring back lightly when pressed in the centre.

Working quickly while the okonomiyaki is still very hot, use a squeeze bottle or spoon to draw parallel lines of okonomiyaki sauce across the surface, spaced about 2 cm apart. Repeat with Kewpie mayonnaise lines perpendicular to the sauce. The lines should not be completely mixed — the two-sauce crosshatch is a visual signature of the dish. Scatter bonito flakes over the top: the heat from the pancake will animate them, making them curl and wave like living things. Finish with aonori (dried green seaweed flakes) and serve immediately at the table.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: West African Okra Stew
description: A dense, richly seasoned tomato and palm oil base into which shredded okra is stirred to release its natural mucilaginous thickener, building a silky, savory pot fragrant with crayfish and dried fish. Eaten over fufu, rice, or eba, it is a complete meal in a single pot.

ingredients.text: 1 piece Scotch bonnet pepper, seeds in or out to taste
80 g Stockfish (pre-soaked and shredded) or dried fish
150 ml Fish or chicken stock, or water

instructions: Heat the palm oil in a heavy pot or Dutch oven over medium heat until it liquefies and shimmers — palm oil is solid at room temperature and needs a moment. Add the diced onion and whole or roughly chopped scotch bonnet. Fry, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft, translucent, and beginning to take on color at the edges, about 7–8 minutes. The palm oil and onion together form the aromatic foundation of the stew. The kitchen will fill with the unmistakable, earthy fragrance of red palm oil — this is correct.

Add the fresh tomatoes and tomato paste to the pot. Stir to combine and increase heat slightly. Cook uncovered, stirring frequently, until the tomatoes have completely broken down and the mixture has reduced substantially — about 12–15 minutes. The critical sign you are looking for is the oil rising to the surface and pooling at the edges of the pot. In Nigerian cooking this is called 'the oil floating' and signals that the water from the tomatoes has been driven off and the stew base is properly fried and concentrated.

Add the ground crayfish, pre-soaked shredded stockfish, and stock or water. Stir thoroughly and taste — the crayfish adds an intense, oceanic umami note and a faint sweetness that is the backbone of West African stews. If using stockfish, it should be pre-soaked for 24–48 hours and is already softened; dried fish (e.g. eja osan) goes in dry and rehydrates in the pot. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 minutes to marry the flavors. Taste and begin adjusting salt at this stage.

Prepare the okra according to preferred texture: for a very slimy (draw) stew — traditional and prized in many regions — shred the okra by grating on a box grater or pulsing briefly in a food processor. For a less mucilaginous version with discrete rounds, slice crosswise into 1 cm coins. Both methods release the mucilage that thickens the stew; shredding releases far more and produces a denser, more viscous result. Whichever method you use, the okra should be cut just before adding to the pot to prevent oxidation.

Add the okra to the simmering base. Stir once to incorporate, then resist the urge to stir vigorously or frequently — excessive stirring breaks down the okra and makes the stew overly slimy rather than silky. Cook on medium-low heat for 8–12 minutes, stirring gently only 2–3 times, until the okra is fully tender and the stew has thickened to a viscous, glossy consistency. Taste and adjust salt. The stew should be thick enough to mound slightly on a spoon and should coat the back of it. Serve over fufu, pounded yam, eba, or steamed rice.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Olive Oil Lemon Cake
description: A tender, golden single-layer cake with a crackly sugared top, its crumb perfumed with rubbed lemon zest and the faint grassy pepper of good olive oil, finished with a sharp lemon glaze.

ingredients.text: 2 whole Lemons, zested and juiced (about 60 ml juice)
160 ml Extra-virgin olive oil, mild and fruity

instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Grease a 9-inch (23 cm) round cake pan with olive oil and line the bottom with parchment. Zest both lemons directly into the granulated sugar in a large bowl, then rub the zest into the sugar with your fingertips for 1–2 minutes. Juice the lemons and set the juice aside; you need 45 ml for the batter and about 20 ml for the glaze.

Add the eggs to the lemon sugar and whisk vigorously for about 1 minute until pale and slightly thickened. Whisk in the olive oil in a slow stream so it emulsifies, then the milk and 45 ml of lemon juice. In a separate bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder, and salt; add to the wet ingredients and whisk gently just until no dry flour remains. Scrape into the pan and sprinkle the turbinado sugar evenly over the top.

Bake on the middle rack for 40–45 minutes, until the top is golden, the edges pull away from the pan, and a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cool in the pan 15 minutes, then run a knife around the edge and turn out onto a rack, right-side up.

Whisk the powdered sugar with about 20 ml of the reserved lemon juice until smooth and thick but pourable, adding juice drop by drop. When the cake has cooled to just warm (about 30 minutes on the rack), spoon the glaze over the top and let it drip down the sides. Let it set 15 minutes before slicing.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: One-Pot Cherry Tomato and Basil Spaghetti
description: Dry spaghetti, halved cherry tomatoes, sliced garlic and onion all start together in a wide pan of cold water, and as the pasta cooks its starch and the bursting tomatoes reduce into a sweet, glossy sauce that clings to every strand.

ingredients.text: 600 g Cherry or grape tomatoes, halved
150 g Yellow onion, halved and thinly sliced
20 leaves Fresh basil leaves, half left whole, half torn to finish
45 ml Extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish
0 to taste Black pepper, freshly ground

instructions: Use a 12-inch (30 cm) straight-sided skillet or wide braiser the spaghetti can lie flat in. Lay the dry spaghetti in the pan, then scatter over the tomatoes, onion, garlic, red pepper flakes and half the basil (whole leaves). Add the olive oil, salt and the cold water — the pasta should be just submerged.

Bring to a rolling boil over high heat. As soon as the pasta softens (about 2 minutes), start turning it with tongs every 30–60 seconds so it doesn't clump. Keep at a vigorous boil, uncovered, for 9–11 minutes, until the pasta is al dente and the water has reduced to a few tablespoons of glossy, orange-red sauce. Press some of the tomatoes against the side of the pan as they soften.

Off the heat, add the Parmesan, a drizzle of olive oil and a few grinds of black pepper, and toss vigorously for 30 seconds so the cheese emulsifies into the sauce. Let stand 2 minutes. Fold in the remaining torn basil, taste for salt, and serve with extra cheese.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Onigiri
description: Hand-pressed Japanese rice balls — seasoned short-grain rice shaped into triangles around a savory filling and wrapped in nori, the most perfect portable lunch ever devised.

ingredients.text: 1 tsp Fine sea salt (for wetting hands)
6 pieces Umeboshi (pickled plum) or tuna mayo filling
3 sheets Nori sheets, cut into wide strips
0.5 tsp Fine sea salt (for seasoning rice)

instructions: Rinse the rice in cold water, gently swirling with your hand and draining, until the water runs almost clear — typically 4–5 rinses. This removes excess surface starch that would make the rice gluey. Drain in a sieve for 10 minutes. Combine the rinsed rice and cold water in a heavy pot or rice cooker. If using a pot: bring to a boil over high heat, then immediately reduce to the lowest possible flame, cover tightly, and cook for 13 minutes without lifting the lid. Remove from heat and let steam, still covered, for 10 more minutes. The steaming step is not optional — it equalizes moisture throughout each grain. Uncover and fluff gently with a rice paddle or wide spatula, folding rather than stirring, which would break the grains.

While the rice is still warm (not hot — hot rice will scald your hands when shaping), sprinkle the salt evenly over the surface and fold it in gently with the rice paddle, turning the rice over itself rather than stirring. Taste: the rice should be lightly, evenly salty — just enough to taste the seasoning on the first bite, not overpowering. The filling will add more salt, so err on the mild side. Cover the seasoned rice with a damp cloth to prevent drying. Prepare a small bowl of water mixed with a pinch of salt for wetting your hands before shaping — this prevents sticking and adds a slight crust to the outside of the onigiri.

Wet both palms with the salted water and shake off excess — damp hands, not wet. Scoop a palm-sized handful of warm rice (about 120–130 g) and flatten it in your palm. Place the filling (an umeboshi, or a teaspoon of tuna mayo) in the center and fold the rice over it, pressing gently to encase the filling completely. Now cup the rice in both hands and press firmly into a triangle by positioning your dominant hand in a V-shape (like an arrowhead) on top, and curving your other hand across the flat base. Apply firm, even pressure from three sides simultaneously, rotating the triangle a quarter-turn and pressing again. Repeat 4–6 times — you want a compact, dense triangle that holds its shape but isn't rock-hard. Each press should feel definitive.

For the classic presentation: cut a nori sheet into a wide strip just wide enough to cover one face of the triangle and overhang on both sides. Press the nori firmly against the bottom face and fold the overhang up over the two sides. The nori should grip naturally onto the rice surface — press gently but firmly all over. Serve immediately for maximum nori crunch: nori begins to absorb moisture from the rice within 10–15 minutes and will become leathery if left to sit. For packed lunches, wrap the nori separately in a small piece of foil and press it onto the rice just before eating — the classic convenience store trick for preserving the crunch.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Gâteau Opéra
description: Six alternating layers of coffee-soaked joconde almond sponge, espresso buttercream, and bittersweet chocolate ganache, assembled flush and finished with a mirror-dark chocolate glaze — the apex of French patisserie elegance.

ingredients.text: 3 parts Simple syrup (equal sugar and water, cooled)

instructions: Beat the almond flour, icing sugar, and whole eggs with a whisk or mixer until the batter is ribbon-stage — pale, voluminous, and falling from the whisk in a wide, sustained ribbon. Sift in the all-purpose flour and fold in. Separately, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, rain in the caster sugar, and whip to a stiff meringue. Fold the meringue into the almond batter in three additions, then fold in the cool melted butter. Spread thinly across two large, parchment-lined baking sheets to a 5 mm thickness. Bake at 200 C / 390 F for 8-10 minutes until just golden and springy. Cut into three equal rectangles for assembly.

Dissolve the espresso powder in the hot water and stir in the simple syrup until fully combined. Allow to cool to room temperature. The soak should taste intensely of coffee and sweet — stronger than you would enjoy as a drink, because the joconde absorbs it and dilutes it. The soak must be at room temperature or cooler when applied — a warm soak will damage the texture of the assembled layers.

Beat the softened butter on medium speed until very pale and fluffy — 3-4 minutes. Dissolve the espresso powder in a teaspoon of hot water to a paste, and add it to the butter. Beat in the icing sugar a third at a time, beating well between additions. The finished buttercream should be very pale (the coffee lightens as it aerates), extremely smooth, and stiff enough to hold a clean edge when spread. If it looks curdled, beat longer — the warmth of friction will smooth it.

Finely chop the dark chocolate and place in a heatproof bowl. Heat the double cream to just below simmering — small bubbles at the edge, not a rolling boil. Pour the hot cream over the chocolate in one go. Leave undisturbed for 1 minute, then begin stirring from the centre outward in small circles, gradually widening as the ganache emulsifies. It will seize at first, then suddenly become smooth and glossy. Allow to cool at room temperature, stirring occasionally, until it thickens to a spreadable but not stiff consistency.

Line a flat tray with parchment. Layer 1: place a joconde rectangle down and brush generously with coffee soak until visibly dark and moist. Spread an even 3-4 mm layer of chocolate ganache. Layer 2: place the second joconde sheet, brush with soak, and spread an even 3-4 mm layer of coffee buttercream. Layer 3: third joconde sheet, final brush of soak, and a second layer of ganache. The top must be perfectly flat — press a clean baking sheet on top gently and refrigerate for at least 1 hour to set the layers solid before glazing. Each layer must be even and the overall structure must be perfectly level.

Melt the dark chocolate gently over a bain-marie or in short microwave bursts. Stir in the neutral oil until completely smooth and fluid — the oil prevents the glaze from setting too hard and gives it a mirror finish. Allow to cool to 35-38 C / 95-100 F — just above body temperature — before pouring. Remove the assembled cake from the refrigerator and set on a rack over a tray. Pour the glaze over in one smooth motion from the centre outward, tilting the rack if needed to coat the entire surface in a single fluid layer. Refrigerate for 20 minutes until the glaze is set and mirror-bright. Trim all four edges with a hot, clean knife to reveal the cross-section of perfect layers. Dust with gold leaf or write 'Opéra' in chocolate if desired.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Osso Buco alla Milanese
description: Milan's great veal braise — cross-cut shanks simmered in white wine and broth until the marrow trembles in its socket and the sauce turns the colour of old amber. A shower of gremolata cut through the richness: raw garlic, lemon zest, and parsley that wake the whole dish up.

ingredients.text: 1500 g Veal osso buco (cross-cut shanks, 4–5 cm thick, tied with kitchen twine)
250 ml Dry white wine (Pinot Grigio or Soave)
1 to taste Fine sea salt and black pepper
1 lemon Lemon zest (finely grated, for gremolata)
15 g Flat-leaf parsley (finely chopped, for gremolata)

instructions: Pat the veal shanks completely dry with paper towel — any surface moisture will steam instead of sear. Season generously on all sides with salt and pepper. Heat the butter and olive oil in a wide, heavy Dutch oven or braiser over medium-high heat until the butter foams and subsides. Sear the shanks flat-side down in batches, never crowding, for 3–4 minutes per side until a deep mahogany crust forms. Turn and sear the bone-edges briefly. Remove and rest on a plate.

Lower the heat to medium. Add the carrot, celery, and onion to the pot and cook in the remaining fat, scraping up the fond with a wooden spoon as the vegetables release their moisture, for 8–10 minutes until soft and lightly golden at the edges. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well, and cook for another 2 minutes until the paste darkens from bright red to a deep brick colour and smells toasty and sweet.

Pour in the white wine all at once and increase the heat to medium-high. Scrape the pot floor vigorously as it comes to a boil, dissolving all the fond into the liquid. Let it reduce by half, about 4–5 minutes, until the raw alcohol smell cooks off and is replaced by a mellow, fruity fragrance.

Pour in the warm stock and add the bay leaves and thyme, tucking them under the liquid. Nestle the seared shanks back into the pot standing upright, marrow-bone facing up — this keeps the marrow in the socket as it softens. The liquid should come halfway up the shanks. Bring to a bare trembling simmer, cover tightly, and transfer to a 160°C / 325°F oven. Braise for 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours, basting the shanks once or twice, until the meat is completely tender and pulling away from the bone at the edges.

Carefully lift the shanks onto a warm plate and cover loosely with foil. Discard the bay leaves and thyme sprigs. Taste the braising liquid and skim any fat floating on the surface. If the sauce is thin, simmer it uncovered over medium heat for 5–10 minutes until it reduces to a coating consistency — it should nappe a spoon with a light, glossy sheen. Season with salt and pepper and remove the twine from the shanks.

Mix the finely grated lemon zest, chopped parsley, and minced garlic together in a small bowl to make the gremolata. It should be combined but not mashed — the texture of each element should remain visible. Spoon the shanks onto plates or saffron risotto, ladle over the sauce, and scatter a generous pinch of gremolata over each shank at the very last moment. Do not stir the gremolata into the braise — its freshness is meant to contrast the richness.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Oysters with Mignonette Granita
description: French raw oysters served on crushed ice with a mignonette granita — shallot and sherry vinegar frozen into sharp, icy crystals that melt over the cold oyster, heightening the brine without masking it. The simplest luxury in the kitchen.

ingredients.text: 900 g Live oysters (Fines de Claire, Belon, or Kumamoto)

instructions: Combine the sherry vinegar, very finely minced shallots, cracked black pepper, and cold water in a small bowl. Stir to combine. Taste: it should be sharply acidic with a pungent shallot note and a flicker of pepper heat. Adjust the balance with a touch more water if very sharp, or an extra pinch of cracked pepper for more heat. The shallots will soften slightly in the vinegar over time.

Pour the mignonette liquid into a wide, shallow freezer-safe dish — the thinner the layer, the faster and more evenly it freezes. Place in the freezer. After 45 minutes, drag a fork across the partially frozen surface to break it into crystals. Repeat every 30 minutes for 2 hours total, until you have a loose, shimmering mass of sharp vinegar-shallot ice crystals.

Hold each oyster in a folded kitchen towel, flat shell up, hinge toward you. Insert an oyster knife into the hinge at a 45-degree angle. Apply firm, twisting pressure until the hinge pops. Slide the knife along the inner surface of the flat top shell, severing the adductor muscle. Discard the flat top shell. Sever the muscle on the bottom cup shell as well. Check the liquor: it should be clear and faintly salty — milky or muddy liquor means the oyster is stressed. Arrange on the crushed ice immediately.

Arrange the shucked oysters in their cups on a large platter of crushed ice — the ice keeps them cold and holds them level. Place a half-teaspoon of mignonette granita on top of each oyster just before serving. Add a tiny pinch of flaky salt if the oysters are very mild. Serve immediately, before the granita melts completely.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Oysters Rockefeller
description: Plump raw oysters baked on their half-shell under a blanket of creamed spinach, Pernod, and golden breadcrumbs — the grand New Orleans appetizer of 1899, as rich as its namesake.

ingredients.text: 12 oysters Fresh oysters on the half-shell, shucked (cup side up)
3 parts Baby spinach, washed and dried
0.5 parts Shallots and garlic, finely minced together
0.3 parts Pernod or Ricard anise liqueur
0.1 parts Fresh tarragon, leaves only, finely chopped
0.5 parts Panko breadcrumbs and finely grated Parmesan, mixed 2:1

instructions: Melt the butter in a wide sauté pan over medium heat. Add the minced shallot and garlic. Sweat gently for 4–5 minutes, stirring often, until completely translucent, soft, and sweet-smelling. The alliums must dissolve completely into the butter — any residual crunch will be unpleasant in the final topping spooned over delicate oyster flesh. Season lightly with salt.

Add the baby spinach to the pan in large batches, tossing with tongs to wilt each batch before adding the next — it will reduce to a quarter of its raw volume. Once all the spinach is wilted and any pooled water has evaporated, pour in the Pernod and let it sizzle and reduce for 30 seconds. Add the cream and increase heat to medium-high. Stir and reduce until the mixture is thick enough that a wooden spoon leaves a clear channel along the pan base. Remove from heat, stir in the tarragon, and season carefully with salt and cayenne.

Preheat the oven to 220°C (425°F), or preheat a grill/broiler to its highest setting. Arrange the oysters on their half-shells on a baking tray filled with rock salt or crumpled foil to keep them level — a tilted oyster loses all its precious liquor. Spoon a generous teaspoon of the Rockefeller topping over each oyster, leaving a thin rim of shell exposed. The topping should mound slightly above the shell edge. Combine the panko-Parmesan mixture and scatter evenly over each topped oyster.

Bake at 220°C (425°F) for 8–10 minutes, or broil for 3–4 minutes, until the breadcrumb topping is deeply golden-brown and the edges of the oyster flesh are just beginning to curl. The oyster itself should still be plump and juicy — it cooks almost entirely from the heat of the topping above it. If using a broiler, watch constantly: it goes from golden to burnt in under a minute.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pad See Ew
description: Wide flat rice noodles stir-fried at ferocious wok heat with egg, Chinese broccoli, and sweet soy sauce until lightly charred — a dish that lives or dies by the 'wok hei' smoky breath of the fire.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Fresh wide rice noodles (sen yai, 2-3 cm wide)
40 parts Chicken breast or thigh (thin sliced) or firm tofu
35 parts Gai lan (Chinese broccoli, cut in 5 cm lengths)
10 parts Kecap manis or dark sweet soy sauce
12 parts Neutral oil (high smoke point — canola or grapeseed)

instructions: Slice the chicken into thin, even pieces no more than 5 mm thick. Toss with half the oyster sauce and half the light soy sauce. Rest at room temperature for 10 minutes. Separately, mix the remaining oyster sauce, light soy sauce, dark sweet soy (kecap manis), and sugar in a small bowl to create the stir-fry sauce. If using fresh rice noodles that are refrigerator-cold, separate them gently by hand and bring to room temperature — cold noodles will drop the wok temperature dramatically and result in steaming rather than charring.

Heat the wok over the highest heat your stove produces until it smokes visibly. Add half the oil and the minced garlic — it should sizzle and turn golden within 15 seconds. Add the chicken immediately and spread into a single layer. Let it sit undisturbed for 60 seconds to develop a sear, then toss. Cook until just cooked through, about 2 to 3 minutes total. Remove the chicken from the wok and set aside. The wok must be back at maximum heat before adding noodles.

Return the wok to maximum heat and add the remaining oil. Add the separated rice noodles in a single layer as much as possible. DO NOT stir for 60 to 90 seconds — let them sit directly against the wok to char and blister slightly. Then add the gai lan pieces. Toss everything together 3 to 4 times with long chopsticks or a wok spatula. Push everything to one side of the wok.

Clear a space in the center of the wok and crack the eggs directly into it. Let them set for 10 to 15 seconds until the whites are just opaque at the edges, then scramble them lightly with the spatula. Before they are fully set, fold the noodles over the egg and toss together so the soft curds distribute through the noodles. The egg should be cooked but still soft — not dry scrambled egg shreds.

Pour the prepared sauce over the noodles and egg. Return the seared chicken to the wok. Toss everything together vigorously for 60 seconds until the sauce has coated every component and the noodles look uniformly dark and glossy. Taste and adjust — pad see ew should be predominantly sweet from the dark soy with a savory backbone. Plate immediately; the noodles clump as they cool.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pad Thai Sauce
description: The amber-dark sauce that defines pad thai — a careful balance of sour tamarind, sweet palm sugar, and funky fish sauce that caramelises around the rice noodles in the wok, creating the sticky, slightly charred edges that street vendors call the hallmark of a well-made plate.

ingredients.text: 3 parts Tamarind paste (from a block, not concentrate)
2 parts Palm sugar (jaggery), grated or crumbled
2 parts Fish sauce (Tiparos or Megachef preferred)
0.25 parts Dark soy sauce (for colour, optional)

instructions: If using block tamarind: break off 60 g and soak in 120 ml of warm (not boiling) water for 15 minutes. Work the softened block with your fingers, squeezing and pressing until all the pulp dissolves into the water. Pour the mixture through a fine sieve, pressing hard on the solids to extract all the liquid. Discard the fibres and seeds. You need a thick, dark-brown liquid, about 3 tablespoons of concentrated paste per portion of sauce. If using tamarind concentrate from a jar, thin with a little water to a pourable consistency.

Combine the tamarind liquid, palm sugar, fish sauce, oyster sauce, and dark soy sauce in a small saucepan. Set over low-medium heat and stir continuously until the palm sugar dissolves completely — palm sugar lumps are denser than white sugar and need gentle heat and patience. Once dissolved, raise heat slightly and bring to a very gentle simmer for 2–3 minutes. The sauce will darken slightly and thicken a little as moisture evaporates. Remove from heat.

Taste the sauce critically on a clean spoon — pad thai sauce should hit sour first, then sweet, then salty, with a savoury undertow. Adjust: too sour → add more palm sugar in small amounts; too sweet → add more fish sauce (not tamarind, which would change the body); flat → add more fish sauce. The sauce should taste noticeably stronger than you want the finished dish, because it will be diluted slightly by noodle water and wok steam during cooking. Store in a jar at room temperature for up to 1 week, or refrigerate for 1 month.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pad Thai
description: Smoke-kissed rice noodles tangled with egg, shrimp, and crunchy peanuts, bound by a glossy tamarind sauce that walks the razor edge between sweet, sour, salty, and savory. Every wok-blast of heat produces a layer of caramelized noodle crust — the hallmark of true street-stall pad thai.

ingredients.text: 200 g Dried sen lek rice noodles (3mm wide)
150 g Raw shrimp, peeled and deveined
20 g Palm sugar, grated (or light brown sugar)
45 ml Neutral oil (rice bran or sunflower)
20 g Garlic chives (or green onion tops)

instructions: Place the dried rice noodles in a large bowl and cover with room-temperature water — not hot, not boiling. Let them soak for 25 to 30 minutes until they are pliable and can be bent without snapping, but still have a firm, slightly chalky bite at their core. They should feel like al dente pasta but more delicate. Drain in a colander and shake off excess water. Do not rinse. The surface starch left on the noodles helps them cling to the sauce in the wok. If you soak them in hot water, they will become fully cooked and turn to mush the moment they hit the wok. Spread them loosely if you need to wait — they stick aggressively once drained.

In a small saucepan over low heat, combine the tamarind paste, fish sauce, and palm sugar. Stir gently until the palm sugar dissolves completely and the mixture is uniform — about 2 minutes. Do not boil; you are dissolving and integrating, not reducing. Taste the sauce: it should hit sour first (tamarind), then salty (fish sauce), then sweet (palm sugar) in a rolling wave, with no single note dominating. The color should be a deep amber-brown, like strong iced tea. Adjust balance now: too sour, add a pinch more sugar; too sweet, add a dash more fish sauce; too flat, add a tiny extra squeeze of tamarind. This sauce is the entire flavor backbone of the dish — getting the balance right before the wok work begins is essential, because there is no time to adjust once you are cooking.

Heat a wok or large heavy skillet over the highest heat your stove allows for a full 2 minutes — the pan should be smoking. Add the oil and swirl to coat. Add the sliced shallots and stir-fry for 90 seconds until they begin to soften and turn golden at the edges. Add the minced garlic and the dried shrimp. Stir-fry constantly for another 60 seconds, keeping everything moving. The dried shrimp will toast and release their deeply savory, oceanic fragrance — the aroma should shift from raw garlic to something roasted and complex. Do not let the garlic burn; it turns bitter fast at this temperature. The entire wok should be billowing with fragrant smoke. If your exhaust fan is not at maximum, open a window.

Add the raw shrimp to the wok in a single layer and press them flat for 30 seconds without stirring, letting them sear against the hot wok surface. Flip once — they should be pink on the seared side. Stir-fry for another 30–45 seconds just until they are just cooked through and curled into a C-shape. Do not overcook; they will return to the wok heat twice more. Remove the shrimp to a plate and set aside. They should be 90% cooked — just opaque, still glossy, not rubbery. Leaving them slightly underdone here is intentional: they will finish in the final toss with the noodles.

Return the wok to maximum heat. Add the drained noodles to the wok and immediately pour the pad thai sauce over them. Toss constantly for 60–90 seconds, folding the noodles through the sauce with tongs or a long spatula — the sauce will absorb and caramelize against the wok surface. Push the noodles to one side of the wok to expose the center. Crack both eggs into the exposed center and let them set for 15 seconds, then scramble loosely before the whites fully set. When the eggs are still glossy and 80% cooked, drag the noodles back over the eggs and fold everything together. The eggs should coat the noodles in broken golden ribbons, not clump into a dry omelette. Return the shrimp to the wok, toss once or twice, and plate immediately.

Plate the pad thai in a mound. On one side, pile the bean sprouts and garlic chives raw — they should be cold and crunchy against the hot noodles, providing textural contrast. Scatter the crushed peanuts over the top. Serve with a lime wedge pressed against the mound and a small pile of dried chili flakes on the side. Never mix the garnishes into the noodles before serving — each diner should mix their own, squeezing the lime and adjusting chili to taste. The pad thai is traditionally served with additional condiments on the side: fish sauce with floating chilies, more sugar, more chili flakes, and white vinegar — the four flavors of the Thai table.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Paella Sofrito
description: The dark, jammy foundation of every great paella — tomatoes and peppers cooked down to a concentrated, saffron-kissed paste that smells of a Valencia market at noon, caramelized and deep.

ingredients.text: 1.5 parts Red bell pepper, finely diced
6 parts Ripe tomatoes, grated on a box grater (discard skins)
0.01 parts Saffron threads, steeped in 2 tbsp warm water
0.2 parts Fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped

instructions: Crumble the saffron threads into a small bowl or ramekin. Pour 2 tablespoons of warm (not boiling) water over them and let steep for at least 10 minutes. The liquid will turn a vivid amber-gold. Heating the saffron in warm water releases its crocin pigments and safranal aroma compounds far more efficiently than adding dry threads directly to a hot pan.

Warm the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan (the paella pan if available) over medium heat. Add the onion first and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8-10 minutes until soft and translucent with golden edges. Add the garlic and red pepper and cook for another 5 minutes, stirring frequently. The vegetables should be completely soft and starting to caramelize at the edges — not raw, not browned.

Add the grated tomatoes, smoked paprika, and salt to the pan. Stir to combine and cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, for 20-25 minutes. The sofrito is done when the tomato water has fully evaporated, the mass has darkened from bright red to a deep brick-red, and the oil has begun to separate and pool at the edges of the paste. This concentration step is not optional — a watery sofrito produces gummy, bland paella.

Pour the saffron water (liquid and threads) over the concentrated sofrito. Stir vigorously to incorporate — the paste will sizzle and tighten momentarily as the liquid contacts the hot oil. Cook for 2 more minutes to drive off the water and let the saffron flavor fully bloom into the paste. Remove from heat, stir in the fresh parsley, and use immediately as the base of your paella, or cool and refrigerate for up to 3 days.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Paella Valenciana
description: The original paella — chicken, rabbit, green beans, and white beans cooked in saffron-gold rice over an open fire or gas burner in a wide carbon-steel pan, until the socarrat crust crackles and perfumes the whole kitchen with toasted rice.

ingredients.text: 0.5 parts Large white butter beans, cooked
0.5 parts Ripe tomato, grated on a box grater
0.05 parts Sweet pimentón de la Vera (paprika)

instructions: Place the paella pan (40–50 cm for 4 people) over medium-high heat. Add the olive oil and heat until shimmering but not smoking. Season the chicken and rabbit pieces generously with salt. Add them to the pan skin-side down and sear without moving for 5–7 minutes per side until deeply golden-brown all over. The meat does not need to cook through — it will finish in the rice. Work in batches if the pan is crowded. The golden fond on the pan bottom is flavor. Leave it.

With the meat pushed to the sides, add the garlic to the center of the pan and fry 30 seconds until golden. Add the grated tomato — it will sizzle fiercely. Stir and cook the tomato in the center of the pan for 8–10 minutes, spreading it across the pan, until it has lost all its raw smell, darkened from red to a concentrated brick, and the oil has separated from the tomato solids. Add the sweet paprika and stir for 30 seconds only — paprika burns very quickly. This sofrito is the flavor spine of the entire dish.

Bloom the saffron in a ladleful of hot stock for 2 minutes. Add the green beans and white beans to the sofrito; stir for 1 minute. Scatter the rice evenly across the entire pan and stir to coat each grain with the sofrito. Pour in all the hot saffron-infused stock at once. Stir once to distribute the rice evenly — this is the last time you stir. From this point on, do not touch the rice. Taste the stock and adjust salt now, before the rice absorbs everything. Cook over medium-high heat for 8–10 minutes until the stock has reduced to the level of the rice. Reduce to medium-low and cook a further 8 minutes. In the final 2 minutes, raise the heat to medium-high to form the socarrat.

Remove the pan from the heat and drape loosely with a sheet of aluminium foil or a clean kitchen towel. Rest for exactly 5 minutes — no longer, or the socarrat will steam and go soft. This rest allows the rice to finish absorbing any remaining liquid and the steam to redistribute moisture evenly. Remove the foil and serve directly from the pan at the table. Scrape the socarrat from the bottom with a spoon and offer a piece to each diner — it is the most coveted part.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pain au Lait
description: French milk bread rolls so impossibly pillowy that pulling one apart from the tray releases a cloud of buttery steam — enriched with whole milk, butter, and just enough sugar to make the crust gild golden, the crumb white and tender as a cloud.

ingredients.text: 2 large Egg (for dough and egg wash)

instructions: Warm the milk gently to 38-40 C (body temperature — warm but not uncomfortable when dipped into with a wrist). Whisk in the sugar and active dry yeast and leave to stand for 8-10 minutes until a creamy, foamy layer forms across the surface. Milk's natural lactose and fat accelerate yeast activity significantly compared to a water-based activation — you should see full foam in 6-7 minutes. Beat one egg and set aside for the egg wash; add the second egg to the foamed milk and whisk briefly to combine before proceeding to mixing.

Combine flour and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook (this enriched dough benefits from machine kneading, though hand-kneading is possible). Add the yeast-milk mixture and mix on low for 2 minutes until a shaggy dough forms, then increase to medium-low and knead for 5-6 minutes until the dough is smooth but still slightly tacky. Do not add butter yet — the fat must be incorporated after the gluten network is established. Adding butter too early prevents proper gluten development and produces a crumbly loaf.

With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter in 4-5 small additions, allowing each piece to fully incorporate before adding the next. The dough will appear to fall apart as the fat coats the gluten strands — this is normal and temporary. After the final addition, increase to medium speed and knead for 6-8 more minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly from the bowl — this is the window test for enriched dough. The finished dough will be noticeably softer, shinier, and more extensible than a lean dough. It should not be sticky at this stage.

Shape the dough into a ball, place in a buttered bowl, and turn once to coat. Cover with plastic wrap and let rise at warm room temperature (24-26 C) for 60-90 minutes, until the dough has doubled. Enriched doughs proof more slowly than lean doughs due to the fat and sugar inhibiting yeast activity — do not rush. A common error is baking an under-proofed enriched loaf and getting a dense, brioche-like brick. After the first rise, gently deflate the dough and divide into 12 equal portions (about 50-55g each if working with 500g flour).

Working on a lightly floured surface, flatten each portion gently into a small disc, then fold the edges into the center and flip so the seam is underneath. Cup your hand over the dough and rotate it with a circular motion on the un-floured part of the surface — the friction builds surface tension and pulls the roll into a tight, smooth sphere. Arrange the rolls in a lightly buttered baking dish with the rolls touching each other — this produces the characteristic pull-apart structure that makes pain au lait so comforting. Cover with a damp cloth and proof for 45-60 minutes at room temperature until visibly puffy and the rolls have grown into each other.
