Bring a large pot of generously salted water (as salty as pasta water) to a rolling boil. Drain the soaked rice and add to the boiling water. Parboil for exactly 5-7 minutes, stirring once. Test frequently from minute 5: the rice should be cooked on the outside but still have a distinct chalky white line at the very center when bitten. Drain immediately through a fine colander and rinse with cold water to stop cooking.

Heat the oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot (nonstick or well-seasoned) over medium-high heat until shimmering. Whisk the yogurt with a ladleful (about 15 parts) of the drained parboiled rice and the bloomed saffron water. Spread this yogurt-rice mixture across the bottom of the hot pot in an even layer — this forms the tahdig. Mound the remaining parboiled rice over the top in a pyramid, keeping it away from the pot sides. Drizzle the remaining saffron water over the top. Wrap the lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel (to absorb steam) and place on the pot. Cook over medium-high heat for 10 minutes to set the crust, then reduce to the lowest possible heat.

After 45-55 total minutes of steaming, remove the lid. Scoop out the fluffy upper rice onto a serving platter and scatter the saffron-stained grains and barberries over the top for color. Now the moment of truth: place a large flat platter over the mouth of the pot and invert in one decisive motion. The tahdig should release as a single, golden disc — crackling and glossy. If it sticks, return to low heat for 2 more minutes.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Persian Chelo Rice with Tahdig
description: The crown jewel of the Iranian table — long-grain basmati parboiled, drained, and steam-finished over a shield of butter and potato that becomes the tahdig: an impossibly crisp, golden-amber crust that is the most fought-over piece on any Persian platter.

ingredients.text: 30 g Fine sea salt (for soaking and parboiling)
60 g Unsalted butter or vegetable oil
0.5 g Saffron strands (bloomed in hot water)

instructions: Rinse the basmati in cold water until the water runs clear — at least 5-6 rinses. Soak in cold water with 1 tablespoon of salt for 30 minutes minimum (up to 4 hours). The soaking hydrates the grain, which allows it to elongate dramatically during steaming. Drain and rinse once more.

Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil (should taste like seawater). Add the drained rice. Parboil uncovered for exactly 5-7 minutes, stirring gently once. A grain is ready when it has elongated and is tender at the outside but still has a firm, white core when bitten — like pasta 2 minutes before al dente. Drain immediately into a sieve and rinse with cold water to stop cooking. The rice is only half done at this point.

Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed non-stick pot over medium-high. Layer sliced potato in a single even layer on the bottom. Mound the parboiled rice on top in a gentle pyramid — do not press it. Drizzle the bloomed saffron over the top third. Wrap the pot lid in a clean cloth to absorb condensation, place on tight. Cook on medium-high for 3 minutes, then reduce to the lowest possible heat. Steam for 35-45 minutes. To serve: invert the entire pot onto a serving platter so the golden tahdig comes out on top.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Persian Saffron Rice (Chelow)
description: The crown jewel of Iranian cooking — long-grain basmati that has been soaked, parboiled, and then steamed over a low flame wrapped in a cloth to create a golden, shatteringly crisp crust called tahdig at the bottom of the pot while the rice above remains separate, elongated, and perfumed with saffron.

ingredients.text: 0.5 parts Saffron threads, bloomed in 3 tbsp hot water
15 parts Lavash bread or thin flatbread (optional tahdig base)

instructions: Rinse the basmati rice in several changes of cold water until the water runs clear — this removes surface starch that would make the cooked grains clump. Add salt to cold water (about 1 tablespoon per 2 cups rice) and soak the rinsed rice for 30–60 minutes, up to overnight in the refrigerator. Soaking allows the grain to begin absorbing water, which ensures it cooks evenly all the way through during the rapid parboil and prevents the exterior from overcooking before the center is done.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a vigorous boil — the water should taste pleasantly salty, like pasta water. Add the drained soaked rice and cook, stirring occasionally, for exactly 5–7 minutes. The rice is ready to drain when each grain has grown significantly in length and is just tender at the exterior but still has a firm, white, chalky core when bitten. The center should still have a snap. Drain immediately in a fine colander and rinse briefly with cool water to stop cooking.

In a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid, heat the oil over medium heat. If using lavash, place a single layer over the oiled pot bottom, pressing to the edges. If using potato, layer thin slices over the base. Add 2 large spoonfuls of parboiled rice and spread to cover the lavash. Mound the remaining parboiled rice in a cone shape over the top — do not press or pack it. Create 5–6 holes down through the rice mound with the handle of a wooden spoon to allow steam to rise from below. Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen cloth (this absorbs steam and prevents condensation dripping back onto the rice).

After 5 minutes on medium-high, reduce to absolute minimum heat (use a heat diffuser if available). Steam for 45 minutes. While the rice steams, bloom the saffron in hot water for 5 minutes, then mix with 2 tablespoons of melted butter. At the 45-minute mark, remove the lid and drizzle the saffron butter over 3–4 spoonfuls of rice in a separate bowl — stir to coat, then return this golden-orange rice to the top of the pot as a garnish. Replace lid for 5 more minutes. To serve: invert the pot onto a large round platter in one decisive motion. The tahdig should release with a satisfying thud.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Persian Tahdig (Crispy Rice)
description: Rice that is as much about its golden, shattering crust as the fluffy grains above it — parboiled, rested, steamed under a towel-wrapped lid for an hour until the bottom transforms into a burnished disk that comes away from the pot in one dramatic, crackling sheet.

ingredients.text: 3 parts Fine sea salt (for parboiling water)

instructions: Rinse the rice in cold water until the water runs clear — this removes excess surface starch that would otherwise glue the grains together. Soak in cold, lightly salted water for 30 minutes minimum, 2 hours ideally. Drain. Bring a large pot of heavily salted water (it should taste like the sea) to a vigorous boil. Add the soaked, drained rice and parboil for exactly 6–7 minutes, stirring gently once. The rice is done when the outside is fully cooked but the center still has a small chalky core — bite a grain to check. Drain immediately in a colander and rinse briefly with lukewarm water to stop the cooking.

In a heavy-bottomed, non-stick pot (24–26cm diameter), heat the oil over medium heat until shimmering. For a plain crust: add 2–3 tablespoons of water to the oil and let it sizzle, then immediately pile in all the parboiled rice, mounding it slightly in the center. Do not press or compact it — use a spoon handle to poke 5–6 holes down through the rice to allow steam to travel upward. For a potato tahdig (beloved variation): place thin potato slices in the oiled pan in a single overlapping layer before adding the rice. Scatter the cubed butter over the top of the mounded rice.

Wrap the pot lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel, securing the corners at the top so they do not hang near the burner. Place the lid on the pot — the towel absorbs condensation that would otherwise drip back down and make the rice wet. Set heat to medium-high for 3 minutes to start building the crust, then reduce to the absolute lowest simmer your burner offers. Cook undisturbed for 40–45 minutes. Do not lift the lid. The golden crust develops from below through even, gentle heat — disturbing this process resets it.

The unmolding is the theater of tahdig. Place a large serving platter on top of the pot. With one decisive, confident motion, flip the entire pot over onto the platter — like unmolding a cake. If the tahdig releases cleanly, you will hear it land in one piece. If it sticks, place the pot back on the cold sink bottom for 30 more seconds, then try again. Alternatively, serve family-style by first spooning the fluffy top rice onto the platter, then carefully lifting the crust in one piece to place on top, golden-side up.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Persillade
description: The most elemental French condiment — flat-leaf parsley and raw garlic chopped together until the garlic perfumes the parsley and the parsley tempers the garlic, ready to finish a sauté, crown a roast bone, or scatter over roasted vegetables.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Flat-leaf parsley, leaves and tender stems

instructions: Peel the garlic cloves and mince them very finely with a sharp knife. Scatter the salt over the minced garlic on the cutting board. Using the flat side of the chef's knife, smear the garlic and salt across the board in long, forward strokes, then scrape it back with the blade and repeat — alternating between chopping and smearing. After 2–3 minutes of this motion, you have a smooth, sticky garlic paste. The salt abrades the garlic, releasing its juice and breaking down the cell walls to give a milder, more integrated flavor than raw chunks.

Pile the parsley leaves on the garlic paste on the cutting board. Chop together with a rocking motion, folding the mixture back toward the center as the parsley spreads outward. The goal is integration, not obliteration: you want the garlic paste fully coated in parsley oil and the parsley finely minced, but not reduced to a wet green mash. Keep chopping and folding until the mixture is uniform, fragrant, and vivid green. If using olive oil, drizzle it over the finished persillade and fold through — this both preserves the color and makes the persillade easier to scatter.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Peruvian Aji Amarillo Paste
description: The sun-orange soul of Peruvian cooking — ají amarillo chilis blanched to remove harshness, then blended with a slick of oil into a vivid, fruity, moderately hot paste that is the essential base for ceviche, causa, and ají de gallina.

ingredients.text: 500 g Fresh ají amarillo chilis (or frozen)

instructions: Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Meanwhile, wearing gloves, remove the stems from the ají amarillo. Score each chili lengthwise with a paring knife and remove the seeds and white veins — these hold the harshest heat and removing them gives the paste a moderate, fruity heat rather than a face-melting one. Add the chilis to the boiling water. Blanch for 3 minutes. Drain, discard the blanching water, and repeat the blanch with fresh boiling water two more times. Three blanches is the traditional method for removing the raw, sharp bitterness of the ají amarillo while preserving its distinctive fruity flavor and vivid orange color. Do not skip the multiple blanches.

Transfer the drained, blanched chilis to a blender. Add the neutral oil and salt. Blend on high for 2–3 minutes until completely smooth — the paste should be velvety with no fiber or skin texture. If the blender struggles, add water one tablespoon at a time. Taste and adjust salt. The finished paste should taste of fruity, tropical warmth — think a moderately hot chili with notes of mango and passion fruit. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve if you want a particularly silky paste for refined applications like causa. Store refrigerated in an airtight jar for up to 2 weeks, or freeze in ice cube trays for up to 6 months.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Peruvian Ceviche with Leche de Tigre
description: Thin-sliced sea bass cured in punishing lime juice and ají amarillo until the flesh turns white and tender, served in its own milky tiger's milk that you are expected to drink at the end.

ingredients.text: 150 g Red onion, thinly sliced into half-moons
20 g Ají amarillo paste (or 2 fresh chilies)
15 g Fresh cilantro, leaves and thin stems
80 g Choclo corn kernels (or corn on the cob)
100 g Camote (sweet potato), cooked and sliced

instructions: Ensure the fish is as cold as possible — partially freeze for 20 minutes if needed for cleaner cuts. Cut into 2cm cubes against the grain of the flesh. Uniformity matters: irregular pieces cure at different rates, leaving some over-cured and chalky while others are still raw. Place immediately in a chilled ceramic or glass bowl.

Season the fish cubes with salt and toss to coat. Add the garlic, ginger, and ají amarillo paste. Pour the lime juice over all — there should be enough to fully submerge the fish. Toss gently. The acid cure begins immediately: for Peruvian ceviche, the ideal cure time is just 3–5 minutes for a tender, barely-cooked interior. Taste at 3 minutes — the fish should be white on the exterior but still slightly translucent at the very center.

Add the sliced red onion and half the cilantro to the ceviche and toss once. Taste and adjust salt and ají amarillo level. Serve immediately in chilled bowls — pour the full leche de tigre over and around the fish. Arrange the choclo corn and sliced camote on the side. Scatter remaining cilantro over. The leche de tigre is not a by-product — it is the whole point. Serve with a spoon.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Picarones
description: Peru's beloved fried doughnuts — rings of sweet potato and butternut squash dough, yeast-risen and crisp on the outside, pillowy within, drizzled with chancaca syrup spiced with anise and cinnamon.

ingredients.text: 250 g Orange-flesh sweet potato, cooked and mashed
250 g Butternut squash, cooked and mashed
250 g Chancaca (raw cane sugar block) or dark muscovado sugar

instructions: Ensure the sweet potato and squash mashes are cooled to lukewarm — warm enough to activate the yeast, cool enough not to kill it (38°C / 100°F is ideal). Combine the mashes in a large bowl. Dissolve the yeast in 3 tablespoons of warm water with a pinch of the sugar and leave 5 minutes until foamy. Add the foamy yeast, remaining sugar, salt, and anise seeds to the mash. Add the flour gradually, mixing to form a soft, slightly sticky dough. It will be softer and stickier than bread dough due to the vegetable moisture — do not add too much flour.

Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a damp cloth. Leave in a warm place (25-28°C / 77-82°F) for 1-2 hours until the dough has roughly doubled in volume and looks airy and loose. The dough will also become even stickier as the yeast activates — this is normal. The anise aroma will become more pronounced.

Break or chop the chancaca into pieces. Combine with water, cinnamon stick, cloves, and orange peel in a saucepan. Heat over medium, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Once dissolved, bring to a gentle boil and cook for 10-12 minutes until syrupy and fragrant. Strain out the spices and peel. Keep warm. The syrup should be dark, spiced, and thick enough to drizzle.

Heat the oil to 175°C (345°F) in a deep, wide pan. Wet your hands thoroughly. Grab a golf ball-sized portion of dough, poke a hole through the center with your finger, and stretch into a ring shape (about 10cm diameter) directly over the hot oil. Drop it in. Fry in batches of 3-4, turning once after 2-3 minutes, until both sides are deep golden-brown. Total frying time is 4-5 minutes per batch. The dough will expand in the oil. Drain on paper towels.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pesto alla Genovese
description: The mortar-pounded green of Liguria — young basil bruised against marble with garlic and pine nuts until it bleeds an electric, grassy oil, then bound with two cheeses and a slow thread of fruity Riviera olive oil into a coarse, glistening emerald paste that smells of summer the instant it touches hot pasta.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Genovese basil leaves (small, young, picked from the tips)
6 parts Garlic clove, peeled and green germ removed
4 parts Coarse sea salt (acts as the abrasive in the mortar)
15 parts Pecorino Sardo (mature, sharp), finely grated
90 parts Ligurian extra-virgin olive oil (mild, fruity, low-bitter)

instructions: Drop the peeled, de-germed garlic and the coarse salt together into a marble mortar. Crush with a circular grinding motion of the wooden pestle — not a pounding hammer — until the garlic dissolves into a smooth, wet paste. The salt crystals do double duty: they shred the garlic's cells and draw out its moisture, so a little goes a long way and the harsh raw bite is tamed before any basil ever touches it.

Add the pine nuts to the garlic paste and grind them down with the same patient circular motion. They are soft and oily, so they break quickly into a thick, sandy cream that loosens the garlic and rounds out its sharpness. Work until you have a cohesive, buttery base with no whole nuts left — this fat-rich layer is what will carry and protect the basil's color in the next step.

Add the basil a generous handful at a time, pressing and rolling the leaves up the sides of the mortar with the pestle rather than smashing them flat. The goal is to bruise and tear the leaf cells so they weep their oils — a rotating, wall-scraping motion does this without overheating. Add more basil only as the previous handful breaks down. Work fairly briskly; the longer the cut basil is exposed to air and friction heat, the faster it oxidizes from electric green toward muddy olive.

Stir the two grated cheeses into the basil paste; they thicken it into a dense, clay-like mass. Now switch to a spoon or the pestle and work in the olive oil in a slow thread, beating it into the paste a little at a time the way you would mount a sauce, until the pesto turns glossy, loose, and pourable but still coarse. Taste: it should be lush, salty from the cheese, and almost too intense on its own — it is meant to be cut by hot starchy pasta water at the moment of saucing. Use within a few hours, the surface filmed with a little extra oil to seal it from the air.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pho Broth
description: The soul of pho bo — beef bones simmered for hours into a crystal-clear amber broth, perfumed with charred onion and ginger and a fistful of toasted spice, then balanced on a knife's edge of fish sauce. Clean, aromatic, and deceptively deep.

ingredients.text: 2 % Whole spice (star anise, cinnamon stick, cloves, coriander seed, fennel seed)

instructions: Cover the bones and meat with cold water in a large pot and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Boil hard for 5-7 minutes — a gray, foamy scum will erupt to the surface. Dump everything into a colander, discard the cloudy water, and scrub each bone under running water to remove every trace of coagulated blood and grit. This brutal first wash is the single most important step for a clear broth.

Hold the halved onions and whole ginger directly over an open flame, or place cut-side down in a dry cast-iron skillet over high heat. Char until the surfaces are blackened and blistered, 8-10 minutes, turning so every face takes color. Don't be timid — you want genuine black char, not just golden. Rinse off any loose ash under the tap and leave the rest.

Toast the star anise, cinnamon, cloves, coriander, and fennel in a dry skillet over medium heat, shaking constantly, for 3-4 minutes until fragrant and the seeds begin to pop. Don't let them smoke. Tie the spices in a small muslin bag or cheesecloth bundle so they can be lifted out cleanly later.

Cover the clean bones and meat with fresh cold water and bring to a bare simmer — never a boil. Add the charred onion and ginger and the spice bag. Hold at the gentlest simmer, surface barely shivering, for 4-6 hours. Skim foam and surface fat patiently every 20-30 minutes for the first hour. Pull the brisket out at 90 minutes once it is tender (save it for slicing into the bowls); let the bones keep going. Top up with hot water if the level drops below the bones.

Return the strained broth to the pot over low heat. Season with fish sauce, rock sugar, and salt, adding in stages and tasting as you go. The goal is a savory broth with a whisper of sweetness and a deep umami hum — it should taste slightly stronger than you'd sip on its own, because rice noodles and raw beef will dilute it in the bowl. Adjust until balanced.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Quick Pickled Jalapeños
description: Vinegar-bright, gently fiery pickled jalapeños ready in 30 minutes — crisp, olive-green rings that cut through richness and outlast any store-bought jar.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Fresh jalapeños, sliced into 6 mm rings

instructions: Combine the vinegar, water, sugar, and salt in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar and salt are completely dissolved. Remove from heat as soon as the brine is clear — do not boil hard or reduce, as this concentrates the acidity unpredictably.

Sterilize one or two glass jars with boiling water and drain upside down. Pack the jalapeño rings tightly into the warm jars, tucking the smashed garlic, peppercorns, and oregano throughout. Press down firmly to maximize density — the jalapeños will soften slightly in the brine and you want them packed.

Pour the warm brine over the packed jalapeños until they are completely submerged with a 1 cm headspace above the brine. Gently tap the jar on the counter to release any trapped air bubbles. If jalapeños float above the brine, weigh them down with a small resealable bag filled with brine.

Allow the jar to cool to room temperature (about 15 minutes), then seal with a lid and refrigerate. The jalapeños are edible after 30 minutes but are dramatically better after 2 hours once the brine has penetrated to the center. They keep refrigerated for up to 3 weeks.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pickled Red Onions
description: Thin-sliced red onions submerged in a vinegar brine with a pinch of sugar and salt, left for as little as 30 minutes — turning from sharp and raw to bright magenta, tender, and mellow.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Red onion (halved, sliced paper-thin on a mandoline or knife)

instructions: Halve the red onion through the root, then slice as thinly as you can manage — ideally 2 mm or less on a mandoline, or with careful knife work following the grain. The thinner the slice, the faster the pickle penetrates and the more tender the result. Uniformity matters: thick and thin slices pickle at different rates and you end up with some raw and some limp.

Combine the vinegar, water, sugar, and salt in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir constantly until the sugar and salt are fully dissolved, about 2 minutes. Add the peppercorns and bay leaf and remove from the heat. The brine does not need to boil — you are only dissolving solids, not cooking the onions. Allow to cool for 5 minutes before pouring.

Pack the sliced onions into a clean glass jar, pressing down gently so they sit below the rim. Pour the warm (not boiling) brine over the onions, submerging them completely. Press the onions down with a fork if needed — any exposed to air will not pickle and may discolour. Seal the jar loosely or lay a small piece of plastic wrap across the top. Leave at room temperature for at least 30 minutes; 1 hour is better.

After 30 to 60 minutes at room temperature, transfer the sealed jar to the refrigerator. The pickle is ready to eat immediately but will continue to improve over the next 24 hours as the onions soften slightly and the brine penetrates fully. Use within 2 to 3 weeks. The brine will turn a vivid magenta that will stain — keep a cloth nearby when pouring.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pico de Gallo
description: Mexico's fresh, chunky tomato salsa — ripe tomato, white onion, jalapeño, cilantro, and lime juice cut fine and macerated just long enough for the juices to pool in the bowl.

ingredients.text: 100 % Ripe Roma or vine tomatoes, seeds removed, fine dice
8 % Jalapeño or serrano, seeds and ribs removed for medium heat, minced
8 % Fresh cilantro, leaves and tender stems, chopped

instructions: This is a knife-skill recipe. Begin with the onion: dice it very fine (3–4 mm), then place in a small bowl and rinse with cold water to reduce the harsh raw bite — squeeze dry in a paper towel. Core and halve the tomatoes, scoop out the seeds and gel with a spoon (this prevents the finished salsa from becoming watery), then dice the flesh into 5–8 mm pieces — not too fine or the salsa turns mushy, not too coarse or it won't coat a chip. Mince the jalapeño as fine as possible; start with only half if uncertain about heat level. Chop the cilantro coarsely — it will macerate and soften, so you don't want it minced to nothing.

Combine all the diced vegetables in a bowl. Add the cilantro, lime juice, and salt. Fold gently with a spoon — do not stir vigorously or the tomatoes will break down. Taste immediately: the lime should be assertive and the salt should pop everything forward. Do not under-salt; pico de gallo needs more salt than feels comfortable when tasting from a plain spoon because it is served with unsalted tortilla chips or plain corn. Let the pico sit for 10 minutes before serving so the salt draws out the tomato juices and they pool in the bowl, creating a natural light brine.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pierogi Dough
description: A supple, silky dumpling dough that rolls impossibly thin without tearing — pale and smooth as chamois leather, pliable enough to pleat easily, yet firm enough to survive a rolling boil.

ingredients.text: 5 parts Unsalted butter, melted (for boiled finish)

instructions: Mound the flour on a clean work surface and make a wide well in the center. Add the egg yolks, sour cream, warm water, and salt to the well. Beat the wet ingredients gently with a fork, then gradually incorporate the flour from the inner walls of the well, stirring in a widening spiral. When the mixture becomes too thick to stir, begin kneading with your hands — flour from the edges inward, pressing and folding. The dough will come together into a rough, slightly sticky mass.

Knead the dough on a lightly floured surface for 5-8 minutes using a push-fold-turn rhythm: push the heel of your hand forward, fold the dough back over itself, rotate a quarter turn, repeat. The dough transforms from rough and lumpy to smooth and supple. It should not require much flour — add only enough to prevent sticking. Once smooth, wrap tightly in plastic wrap and rest at room temperature for 30 minutes. This rest is essential: it relaxes the gluten so the dough can be rolled paper-thin without springing back.

Divide the rested dough into two halves (keep one half covered while working the other). On a lightly floured surface, roll with a rolling pin from the center outward, turning the sheet a quarter turn after every 3-4 passes. The goal is a uniform sheet 2mm thick — thin enough to be almost translucent when held up to light, but not so thin it tears. Cut circles with a 7-8 cm round cutter or an upturned glass. Re-roll scraps once.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Work in batches — no more than 8-10 pierogi at a time to prevent sticking and temperature drops. Lower the pierogi gently with a slotted spoon. They will sink to the bottom, then float up as they cook. Once they float, cook for a further 2-3 minutes for a total of 4-5 minutes from entry. Remove with a slotted spoon, drain, and toss immediately with melted butter to prevent sticking.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pierogi
description: Poland's answer to the dumpling: a thin, yielding dough pocket sealed around a filling of farmer's cheese and potato so creamy it collapses on the tongue, finished in brown butter with onions that have cooked into sweetness.

ingredients.text: 60 parts Russet potatoes, boiled and riced

instructions: Combine the flour and a pinch of salt in a bowl. Add warm water gradually, mixing with a fork until shaggy. Turn out and knead by hand for 8–10 minutes until the dough is completely smooth, supple, and slightly tacky but not sticky. The dough should have the elasticity of an earlobe. Wrap tightly in cling film and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature — resting is non-negotiable, as it relaxes the gluten so the dough can be rolled paper-thin.

Sauté half the diced onion in butter until golden, then set aside to cool. In a bowl, combine the riced potatoes, farmer's cheese, and sautéed onion. Season aggressively with salt and white pepper — the filling will be encased in unseasoned dough, so it must carry all the flavor. Mix until just combined; do not overwork or the potato becomes gluey. Taste and adjust salt until the filling tastes pleasantly salty on its own.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the rested dough to 2–3mm thickness — thin enough to see the shadow of your hand through it. Cut circles using a 8–9cm cutter or glass. Place a generous teaspoon of filling in the center of each circle. Fold the dough over the filling and press the edges firmly together, crimping with a fork or a tight finger-pinch. Sealed edges must be completely airtight — any opening will burst during boiling.

Bring a large pot of heavily salted water to a rolling boil. Add pierogi in batches — do not crowd. They will sink, then float to the surface after 2 minutes. After they float, cook 2 minutes more for a total of 4–5 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon. For the classic finish, melt butter in a wide pan over medium heat, add the remaining diced onion and cook until golden. Toss the boiled pierogi in the browned butter for 2 minutes until lightly crisped on one side.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Bacalà al Pil-Pil
description: The Basque art of coaxing salt cod's own gelatin into an emulsified olive-oil sauce — a gentle, circular swirl of the pan builds a creamy, ivory emulsion without a drop of cream or butter, sustained entirely by the fish's own collagen.

ingredients.text: 100 % Desalted salt cod (bacalao), skin-on fillets, soaked 48 hr in cold water
3 % Dried guindilla chili peppers (or dried cayenne)
0.5 % Fine sea salt (taste before adding — the cod carries salt)

instructions: If not already desalted, submerge the salt cod in a large bowl of cold water in the refrigerator. Change the water every 8–12 hours for 48 hours. The fish is ready when a small piece tastes pleasantly salty rather than overwhelming. After desalting, remove the fillets from the water and pat them completely dry on multiple layers of paper towel, then leave them uncovered on a rack at room temperature for 20 minutes. This drying step is critical: surface moisture is the enemy of the emulsion — it will cause the gelatin to dilute into water rather than binding with the oil. Run your fingers over the skin; the fillets should feel dry and faintly tacky, not wet.

In a wide, shallow clay cazuela or heavy skillet, combine the olive oil, sliced garlic, and dried chilis over the lowest possible heat. When the garlic begins to sizzle gently (about 2 minutes), nestle the cod fillets in skin-side up. The oil should never bubble aggressively — it should hover around 60–70C / 140–160F, which is well below a fry. Cook for 12–15 minutes, periodically tilting the pan to baste the fish with the warm oil. You will begin to see small white droplets forming at the edges of the fillets — this is the gelatin leaching from the fish into the oil. This is the raw material for the emulsion. When the fish is just cooked through and beginning to flake, gently remove the fillets with a slotted spatula onto a warm plate. Reserve every drop of the oil with its garlic and gelatin droplets.

This is the defining technique of the dish. With the reserved warm oil still in the pan over the lowest heat, begin moving the pan in slow, continuous circles — tilting it forward, sideways, backward, in a hypnotic, patient swirl. Do not stir, do not whisk. Just swing the pan. As you do this, the gelatin droplets begin to bind with the olive oil, and after 5–10 minutes a pale, creamy emulsion starts forming at the edges of the pan and slowly spreading to the center. The sauce goes from oily to ivory-white and slightly thickened, like a very loose aioli. If at any point it looks like it's about to split — the oil separates from the white mass — add a teaspoon of cold water and slow down the swirl. Taste and adjust salt very carefully. A pil-pil sauce that holds is one of the great quiet miracles of the kitchen.

Gently lower the reserved cod fillets back into the emulsified sauce, skin-side up, and tilt the pan to baste them with the sauce. The residual heat of the sauce will warm the fish through without further cooking. Taste the sauce carefully and add a pinch of salt only if needed — the fish and oil will have already contributed significant salt. To serve, bring the cazuela directly to the table. Tear crusty bread and drag it through the ivory sauce. The dish should be served warm, not hot — pil-pil breaks at temperatures above 80C, so never return it to a burner at this stage.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Butter Pilaf
description: The pillar of Central Asian and Turkish cooking — long-grain rice toasted in butter until translucent and nutty, then steamed in stock with onion and carrot until each grain is firm, separate, and fragrantly golden.

ingredients.text: 300 g Basmati or long-grain white rice
1 head Whole head of garlic (unpeeled, optional)

instructions: Rinse the rice under cold running water, swirling with your hand, until the water runs nearly clear — this removes excess surface starch that would cause the grains to clump. Transfer to a bowl and cover with cold water. Soak for 30 minutes. This hydrates the outer layers of the grain so they can expand uniformly under steam without the center remaining chalky. Drain thoroughly before cooking.

Melt the butter in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid over medium heat until it foams and then settles — this is clarified butter temperature, ideal for frying. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring often, for 5-6 minutes until completely soft and just beginning to turn golden at the edges. Add the carrot julienne and cumin seeds and cook for 3 more minutes until the carrot softens slightly. The pot should smell of warm butter, sweet onion, and earthy cumin.

Add the drained rice to the pot with the aromatics and stir to coat every grain in the butter. Spread the rice in an even layer and cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, for 2-3 minutes. The grains will turn from opaque white to a slightly translucent, glassy appearance, and the pot will smell of warm, toasted grain — like popcorn but delicate. This toasting step coats each grain in fat, which keeps them separate during steaming.

Pour the hot stock over the toasted rice — it will hiss and steam immediately. Add salt and black pepper. If using, nestle the whole unpeeled head of garlic into the center of the rice, cut side down (it perfumes the steam without making the pilaf garlicky). Stir once to distribute everything. Bring to a full boil over high heat, then immediately reduce to the absolute lowest setting. Cover tightly with the lid and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid once.

Remove the pot from heat and let it rest, completely undisturbed with the lid on, for 10 minutes. This is not optional — it is the moment the steam redistributes through the grains, equalizing moisture and ensuring even texture. After 10 minutes, remove the lid and the garlic head (if used). Using a fork or the handle of a wooden spoon, gently fluff the rice from the bottom up with light, lifting motions — never press down or stir aggressively, which would crush the grains.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pineapple Upside-Down Cake
description: A golden sponge baked over a glossy layer of caramelised pineapple rings and brown sugar, then inverted to reveal a lacquered, jewel-bright topping that smells of caramel and tropical fruit.

ingredients.text: 60 parts Canned or fresh pineapple rings
40 parts Dark brown sugar (for caramel base)
30 parts Unsalted butter (for the caramel base)
80 parts Unsalted butter, softened (for the sponge batter)

instructions: Preheat oven to 175°C (350°F). Place a 24cm oven-safe skillet or round cake tin directly on the stovetop over medium heat. Add the butter and let it melt. Add the dark brown sugar and stir briefly to combine, then leave undisturbed for 2 minutes until it bubbles and darkens slightly. The caramel does not need to be fully made at this point — it will finish in the oven — but the butter and sugar should be melted and fragrant. Remove from heat.

Lay the pineapple rings over the hot caramel in the pan, fitting them snugly — one in the centre and as many as will fit around the edge without overlapping. Press them gently into the caramel. If using canned pineapple, pat the rings thoroughly dry first — excess juice will water down the caramel and prevent the fruit from browning properly. Place a maraschino cherry or dried cherry in the centre of each ring if desired.

In a bowl, beat the softened butter and caster sugar together with an electric mixer for 3 minutes until pale and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each addition. Sift in the flour and baking powder and fold until just combined — a few turns with a spatula rather than vigorous beating. The batter should be smooth, thick, and fall from the spatula in slow ribbons. A small splash of milk or pineapple juice from the tin can loosen it to the right consistency.

Pour the batter carefully over the pineapple arrangement, spreading gently to the edges to cover everything evenly without disturbing the fruit arrangement. Bake at 175°C for 30–35 minutes until the sponge is deep golden and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. Remove from the oven and rest for 5 minutes — not longer. Run a knife around the edge, place a large serving plate on top, and invert decisively in one motion. Lift the pan straight up. Any caramel clinging to the pan can be scraped off and poured over the top.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Piri Piri Sauce
description: A vivid, oil-bright red sauce from the African bird's eye chili — simultaneously fiery and fruity, with a lemon-garlic sharpness that makes grilled chicken sing and your lips tingle long after the last bite.

ingredients.text: 4 parts Bird's eye chilies (fresh or dried and rehydrated), stems removed
2 parts Red bell pepper, roughly chopped and roasted
3 parts Neutral oil (sunflower or light olive)
0.3 parts Fresh oregano leaves (or 0.5 tsp dried)

instructions: Place the red bell pepper pieces and whole garlic cloves on a baking tray under a very hot broiler (240C/460F) or directly over a gas flame using tongs. Roast until the pepper skin is blackened and blistered in patches and the garlic is golden-brown and soft inside. The pepper takes 10-15 minutes, the garlic 8-10 minutes. Transfer to a bowl, cover with cling film, and steam for 5 minutes. Peel the pepper skin off — the char and steam loosens it.

Combine the chilies, peeled roasted pepper, roasted garlic, lemon juice, vinegar, oil, salt, oregano, and paprika in a blender or food processor. Blend on high for 2 minutes until completely smooth and emulsified. If the sauce is too thick, add a tablespoon of water and blend again. Taste carefully — the heat will be significant. Adjust with more lemon for brightness or more salt for depth.

For a cooked piri piri (preferred for marinating and shelf stability): pour the blended sauce into a small saucepan and simmer over low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Cooking mellows the raw chili edge, deepens the roasted pepper flavor, and extends refrigerator life to 2 weeks. For a fresh, vibrant table sauce, skip this step and use raw. Cool completely before jarring.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pisco Sour
description: Peru's national cocktail — a dry, citrus-bright pisco shaken hard with fresh lime juice, simple syrup, and raw egg white until it froths into a cloud, served in a chilled coupe with three drops of Angostura bitters bleeding into the foam.

ingredients.text: 30 ml Fresh lime juice (key lime preferred)

instructions: Combine the pisco, lime juice, simple syrup, and egg white in a cocktail shaker with no ice. This is the 'dry shake' — shaking without ice to build a preliminary foam from the egg white protein before dilution with ice. Shake as hard and as long as you can for 30–45 seconds. The shaker will feel almost impossible to open from the vacuum. The egg white requires the heat and full force of this dry shake to denature and foam — a half-hearted shake produces a thin, watery foam cap that collapses in seconds.

Add a generous scoop of ice cubes to the shaker containing the dry-shaken base. Shake vigorously again for 15–20 seconds. This second shake chills, dilutes, and further aerates the cocktail. The colder temperature helps set the foam into a more stable structure. The shaker will frost over on the outside — this is your cue that the drink is cold enough.

Double-strain the cocktail through a Hawthorne strainer and a fine-mesh sieve into a chilled coupe glass — the fine strainer catches ice shards that would crater the foam. Pour from a low height so the foam lands cleanly on top rather than splashing against the sides. The foam should dome slightly above the rim of the glass. Immediately add three drops of Angostura bitters to the center of the foam. Use a cocktail pick or toothpick to drag the drops through the foam in a spiral or line — the bitters bloom in the white foam like ink in water, creating the classic pisco sour pattern.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pistou
description: Provence's uncooked basil paste — raw garlic pounded with fresh basil and olive oil into a vivid green sauce that smells like a garden in August. Unlike its Ligurian cousin pesto, pistou contains no nuts and no cheese, meaning all the flavors are immediate and transparent, with nowhere for the basil to hide.

ingredients.text: 60 g Fresh basil leaves (packed, no stems)

instructions: In a mortar, pound the garlic cloves with the coarse salt until a completely smooth, white paste forms. The salt crystals act as an abrasive and draw out the moisture from the garlic. This step is crucial — any remaining garlic chunks will make the sauce harsh and unpleasant. If using a food processor instead, mince the garlic as fine as possible before proceeding.

Add basil leaves to the mortar in two or three batches. Pound and grind with a circular pressing motion — not sharp strikes — until each batch is completely incorporated before adding the next. The goal is to bruise and crush the cells to release the oils, not to create friction heat. If using a food processor, pulse briefly in short bursts — blending too long heats the basil and turns it black.

Stream in olive oil a little at a time, stirring and pressing the paste against the sides of the mortar to incorporate. The sauce will loosen and become glossy as the oil emulsifies with the water content of the basil. Add a small squeeze of lemon juice if using. The consistency should be thick enough to coat a spoon but fluid enough to pour. Use immediately — pistou begins to oxidize and lose its vivid color within 30 minutes.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Greek Pita Bread
description: Soft, pillowy rounds that inflate into perfect steam-pockets in a furiously hot oven — they emerge with a pale gold crust, a tender crumb, and a hollow belly just waiting to be torn open and filled.
instructions: Combine flour, instant yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Add warm water and olive oil. Mix with a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains, then use your hand to bring it into a rough ball. The dough should be moderately soft and slightly sticky — noticeably softer than pizza dough but not as wet as focaccia. Turn out onto a lightly floured surface.

Knead for 8 minutes on a lightly floured surface using a push-fold-rotate motion. The dough will transform: from sticky and rough to smooth, elastic, and barely tacky. After 8 minutes it should pass the basic stretch test — pull a small piece and stretch it a few inches without it tearing immediately. Shape into a ball, lightly oil the surface, and place in a clean bowl.

Cover the bowl with a damp towel or plastic wrap. Let rise at room temperature (22–25 C) for 60–75 minutes until doubled. While the dough rises, place a heavy baking stone or inverted cast-iron pan on the top rack of the oven. Preheat the oven to its maximum temperature — 260 C (500 F) or higher — at least 30 minutes before baking. A screaming-hot surface is essential for pita to puff.

Punch down the dough and divide into 8 equal portions (about 70 g each). On a lightly floured surface, roll each portion into a smooth ball. Cover and rest 10 minutes so the gluten relaxes. Then roll each ball with a rolling pin into a round 18–20 cm across and about 4–5 mm thick. Do not roll too thin — a pita that is too thin won't form a proper pocket. Place on a sheet of parchment and rest 15 minutes before baking.

Working in batches of 2–3 (however many fit on your baking stone), use a peel or the back of a flat baking sheet to slide pita rounds directly onto the screaming-hot stone. Bake for 3–4 minutes — no more. You will see the pita begin to puff dramatically about 60–90 seconds in, inflating into a dome. Once fully puffed and barely pale gold on top, remove. Do not over-bake — the goal is a soft, pliable pita, not a crisp one. Wrap immediately in a clean towel to keep soft.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Polenta
description: Coarse cornmeal stirred into a slow whirlpool until the grains burst, swell, and pull away from the pot in a single glossy mass — patient, golden, and finished with a knot of butter and a storm of cheese.

ingredients.text: 500 parts Water (or half water, half milk)

instructions: Pour the water into a heavy-bottomed pot — copper or thick-clad steel holds heat best and resists scorching. Add the salt and bring to a bare simmer over medium heat. The water should be hot and lazily steaming, with small bubbles trembling at the edges, NOT at a rolling boil. A violent boil flings cornmeal everywhere and seizes it into lumps.

Stir the simmering water into a slow whirlpool with a whisk. While it spins, add the cornmeal in a thin, steady rain from your fist — never dump it. Whisk constantly as you pour so each grain disperses before the next lands. Once all the cornmeal is in, switch to a sturdy wooden spoon. The mixture will look loose and milky, like thin cream.

Drop the heat to its lowest setting so the polenta blips rather than boils — a thick bubble should heave up and burst every few seconds, like a slow mud pot. Cook 35-45 minutes, stirring every few minutes with the wooden spoon, scraping the bottom and corners to prevent scorching. The polenta is done when the grains have lost all grittiness and the mass pulls cleanly away from the sides of the pot as you stir.

Off the heat, beat in the cold butter and grated Parmigiano, stirring vigorously until both melt into a glossy, unified cream. For a soft, spoonable polenta, loosen with the warm milk until it slumps slowly off the spoon. Taste and adjust salt. Serve at once in warm, shallow bowls — polenta stiffens fast as it cools.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pollo a la Brasa (Peruvian Rotisserie Chicken)
description: A whole chicken brined in soy sauce, cumin, aji panca, and garlic for 24 hours, then roasted on a rotisserie or in the oven until the skin is burnished and crackled and the meat inside is so juicy and aromatic it needs nothing beyond the bright green aji verde served alongside.

ingredients.text: 30 g Garlic cloves, minced to a paste
40 g Aji panca paste (or dried aji panca, rehydrated)
20 g Fresh mint leaves (for aji verde)
20 g Fresh jalapeño or aji amarillo (for aji verde)

instructions: Whisk together soy sauce, garlic paste, cumin, aji panca paste, smoked paprika, lime juice, salt, pepper, oregano, and oil until uniform. The mixture should be thick, dark, and deeply aromatic — the soy and aji panca together create the characteristic mahogany color of pollo a la brasa.

Dry the chicken thoroughly inside and out. Using your fingers, carefully separate the skin from the breast and thigh meat and push half the marinade directly under the skin, massaging it over the meat. Rub remaining marinade all over the exterior and inside the cavity. Place in a large zip-lock bag or covered dish. Refrigerate 12–24 hours, turning once.

Place chicken breast-side up on a rack in a roasting pan (or on a rotisserie spit). Roast at 200 C (400 F) for 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes. Every 20 minutes, baste with pan drippings. Rotate the pan if using a regular oven. The chicken is done when the thigh joint reads 82 C (180 F) and the skin is deeply burnished. Rest 10 minutes before carving.

Blend mint, cilantro, jalapeño, mayonnaise, and lime juice in a blender until completely smooth and vivid green. Season with salt. The sauce should be bright, herby, creamy, and slightly spicy — the essential accompaniment to cut the richness of the chicken.

Carve the rested chicken: separate the legs, split the breast, cut the wings. Arrange on a warm platter skin-side up so the burnished skin remains visible. Serve the aji verde in a bowl alongside, with fried yuca or papas fritas and a simple salad.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pollo en Adobo
description: Bone-in chicken braised in a deep brick-red Mexican adobo — ancho and guajillo chiles toasted, rehydrated, and blended with vinegar, garlic, cumin, and oregano into a glossy, chile-thick sauce that clings to the meat like varnish.

ingredients.text: 1000 g Bone-in chicken pieces (thighs and legs)
4 whole Dried ancho chiles (stems and seeds removed)
4 whole Dried guajillo chiles (stems and seeds removed)

instructions: Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat until very hot. Toast the stemmed, seeded ancho and guajillo chile pieces in batches by pressing them flat against the hot surface for 10-15 seconds per side — you will see them puff slightly, change color, and release an intoxicating smoky-sweet fragrance. Do not scorch them black: a toasted chile smells of raisin, chocolate, and dried fruit; a burnt chile smells of acrid carbon and will make your sauce bitter. Once toasted, transfer immediately to a bowl and cover with boiling water. Soak for 20-30 minutes until completely soft and pliable.

Drain the rehydrated chiles, reserving 120 ml of the soaking liquid (it has flavor but can be bitter — taste before using). Place the chiles in a blender with the quartered onion, garlic, apple cider vinegar, toasted cumin, oregano, cinnamon, and cloves. Add 60 ml of the soaking water and 60 ml fresh water. Blitz to a completely smooth, thick paste, 2-3 minutes on high. The finished adobo should be the color of dark brick, intensely aromatic, slightly sour from the vinegar, and thick enough to coat a spoon. Pass through a fine-mesh strainer if desired for a smoother texture.

Heat the lard in a large, heavy pot (Dutch oven) over high heat until smoking. Working in batches, sear the salted chicken pieces skin-side down for 4-5 minutes without moving until deeply browned. Turn and sear the other side for 2 minutes. Remove and set aside. Reduce heat to medium. Add the adobo paste to the hot fat — it will splatter furiously. Stand back, then stir constantly for 3-4 minutes, frying the paste in the fat. This step, called freír el adobo, transforms the raw chile paste into a deep, complex sauce: the color darkens, the sharp raw smell mellow to something round and toasted, and the fat begins to bleed out visibly — the Mexican equivalent of bhunao.

Return all the seared chicken pieces to the pot with the fried adobo paste. Pour in the chicken stock and stir to combine — the liquid should come about halfway up the chicken. Bring to a simmer, cover the pot, and cook over low heat for 45-60 minutes until the chicken is completely tender at the bone. The adobo will penetrate every surface of the chicken. A fork inserted at the thigh joint should meet no resistance and the meat should want to pull from the bone.

Remove the lid and increase heat to medium-high. Cook uncovered for 10-15 minutes, turning the chicken pieces frequently and spooning sauce over them. The adobo will reduce and glaze: each piece of chicken becomes lacquered in a thick, glossy, brick-red coating. The sauce should be thick enough that it coats the back of a spoon and holds for a moment. Taste and adjust salt. Serve over rice or with warm tortillas, with pickled jalapeños and sliced white onion alongside.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Ponzu
description: The bright, savory backbone of the Japanese table — sour citrus juice married to soy and steeped over kombu and katsuobushi until it deepens into a tart, mahogany dressing that wakes up everything from chilled tofu to seared fish and shabu-shabu hot pot.
instructions: In a clean glass jar or non-reactive bowl, combine the yuzu juice, rice vinegar, soy sauce, and mirin. Do not heat the citrus — raw juice keeps its high, perfumed top note, and cooking would dull the sourness into something flat and stewed. Stir gently to blend. The liquid should be a deep amber that smells equally of sharp citrus and salty soy, neither one drowning the other.

Wipe the kombu lightly with a damp cloth (never rinse off the white powdery mannitol — that is pure umami) and submerge it in the base along with the katsuobushi. Cover and refrigerate for at least 24 hours, ideally 2 to 3 days. This cold infusion draws glutamate from the kelp and inosinate from the bonito into the acidic liquid, building the deep savory undertone that defines true ponzu. The flakes will swell and slowly sink as they saturate.

Set a fine-mesh sieve lined with a paper towel or cheesecloth over a clean jar and pour the ponzu through, letting it drip without pressing — squeezing the solids forces through bitter, cloudy fines. Discard the spent kombu and bonito. Bottle the strained ponzu and let it rest in the refrigerator at least a few hours so the flavors settle and marry. It keeps refrigerated for several weeks and only improves over the first week.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Porchetta
description: A whole pork belly rolled around a core of fennel pollen, wild fennel fronds, rosemary, and garlic, then slow-roasted for hours until the fat renders completely and the skin transforms into a thunderous, blistered crackling that shatters into a thousand shards at the first cut. Central Italy's greatest street food, sliced and eaten in a bread roll.

ingredients.text: 2000 g Skin-on pork belly, deboned, butterflied flat
20 g Fresh fennel fronds or wild fennel
10 g Fennel seeds, toasted and coarsely ground
8 cloves Garlic cloves, very finely minced

instructions: The night before: lay the pork belly skin-side down. Score the flesh side in a crosshatch pattern about 5 mm deep (this is where the filling will cling). Season the flesh generously with salt — use about half the total salt. Flip the belly and score the skin with a sharp knife in parallel lines about 1 cm apart, cutting only through the skin and just into the fat — do not cut into the flesh. Salt the skin lightly, rub in, and refrigerate uncovered overnight. Dry skin is the key to crackling.

Roughly chop rosemary, fennel fronds, and garlic together on a cutting board until finely minced. Transfer to a bowl. Add ground fennel seeds, black pepper, and olive oil. Stir into a fragrant, moist paste. Taste — it should be aggressively herby and garlicky. This is the soul of the porchetta.

Spread the herb paste evenly over the entire scored flesh side, pressing it into the crosshatch cuts. Roll the belly tightly from one short end, keeping the tension even, ensuring the roll is tight with no air pockets. Tie with kitchen twine at 3 cm intervals — tight enough that the roll holds a drum-like firmness. Rub remaining salt all over the skin. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 2 hours, or overnight if possible.

Take porchetta from the fridge 1 hour before roasting. Preheat oven to 230 C (450 F). Place porchetta on a wire rack over a roasting pan, seam-side down. Roast at 230 C for 30 minutes — this blast of heat begins the crackling. Reduce heat to 160 C (325 F) and roast for 2 to 2.5 more hours until internal temperature reaches 70 C (158 F) at the center.

Rest the porchetta on a wire rack (not a cutting board) uncovered for 20–30 minutes. Resting lets the juices redistribute through the fat and flesh. Do not tent with foil — steam will soften the crackling you worked so hard for. Slice with a sharp, serrated bread knife using a sawing motion — a chef's knife will crack and shatter the crackling rather than cut through it cleanly.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Hong Shao Rou (Red-Braised Pork Belly)
description: Thick-cut pork belly caramelized in rock sugar and braised in soy, Shaoxing wine, and star anise until the fat layers quiver like warm amber silk and the sauce reduces to a dark, lacquered glaze.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Pork belly (skin-on), cut in 4 cm cubes

instructions: Place pork belly cubes in a cold pot, cover with cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat and blanch for 5 minutes, skimming the grey foam vigorously. Drain and rinse each piece under cold running water to remove all grey protein residue. Pat completely dry with paper towels. This step is essential for a clean, clear braising sauce with no off-flavors.

In a wide, heavy pot or wok, heat the neutral oil over medium heat. Add the rock sugar and cook, stirring gently, until it melts and turns a deep amber color — like old whiskey. This takes about 4–6 minutes. Do not walk away. The caramel transitions from clear to pale gold to amber to dark amber very quickly.

Add the pork belly to the hot caramel and toss to coat (stand back — it will spit). Add Shaoxing wine, dark and light soy sauces, star anise, cassia, ginger, and scallion knot. Pour in enough water to just barely cover. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a very low simmer. Cover and braise for 1.5–2 hours, turning the pork every 30 minutes.

Uncover the pot and increase heat to medium-high. Baste the pork continuously with the braising liquid as it reduces and concentrates. Cook for 10–15 minutes, turning the pork gently, until the sauce is thick, glossy, and sticky — it should coat each pork cube in a shiny, lacquered shell. Remove the whole spices, ginger, and scallion knot.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Chashu Pork Belly
description: A rolled pork belly tied tight, seared golden, and braised in soy, mirin, sake, and sugar until the fat is trembling and translucent — the canonical ramen topping.

ingredients.text: 5 parts White sugar (or light brown sugar)

instructions: Lay the pork belly skin-side down on a clean board. Roll it tightly from one short end into a compact cylinder, keeping the roll as even in diameter as possible. Tie at 2 cm intervals with butcher's twine — snug but not so tight that it cuts into the fat. The tight roll ensures even slices for ramen, and the twine holds the shape through the braise. If the belly is very thick or the skin tough, score the skin lightly at 1 cm intervals before rolling to help it render and soften evenly.

Heat the oil in a heavy pan or Dutch oven over high heat until shimmering. Place the rolled belly in the pan and sear, turning every 2 to 3 minutes with tongs, until every surface including the two flat ends is golden-brown. This takes about 10 to 12 minutes total. The skin side will sputter and contract energetically — use a splatter screen if needed. The Maillard crust built here contributes the roasted, caramelized notes that distinguish chashu from a simple braised pork roll.

Remove the seared roll to a plate. Deglaze the hot pan with the sake, scraping all the fond from the bottom. Add the soy sauce, mirin, sugar, water, scallion stalks, and ginger slices. Stir to dissolve the sugar. Return the roll to the pan — the braising liquid should come about halfway up the roll. Bring to a bare simmer, then cover with a tight-fitting lid or a cartouche of parchment paper. Cook over the lowest heat that maintains a gentle simmer, turning the roll every 30 minutes so all sides have equal time submerged, for 2 to 2.5 hours total.

Allow the chashu to cool in the braising liquid to room temperature, then transfer the roll (still in its braising liquid) to the refrigerator and chill overnight, or at minimum 4 hours. Chilling accomplishes two things: the fat solidifies, making clean slicing possible (warm chashu is too soft to slice neatly), and the roll continues to absorb the braising liquid as it cools, deepening the flavor penetration. The chilled braising liquid will set to a dark, jiggly gel — reserve it as a tare or glaze for other applications.

To serve, cut the twine with scissors and slice the chilled roll into rounds of 8 to 12 mm thickness. For ramen service, heat a small non-stick or cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until it just begins to smoke. Lay the chashu slices in without oil — they carry enough rendered fat from the braise. Sear for 45 to 60 seconds per side until the edges caramelize and char at the points and the surface takes on a glorious, lacquered char. Alternatively, brush the slices with a little of the gelled braising liquid and briefly torch them or place under a very hot broiler for 60 seconds to lacquer and caramelize the surface.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pork Belly Confit
description: Skin-on pork belly cured overnight in salt and aromatics, then slow-cooked submerged in its own rendered fat until the collagen surrenders completely — pressed flat overnight and finished with a skin so crisp it shatters like a pane of amber glass.

ingredients.text: 1200 g Skin-on pork belly, whole piece
1000 g Rendered pork fat or duck fat

instructions: Mix together the salt, sugar, lightly crushed garlic, thyme, bay leaves, cracked peppercorns, and juniper berries in a small bowl. Score the skin of the pork belly in a crosshatch pattern with a sharp knife or Stanley blade — cuts 1 cm apart, through the skin and just into the fat layer but not reaching the meat. This scoring promotes even crackling later. Rub the cure mixture thoroughly over every surface of the belly, working it into the score cuts and pressing the aromatics firmly into the flesh. Place skin-side up on a wire rack set over a tray, cover loosely with cling wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8-12 hours).

Preheat the oven to 90°C (195°F). Melt the pork fat in a deep roasting dish or Dutch oven large enough to hold the belly. Place the belly skin-side down, pour in enough warm fat to completely submerge it — the fat should cover the belly by at least 1 cm. Place a piece of parchment over the surface and then the lid or tight foil. Transfer to the oven and cook for 6-8 hours. Do not rush this with higher heat. At 90°C, the collagen in the connective tissue and skin gradually converts to gelatin without ever forcing the fat to fry — the distinction between confit and poaching in fat.

Line a small baking dish or loaf tin with cling wrap, leaving an overhang on all sides. Lift the belly from the fat and place it skin-side down in the lined tin. Fold the cling wrap over the top. Place another baking sheet directly on the cling wrap and weigh it down with heavy cans — at least 2 kg of weight. Refrigerate for a minimum of 6 hours, ideally overnight. The pressing compacts the belly into a uniform slab for clean portioning and forces the fat and gelatin to redistribute evenly throughout.

Portion the pressed belly into individual serving pieces (typically 5-6 cm squares). Place a heavy oven-safe skillet — cast iron ideal — over medium-low heat. Do not add fat; the belly itself will render immediately. Place the portions skin-side down, pressing firmly with a spatula. Cook over medium-low heat for 12-18 minutes without moving — patience here is essential. The fat will slowly render and the skin will progressively crisp and turn translucent amber. It should crackle like glass underfoot when tapped with a spoon. Flip for the final 2 minutes to lightly colour the meat side.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Chashu Pork Belly
description: Rolled and tied pork belly braised in soy, mirin, sake, and sugar until lacquered, sliceable, and deeply caramel-sweet — the ramen topper that makes the bowl.

ingredients.text: 700 g Pork belly slab, skin-on, 600–800 g
3 pcs Scallions, roughly cut in 5 cm sections
30 g Fresh ginger slices, unpeeled, 5 mm

instructions: Lay the pork belly flat, skin-side down. Starting from the shorter end, roll the belly tightly into a compact cylinder, trapping as many fat-to-meat layers as possible within the roll. Tie at 2–3 cm intervals with butcher's twine, pulling each loop firmly so the roll holds its circular cross-section during cooking. A loose roll will unravel and produce uneven slices. The goal is a tight, even cylinder that will hold its shape through 3 hours of braising.

Heat a Dutch oven or heavy pot over medium-high heat with no oil — the belly's own exterior fat will render immediately. Place the roll in and sear, turning with tongs every 90 seconds, until all sides are evenly golden-brown, including the flat cut ends. This sear builds the Maillard flavor base that enriches the braising liquid and creates the lacquered exterior. Total searing time: 8–10 minutes.

Pour the sake into the hot pot and bring to a boil, scraping up the fond from the bottom. Add soy sauce, mirin, sugar, water, scallion, and ginger. Return the pork roll to the pot — the liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the roll. Bring to a very gentle simmer (90°C, barely bubbling — large bubbles will cause the roll to turn tough and the skin to contract unevenly). Cover and braise for 2.5–3 hours, turning the roll every 45 minutes so all sides spend time submerged. The liquid will reduce and deepen.

The key: refrigerate the chashu roll in its braising liquid overnight before slicing. Cold fat and gelatin give the roll structural integrity — room-temperature chashu collapses under the knife. Remove from the liquid (reserve the liquid: it becomes your tare for ramen). Remove all twine. Using a very sharp, thin-bladed knife, slice rounds 1.5–2 cm thick in a single confident stroke — no sawing. For ramen, sear each cold slice in a screaming-hot dry pan for 30 seconds per side to reheat and caramelize the glaze before placing in the bowl.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pork Bone Broth
description: A Cantonese broth of crystalline clarity and extraordinary depth, achieved by blancing bones meticulously and simmering at the precise point where convection lifts collagen but never clouds the liquid — the restraint is the technique.

ingredients.text: 50 parts Pork neck bones or knuckles (split)

instructions: Place all bones in a large pot and cover with cold water. Bring to a full boil over high heat and boil vigorously for 5 minutes. You will see large quantities of grey scum (blood proteins and impurities) accumulate on the surface. Drain the bones and rinse each one individually under cold running water, removing all grey deposits. Also scrub the pot clean. This blanching step is the single most important technique for achieving clear, clean-tasting Cantonese broth — skipping it results in murky, gamy-smelling stock.

Return the rinsed bones to the clean pot. Cover with fresh cold water and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. As it approaches simmer, skim any remaining foam from the surface. Add ginger slices, whole scallions, and Shaoxing wine. Reduce to the lowest possible simmer — the surface should show lazy ripples and occasional bubbles at the edges, but never a rolling boil. A boiling stock becomes cloudy; a simmering stock stays clear. Maintain this temperature for 3.5–4 hours.

Remove the bones with tongs and discard. Line a fine-mesh strainer with a single layer of cheesecloth. Strain the broth slowly, without pressing. Allow to cool slightly, then refrigerate uncovered for 1–2 hours until the fat solidifies on the surface as a cream-colored cap. Remove the solidified fat layer. The broth beneath should be clear, golden, and slightly gelatinous when cold. Season with salt only at the point of use, never in the base stock.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pork Carnitas
description: Michoacán's definitive taco filling — pork shoulder braised slowly in its own rendered lard with orange, cinnamon, bay, and garlic until meltingly tender, then fried in that same fat until the edges shatter into mahogany-brown crackle while the center stays irresistibly juicy.

ingredients.text: 1000 g Pork shoulder (boston butt, cut into large 6cm chunks)
1 whole Orange (1 large — halved, juice squeezed, shells reserved)
1 piece Mexican cinnamon stick (canela, one small piece)

instructions: Pat the pork chunks thoroughly dry with paper towels — surface moisture is the enemy of both rendering and browning. Toss generously with the salt until every surface carries a visible, even coating. Leave at room temperature for 20 minutes while you gather the aromatics. The salt draws the barest trace of moisture to the surface, then the surface dries: this tack helps the lard cling and the seasonings penetrate.

Nestle the pork chunks in a single layer in a heavy wide pot or Dutch oven. Add the lard, then squeeze the orange juice over the top and drop in the spent orange shell halves. Tuck in the onion, garlic, bay leaves, and cinnamon stick. Add just enough cold water to come level with the top of the meat — the water will cook off first, and when it does, the lard takes over. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook uncovered on the lowest heat, never letting it boil, for 1.5 to 2 hours. The water gradually evaporates over the first hour; the pork then quietly poaches in clear lard for the second hour until fork-tender.

Once the water is fully gone and the pork sits in clear lard, raise the heat to medium-high. If using condensed milk, drizzle it in now and stir — the trace of dairy sugar accelerates browning in the authentic Michoacán way. Cook, turning the pieces only every 3 to 4 minutes, until deeply browned and crisp at all the exposed edges and high points. The fat will bubble vigorously around the pieces. Resist the urge to stir constantly — extended contact between meat and hot metal is what builds the crust. Total frying time 8 to 15 minutes.

Transfer the carnitas to a large cutting board and let them rest 5 minutes. The resting is important — the residual heat finishes any remaining pink interior, and the crust sets rather than steaming back soft. Using two forks or your fingers, roughly pull and chop each piece into a mix of large crispy shards and tender shreds. Spoon a tablespoon of the warm reserved lard back over the top to gloss them. Taste and season with a pinch of flaky salt and a squeeze of fresh lime. Serve immediately on warm corn tortillas with white onion, cilantro, lime, and your salsa of choice.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Seared Pork Chops with Apples, Cabbage and Mustard Pan Sauce
description: Thick pork chops seared to a deep golden crust and rested until blushing and juicy, served over tart apples and cabbage softened in the pork fat and a tangy cider-mustard pan sauce glossed with butter.

ingredients.text: 1100 g Bone-in pork rib chops, about 2.5 cm (1 inch) thick
0 to taste Black pepper, freshly ground
400 g Firm, tart-sweet apples (such as Honeycrisp or Pink Lady), cored and cut into 1 cm wedges
300 g Green cabbage, cored and thinly sliced

instructions: Pat the chops dry. If there is a thick fat cap, slash it every 2–3 cm to keep the chops from curling. Season generously on all sides with about 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt total and pepper. Let stand at room temperature 10–15 minutes while you slice the apples, cabbage and shallot.

Heat the oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) heavy skillet (cast iron or stainless) over medium-high heat until it just smokes. Lay the chops in, pressing lightly so they make full contact, and sear without moving 4–5 minutes until deeply browned. Flip, reduce the heat to medium, and cook 3–5 minutes more, turning once more if needed, until an instant-read thermometer inserted near (not touching) the bone reads 140°F (60°C). Stand the chops on their fat edges for the last minute to render it. Transfer to a plate and rest 5 minutes; carryover heat brings them to the USDA-safe 145°F (63°C).

Pour off all but about 1 tbsp fat from the skillet. Over medium-high heat, add the apple wedges in a single layer and cook 2 minutes per side until caramelized at the edges. Add the shallot, cabbage and a pinch of salt and cook, tossing, 4–5 minutes until the cabbage is wilted and browned in spots but still has some bite.

Pour in the cider and stock, add the thyme sprigs, and scrape up the browned bits. Boil 4–5 minutes until reduced by about half. Reduce the heat to low, stir in the mustard and the resting juices from the chops, then swirl in the cold butter a piece at a time until glossy. Stir in the cider vinegar, discard the thyme stems, and season. Return the chops to the pan for 30 seconds to warm, spooning sauce over them, and serve over the apples and cabbage.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Wiener Schnitzel
description: Pork loin pounded thin as a page, encased in three precise coats of flour, egg, and breadcrumb, then fried in a deep wave of clarified butter until the crust billows away from the meat in a golden, gossamer shell that crackles on the first cut.

ingredients.text: 3 large Eggs, lightly beaten with a fork (not whisked)
150 g Fine, dry white breadcrumbs (not panko)

instructions: Place a cutlet between two sheets of plastic wrap or inside a zip-lock bag. Using a meat mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan, pound the meat to an even 3mm thickness with firm, outward strokes — starting from the center and sweeping toward the edges to stretch rather than tear the meat. A properly pounded schnitzel should be uniformly thin across its entire surface, with no thick center or torn holes. Season both sides with salt and white pepper, then let rest for 5 minutes at room temperature so the salt begins to draw moisture to the surface.

Set up three separate wide dishes: flour in the first, beaten eggs in the second, breadcrumbs in the third. Working one cutlet at a time: first dredge in flour, pressing to adhere and shaking off every grain of excess — you want a ghostly, light dusting, not a thick coat. Dip immediately into the egg, allowing the excess to drip off for 3 seconds. Lay in the breadcrumbs and, critically, do NOT press the crumbs into the meat — scatter them over the top, and shake the tray to set them. This loose, unpressed crumb is what allows the crust to soufflé away from the meat in the fat, creating the billowing effect.

Pour clarified butter into a wide pan to a depth of 8–10mm. Heat to 160–170°C — test with a breadcrumb: it should sizzle immediately and turn golden in 30 seconds. Slide in the breaded cutlet. Immediately begin spooning hot butter over the top of the cutlet in a continuous stream while gently moving the pan to keep the fat agitated. This constant basting and movement is how the crust inflates. Fry 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden-amber. Never crowd the pan — fry one cutlet at a time if necessary. Remove to a wire rack (never paper) to drain.

Transfer immediately to warmed plates — schnitzel waits for no one and softens within minutes. Place one lemon wedge alongside, not squeezed over. Serve with potato salad, parsley potatoes, or lingonberry jam. The lemon is squeezed at the table by the diner, and only directly over their portion. Schnitzel eaten 10 minutes after frying is a different, lesser dish — time it to the moment the plates hit the table.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pan-Seared Roasted Pork Tenderloin
description: The most forgiving of the lean cuts — seared in a searing hot pan until mahogany on all sides, finished in a hot oven, then rested until the juices redistribute into a blush-pink, impossibly tender centre.

ingredients.text: 20 g Neutral high-smoke-point oil (avocado or grapeseed)
10 g Fresh thyme sprigs and rosemary

instructions: Remove the silver skin: slide the tip of a thin knife under the silver membrane and angle the blade slightly upward, sawing forward while pulling the skin taut with your other hand. It should come off in one or two strips. Pat the tenderloin completely dry. Combine salt, pepper, smoked paprika, and garlic powder and rub evenly over every surface. Rest uncovered at room temperature for 20 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Heat an oven-safe skillet (cast iron preferred) over high heat for 3 minutes until screaming hot. Add the oil — it should shimmer immediately. Sear the tenderloin for 90 seconds per face, rotating through all four broad faces until every surface is mahogany brown. Use tongs and apply firm downward pressure to maximise contact.

Add the butter, thyme, rosemary, and crushed garlic to the pan. Transfer the skillet to the preheated oven. Roast for 10–12 minutes, basting once halfway through by tipping the pan and spooning the melted herb butter over the tenderloin. Remove when an instant-read thermometer reads 60 C (140 F) at the thickest point — carry-over cooking will bring it to 63 C (145 F).

Transfer the tenderloin to a warm cutting board and tent loosely with foil. Rest for exactly 8 minutes. Do not cut earlier — the temperature will rise 3 degrees and the juices need time to redistribute from the contracted muscle fibres back into the interior.

Using a sharp slicing knife, cut the tenderloin into medallions 1.5–2 cm thick, slicing on a slight diagonal for a broader face. Each slice should reveal a uniform pale-rose interior surrounded by the dark seared crust. Spoon the resting juices and any remaining herb butter over the slices. Serve immediately.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pasteis de Nata
description: The custard tarts of Lisbon: blistered, charred, and caramelised in a furiously hot oven until the surface is a topographic map of dark amber leopard-spots above a trembling, still-barely-set custard of egg yolks, cream, and vanilla, all cradled in a shatteringly thin, flaky puff pastry shell that crumbles into golden debris at the first bite. Dusted with cinnamon, eaten standing up at a marble counter with a bica of espresso.

ingredients.text: 320 g All-butter puff pastry (ready-rolled or block)
5 g Ground cinnamon and icing sugar, to finish

instructions: Combine sugar, water, cinnamon stick, lemon peel, and vanilla bean in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil without stirring and simmer for 3 minutes at 107 C (a light syrup). Remove from heat and steep for 10 minutes to allow the aromatics to infuse deeply. Discard the cinnamon, lemon peel, and vanilla pod — reserve the vanilla seeds if you scraped them in. Cool to room temperature.

Whisk together egg yolks and cornflour in a bowl until smooth. In a saucepan, combine milk, cream, and the cooled syrup. Bring to just below a simmer (small bubbles at the edge). Slowly pour the hot milk over the yolk mixture, whisking constantly. Return the whole mixture to the saucepan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it just begins to thicken to a pourable custard — remove immediately. Strain through a fine sieve.
