description: Bright, tangy tomatillos charred under the broiler with serrano chiles and white onion, then blended raw into a salsa that tastes like green fire — acidic, herbaceous, and dangerously drinkable.

ingredients.text: 1 parts Fresh cilantro, stems and leaves

instructions: Set the oven to broil on high and position a rack 6 inches from the element. Spread the tomatillos (halved if very large), serrano chiles, onion quarters, and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined baking sheet in a single layer. Broil for 5–6 minutes until the tops are spotted black and blistered. Flip everything with tongs and broil for another 3–4 minutes. The tomatillos should be collapsing and oozing their sticky green juice.

Peel the roasted garlic and transfer all roasted vegetables and their accumulated juices into a blender. Add the cilantro, salt, and lime juice. Pulse 4–5 times for a rough texture, or blend for 30–45 seconds for a smoother sauce. Do not over-blend — some texture is traditional and desirable. Taste immediately and adjust salt and lime.

Taste the salsa critically. Add salt in small increments (a pinch at a time), stirring and tasting between each addition, until the tomatillo flavor pops and the salsa tastes bright rather than dull. A properly salted salsa verde should make you immediately want another taste. Add more lime juice if the acidity has faded. Let rest at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving to allow the flavors to settle.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Salt and Pepper Shrimp
description: Cantonese wok-fried whole shell-on shrimp that arrive at the table crackling and fragrant — the shells fried to a shattering crunch you eat whole, the flesh beneath barely cooked and sweet, buried under a confetti of garlic, scallion, and white pepper.

ingredients.text: 600 g Large shell-on, head-on shrimp (prawns), deveined
15 g Fresh red chillies, thinly sliced (optional but traditional)

instructions: Pat the shrimp completely dry with kitchen paper — any surface moisture will cause the oil to spit violently and prevent the shell from crisping. Toss in the cornstarch to coat very lightly — just enough for a barely-there dusting, not a thick batter. Mix in half the salt, white pepper, and the five-spice.

Heat the oil in a wok over the highest possible heat to 190 C (375 F). Fry the shrimp in batches — 8–10 at a time — for exactly 60–75 seconds. The shells will sizzle aggressively and turn bright orange-red. Remove with a spider and drain on a rack. Do not over-fry — the shrimp continue cooking from residual heat.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving about 1 tablespoon in the wok. Return to high heat. Add the garlic, most of the spring onion, and sliced chilli. Stir-fry for 30 seconds until the garlic is golden and fragrant. Add the fried shrimp back to the wok and toss furiously for 30 seconds to coat with the aromatic mixture. Season with remaining salt and white pepper. Drizzle with sesame oil and toss once more. Serve immediately, garnished with remaining spring onion.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Salt and Pepper Squid
description: Rings and tentacles tossed in spiced potato starch and flash-fried until the coating shatters at first bite — finished in the wok with garlic, chili, and spring onion that perfume the crust without softening it.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Fresh squid tubes and tentacles, cleaned
0.5 parts Sichuan peppercorns, toasted and ground
200 parts Neutral oil for deep-frying (peanut or sunflower)
5 parts Long red chili and green chili, thinly sliced
8 parts Spring onions (scallions), cut into 3cm lengths

instructions: Open the squid tubes and score the inside surface in a crosshatch pattern at 5mm intervals — this gives the starch something to grip and helps the squid curl dramatically in the oil. Cut into 4cm pieces. Keep tentacles whole. Dry everything very thoroughly with paper towels.

Combine potato starch, salt, white pepper, and Sichuan pepper in a bowl. Add the dried squid and toss to coat completely. Shake off excess in a sieve — you want a thin, even coating that barely obscures the squid, not a heavy cloak.

Heat oil to 200 C (390 F) in a wok or deep pan — higher than most frying, because squid is wet. Fry in small batches for exactly 90 seconds. The squid will curl and the coating will set. Do not stir for the first 30 seconds so the crust can form. Remove to a rack — immediately.

Pour off most of the frying oil, leaving a thin slick. Over high flame, add garlic, chili, and spring onion. Stir-fry for 20–30 seconds until fragrant and the garlic is barely golden. Add the fried squid back and toss furiously for 15 seconds — just enough to perfume the crust without steaming it soft.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Salt-Baked Branzino
description: A whole branzino buried in a thick egg-white salt crust and baked — the mineral shell seals in steam and moisture, cooking the fish impossibly gently within its own aromatics.

ingredients.text: 600 g Whole branzino (European sea bass), gutted and scaled
1 lemon Lemon, thinly sliced into rounds
30 ml Extra-virgin olive oil, for serving

instructions: Preheat the oven to 190°C (375°F). In a large bowl, combine the coarse sea salt with the egg whites. Mix firmly with your hands until every grain of salt is coated and the mixture resembles wet sand — it should clump when squeezed and hold an impression of your fist. This is the mortar that will seal the fish. If it crumbles and won't hold a shape, add a fourth egg white.

Check the fish cavity is clean and dry. Season the interior lightly with a pinch of salt. Lay the lemon rounds in a shingle pattern along the cavity floor. Pack the fennel fronds, thyme, and parsley in on top of the lemon — the cavity should be visibly full. The herbs will steam inside the crust and perfume the flesh from the inside out without penetrating it externally at all.

Spread a third of the salt mixture onto a rimmed baking sheet in the exact shape and size of the fish, about 1.5 cm thick. Lay the stuffed branzino on top. Pack the remaining salt mixture firmly over the top and sides of the fish, pressing and smoothing it into a solid, even casing at least 1.5 cm thick at every point. Pay special attention to the head and tail — cracks there will let steam escape and dry the flesh. The fish should be completely invisible under the crust. Smooth the surface with wet palms.

Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 25–30 minutes for a 600g fish. The timing scales with fish weight: add 5 minutes per additional 200g. The crust will harden to a rigid, chalky shell and may develop faint ivory-to-beige colouring on top. It will not brown dramatically — the visual cues here are all about the crust hardening. A probe thermometer inserted through the crust should read 58–60°C at the thickest part of the fish. If you do not have a probe, use the timing as your guide.

Bring the baking sheet to the table. Using the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, crack the crust firmly along the spine of the fish. It will fracture in large shards — peel these away and discard. Carefully lift the top fillet free, then remove the spine in one piece. The bottom fillet sits on the lower salt bed — slide a spatula underneath to lift it clean. Serve the fillets on warmed plates with a generous pour of extra-virgin olive oil and the lemon slices from inside the cavity.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Salt-Baked Sea Bass
description: A whole sea bass encased in an egg-white-bound salt crust and baked until the crust sets hard as stone — inside, the fish has steamed in its own juices and the heat of the sealed crust, emerging perfectly cooked, sweet-fleshed, and explosively fragrant with ginger and scallion.

ingredients.text: 700 g Whole sea bass, cleaned and scaled (about 700g)
1500 g Coarse sea salt (not fine — it must be granular)
30 g Fresh ginger, peeled, sliced into coins
4 ea Scallions (spring onions), tied in a loose knot

instructions: Preheat the oven to 200°C (390°F) with a rack in the centre position. Pat the sea bass completely dry — inside the cavity and all over the outside — with multiple changes of paper towels. Dryness is critical: any moisture on the fish surface will steam inside the salt crust rather than allowing the fish to cook in the dry residual heat of the crust. Inspect the fish for any remaining scales by running a finger from tail to head — any that remain will prevent the crust from sealing properly and can embed in the fish.

Lay the ginger slices in an overlapping layer along the length of the cavity floor. Place the knotted scallions on top of the ginger, and tuck the cilantro sprigs around them. Drizzle the Shaoxing wine into the cavity — it will perfume the fish as it steams. Close the cavity by pressing the sides of the fish together gently. The aromatics inside do not season the flesh directly; they create a fragrant steam environment that perfumes the fish from within.

Mix the coarse sea salt and lightly beaten egg whites together with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand that holds its shape when squeezed — it should clump, not crumble. Spread a 1.5cm bed of the salt mixture on a baking tray or oven-proof dish. Lay the stuffed fish on the bed. Pack the remaining salt mixture over and around the entire fish, pressing firmly to build a uniform crust 2cm thick on all sides. Seal any gaps, especially around the tail and head. Bake at 200°C for 25–30 minutes (about 20 minutes per 500g of fish weight, plus 5 minutes for the crust).

At the table, present the salt-crusted dish. Using the back of a heavy spoon or small hammer, crack the crust along the spine with a few firm blows. Lift off the large pieces of crust — the fish skin will often come away with the top crust, revealing bright, pearlescent white flesh beneath. Brush away any salt granules clinging to the flesh with a pastry brush. The fish will not taste salty — the salt crust seasons it only from the outside through the skin, not into the flesh.

Working quickly so the fish does not cool, drizzle the soy sauce evenly over the exposed flesh, followed by the toasted sesame oil — the sesame oil should sizzle faintly as it hits the hot fish. Serve directly from the dish with steamed white jasmine rice and a simple stir-fried green vegetable. Use a tablespoon to scoop portions of the flesh off the spine, keeping the segments as large and intact as possible — this fish deserves to be eaten in generous, moist chunks, not shredded.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Brandade de Morue
description: Provençal salt cod pounded or blended with olive oil and warm milk until it becomes a smooth, ivory emulsion — dense, luxurious, faintly fishy in the best possible way. Spread on crostini or gratinéed in a baking dish, it is the taste of the Languedoc coast in winter.

ingredients.text: 150 ml Extra-virgin olive oil, gently warmed
100 ml Whole milk, warmed to hand temperature

instructions: Place the salt cod skin-side up in a large bowl or deep baking dish and cover with cold water. Refrigerate for 24 hours, changing the water at least 3 times — every 6–8 hours is ideal. The water will turn white and cloudy each time, carrying away the curing salt. After the final soak, taste a thin flake from the thickest part: it should taste pleasantly salty, like a well-seasoned fish, not briny or harsh. If it is still harsh, soak 2 more hours.

Place the desalted cod in a wide pan and cover with fresh cold water. Add the thyme. Bring slowly to a bare simmer — tiny bubbles rising at the edges, the water trembling but not boiling. Poach for 10–12 minutes. Do not boil: boiling at this stage firms the protein into a tough, rubbery slab and breaks the fine flakes. The cod is done when it flakes easily along its natural seams when prodded with a fork. Lift out, discard the poaching water, and let it cool enough to handle.

Remove all skin and bones from the cod — run your fingers carefully through the flakes to find every pin bone. Place the cod and raw garlic in a mortar and pound to a paste, or pulse in a food processor. The goal is to break the fish down into a fine, cohesive mass that will absorb the oil and milk. Do not process to a completely smooth paste yet — a slightly grainy, textured base is correct at this stage. The garlic should be fully incorporated and invisible.

With the cod paste in the mortar or a bowl set over gentle heat (or in a stand mixer with paddle), begin adding the warm olive oil in a thin, slow stream, working it in constantly — exactly like making a mayonnaise. When half the oil is incorporated, add a tablespoon of warm milk. Alternate oil and milk until both are fully incorporated. The brandade will transform from a dense paste to a smooth, fluffy, ivory-white emulsion that is light enough to scoop but rich enough to mound. Season with white pepper and lemon juice. Taste: it should be salty, rich, faintly fishy, and deeply satisfying.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Salt-Crusted Whole Fish
description: A whole fish sealed inside two kilos of egg-white-bound salt and baked until the crust rings like plaster — cracked at the table with a mallet, releasing a cloud of herbed steam and the most perfectly seasoned, juicy fish imaginable.

ingredients.text: 700 g Whole sea bass or sea bream (600-800 g), gutted and scaled
30 ml Extra-virgin olive oil, for serving

instructions: Whisk egg whites to a light foam — no stiff peaks, just broken and fluid. Pour over coarse salt and work with your hands until the mixture resembles wet sand. It should clump when squeezed and hold the shape of your fist. If it won't clump, add water a tablespoon at a time.

Preheat oven to 220 C (425 F). Spread a 1.5 cm layer of salt paste on a baking sheet to form the bed. Stuff the fish cavity with thyme, lemon rounds, and garlic. Lay the fish on the salt bed. Pack remaining salt paste firmly over the entire fish, including head and tail, sealing all seams. Press to compact.

Roast for 25-30 minutes for a 700 g fish. The crust will set and begin to show faint golden spots on its highest points. An instant-read thermometer inserted through the crust into the thickest part of the fish should read 55-60 C (130-140 F). The fish steams inside its own armor.

At the table, crack the crust with the back of a heavy spoon or a small mallet, following the line of the fish's spine. Lift away the top half of the crust in large pieces — it comes off in satisfying slabs. Brush away any salt crystals with a pastry brush. Peel back the skin and serve the fillets with olive oil and lemon wedges. The flesh will be luminous, juicy, and perfectly seasoned.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Saltimbocca alla Romana
description: Veal escalopes blanketed with prosciutto and sage, sautéed in butter until the ham crackles and the white wine pan sauce clings to every fold.

ingredients.text: 300 g Veal escalopes (noce or fesa), 150 g each
8 pcs Fresh sage leaves (2–3 per escalope)
80 ml Dry white wine (Frascati or Pinot Grigio)

instructions: Place each veal escalope between two sheets of plastic wrap. Using the flat face of a meat mallet or the bottom of a heavy pan, pound with firm, even strokes from the center outward — not vertical blows that tear the meat, but angled slides that stretch the fibers. Target 5–6 mm thickness, roughly even across the whole escalope. Season lightly with white pepper only — the prosciutto will provide all the salt needed.

Lay 2–3 sage leaves flat on the top (smooth) side of each escalope. Drape one or two slices of prosciutto over to cover the sage and the entire escalope surface — the ham must extend slightly beyond the meat edges. Secure with one or two wooden toothpicks pierced at an angle through ham, sage, and meat. Season the underside (veal side) very lightly with salt only. Dust the veal side in flour and pat off all excess — you want a gossamer coating, not a thick crust.

Heat a large stainless or carbon steel pan over medium-high heat. Add butter and let it foam and subside — when the first wisps of color appear in the butter, it is ready. Place escalopes prosciutto-side down. Press them flat with a spatula for the first 10 seconds to ensure full contact. Cook prosciutto-side for 2–3 minutes until the ham crackles and has rendered its fat into the butter. Flip and cook the veal side for just 60–90 seconds — veal is lean and overcooks in moments.

Remove the escalopes to a warm plate. Over high heat, pour the wine into the still-hot pan and immediately scrape up the browned bits from the base — these are the flavor. Let the wine reduce by half, about 90 seconds of vigorous bubbling. Remove from heat, add a cold knob of butter, and swirl constantly until the sauce becomes glossy and emulsified. Pour over the escalopes immediately. The dish is best eaten within 3 minutes of plating.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sambal Oelek
description: Indonesia's foundational raw chili paste — fresh red chilies, salt, and a splash of vinegar pounded in a mortar into a coarse, fiery paste whose pure chili heat and fruity freshness serve as the base of countless Indonesian dishes and the perfect condiment for everything else.

ingredients.text: 200 g Fresh red Fresno or Holland chilies (medium heat), stems removed
20 g Fresh red bird's-eye chilies (cabe rawit), for heat boost (optional)
15 ml White vinegar or distilled cane vinegar

instructions: Roughly chop the Fresno chilies into large pieces — halve them lengthwise and cut into thirds. If you prefer a milder sambal, scrape out the seeds and white ribs with a spoon; for full heat, leave them in. If using bird's-eye chilies, leave them whole or halve them. Peel the garlic cloves. This rough prep is all that is needed before the mortar does its work — do not fine-mince. Keep seeds and juice from the cutting board; they are flavour.

Transfer the chopped chilies and garlic to a large granite or stone mortar. Add the salt — salt acts as an abrasive grit that helps break down the fibers faster. Pound with firm, deliberate downward strokes: the pestle should thud, not grind. Begin with harder downward blows to break down the larger pieces, then shift to a rotating, pressing grind for the final paste. The goal is a coarse, rustic paste with visible flecks of chili skin and seeds — not a smooth purée. Sambal oelek's character is its roughness; a blender makes it too uniform and drives off the fresh aroma. Pound for 3–4 minutes total.

Pour the vinegar over the pounded paste and stir to combine. Taste carefully — it should be fiercely hot, brightly acidic, and cleanly salty, with the fresh, fruity aroma of raw chili dominant. Adjust: more salt for presence, more vinegar for brightness and preservation, more garlic pounded in for depth. Transfer to a clean glass jar and press the surface down to eliminate air pockets. Refrigerate. The sambal keeps for up to 2 weeks refrigerated — the vinegar and salt are natural preservatives. The colour will darken slightly from bright scarlet to a deeper red over the first 24 hours as it rests.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sambar
description: A sour, spiced toor dal broth studded with vegetables and built on a tamarind base — simultaneously soup, sauce, and condiment, poured over rice or alongside idli and dosa. The sambar powder is the soul: make your own if you can.

ingredients.text: 80 parts Mixed vegetables (drumstick, eggplant, pearl onions, tomato)
2 parts Dried red chilies (Byadagi or similar)

instructions: Rinse toor dal until water runs clear. Cook in a pressure cooker with water for 3 whistles, or simmer in a covered pot for 30–35 minutes until completely soft. Whisk or mash the cooked dal into a smooth, creamy paste — this will be the body of the sambar.

Combine the mashed dal with tamarind paste, sambar powder, salt, and vegetables in a wide pot. Add enough water to make a thin broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 15–20 minutes until vegetables are completely tender and the broth has unified into a cohesive, sour-spiced gravy.

In a small pan, heat oil over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Add mustard seeds and cover with a lid — they will pop violently within 10 seconds. Uncover, add curry leaves (stand back — they will splatter) and dried red chilies. Stir for 15 seconds, then pour the entire tadka into the sambar.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Samosa Filling
description: Fluffy mashed potato and sweet green peas coarsely folded with a crackling bloom of cumin, coriander seed, ginger, and green chili — the filling that has made samosas irresistible for centuries, fragrant and slightly drier than you expect so it holds its shape inside the crisp pastry shell without steaming it soft. Every bite releases warm spiced starch and a bright herbal finish.

ingredients.text: 500 g Waxy potatoes (Yukon Gold or similar), boiled whole and peeled
100 g Green peas (fresh shelled or frozen, thawed)
1 tsp Coriander seeds, lightly crushed in a mortar
2 whole Green chilies (serrano or Thai), finely minced
3 tbsp Fresh cilantro leaves and tender stems, finely chopped

instructions: Cover the whole, unpeeled potatoes with cold water in a pot. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook until a thin knife slides through the center with zero resistance — about 20–25 minutes depending on size. Do not rush with high heat or the skins will split and the potatoes will absorb too much water. Drain and immediately peel while hot — the skins slip off easily and the potato flesh sheds moisture better when peeled warm. Spread the peeled potatoes on a tray and leave them uncovered for 5 minutes to steam-dry. Then roughly crush them with a fork or your hands into a mix of small chunks and larger broken pieces. Do not mash smooth — the filling needs texture. Some pieces of potato 1–2 cm across are desirable.

Heat the oil or ghee in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the cumin seeds and crushed coriander seeds together — they should sizzle immediately and begin crackling. Let them bloom for about 30–40 seconds until the cumin turns a deep chestnut brown. Do not stop here — add the minced ginger and green chili and stir for 1 minute until the raw ginger smell softens to a sweet, fragrant note. Add the ground coriander, amchur, garam masala, and turmeric. Stir constantly for 60 seconds, scraping the bottom — the ground spices will form a thick, fragrant paste in the fat. This step, called the tadka or bhuna, is critical: the oil carries fat-soluble spice compounds directly into the potato and peas at the moment of contact. If your spice paste smells warm and rounded, with no raw edge, it is ready.

Add the frozen or fresh peas directly to the spiced fat in the pan. Stir and cook for 2 minutes — the peas will warm through and absorb the spiced oil. Add the crushed potatoes all at once and fold everything together using a wide spatula or wooden spoon, working from the bottom of the pan and turning the mixture over itself. You want to evenly coat every piece of potato and pea in the spice blend without turning the mixture into a smooth mash — the filling should retain texture, with visible pieces of potato and peas throughout. Season with salt and stir. Off the heat, fold in the fresh cilantro. Taste: the filling should be intensely flavored — boldly salty, bright with amchur's sour note, and warmly spiced throughout. It needs to be seasoned aggressively because the pastry shell will dilute the intensity. Allow the filling to cool completely before enclosing in pastry — warm filling will steam the pastry and make it soggy.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Samosa with Aloo Filling
description: Crisp, blistered pastry pyramids encasing spiced potato and pea filling seasoned with dried mango powder and garam masala — shatteringly crunchy on the outside with a filling that is simultaneously soft, sharp, and warming. A cup of chai and a plate of these is the perfect North Indian tea-time.

ingredients.text: 50 g Ghee or vegetable shortening (for pastry)
400 g Waxy potatoes (boiled, cooled, and roughly mashed)
10 g Fine sea salt (for both pastry and filling)
800 g Neutral oil for deep frying (sunflower or vegetable)

instructions: Combine flour and half the salt in a bowl. Rub the ghee or shortening into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs and no large fat lumps remain — this is the critical step for a flaky, layered crust. Drizzle in ice-cold water a tablespoon at a time, mixing with a fork after each addition, until the dough just comes together without being sticky. It should feel firmer than a bread dough — this tight, stiff dough is what gives samosas their snap. Knead very briefly — 1 minute only — then wrap tightly and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the frying oil in a skillet over medium heat. Bloom the cumin seeds for 30 seconds until they crackle and darken. Add the green chili and ginger, fry for 1 minute. Add the mashed potatoes and peas and fold gently to combine, trying to keep some potato texture — do not turn it into baby food. Add amchur, garam masala, and the remaining salt. Mix and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the filling is fragrant and slightly dry. Taste: it should be assertively seasoned, sour from the amchur, and warming with spice. The filling must be fully cool before wrapping — warm filling creates steam inside the samosa and makes the pastry soggy.

Divide the rested dough into 10 to 12 equal balls. Roll each ball on a lightly floured surface into an oval roughly 15 cm × 8 cm, 2–3 mm thick — thinner than you think you need. Cut each oval in half across the long axis, giving two D-shaped pieces. Fold each D into a cone: moisten one straight edge with water, overlap the two straight edges by 5 mm, and press firmly to seal. Fill the cone two-thirds full with cooled filling — do not overfill. Moisten the open top edge with water and press firmly to seal into a triangle. Press each seam between your fingers and then press lightly against the work surface to create the flat, pyramid shape. Set on a lightly oiled tray. The sealed edges must be completely watertight — test by gently squeezing each samosa over the sink.

Heat the frying oil in a deep, heavy pot to 160°C (325°F) — lower than you expect. Samosas must fry slowly to develop the characteristic blistered crust: high heat seals the outside before the inside cooks through and the pastry has no time to develop its flaky layers. Lower 3 to 4 samosas at a time into the oil and fry, turning every 2 minutes, for 10 to 12 minutes total until they are an even deep amber-gold on all faces. Raise the temperature to 175°C (350°F) for the final 2 minutes to crisp the exterior. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain upright in a rack or colander, not lying flat — this preserves the crust on all sides.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Potato & Pea Samosas
description: A shattering pastry shell that gives way to a warmly spiced interior of cumin-fragrant potato and bright peas — the hallmark is the dough made with minimal water for maximum flakiness, and the filling cooled completely so the shell never steams from within.

ingredients.text: 20 parts Vegetable shortening or ghee (for rubbing into flour)
80 parts Russet potatoes, boiled and roughly mashed
20 parts Green peas (fresh or frozen, thawed)
8 parts Filling spice blend (cumin seeds, coriander, amchur, garam masala, green chili, ginger)

instructions: Combine flour, fat, salt, and 1 tsp ajwain (carom seeds) if available. Rub the fat into the flour with your fingertips for 3–4 minutes until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs with no loose flour remaining — this is the critical step for flakiness. Add ice-cold water 1 tbsp at a time (about 6–8 tbsp total) until the dough just comes together. It should be firm, stiff, and not sticky. Knead for 2 minutes, then rest covered for 20 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add cumin seeds and let them splutter 10 seconds. Add green chili and fresh ginger, cook 30 seconds. Add roughly mashed potato and peas, then all remaining ground spices. Cook for 3–4 minutes, folding rather than stirring to keep some potato texture. Add amchur (dried mango powder) or lemon juice for tartness and salt to taste. Spread on a plate and cool completely before using.

Divide the rested dough into equal portions and roll each into a thin oval about 18–20cm long and 10cm wide. Cut in half to make two semicircles. Form a cone by folding the straight edge over and sealing with a little water. Fill the cone with 2 tbsp of filling — do not overfill. Pinch the open edge closed firmly, pressing the seam flat. The sealed edge must be completely airtight or the samosa will burst during frying.

Heat oil to 160–170°C (325°F) — lower than standard frying temperature. Slide samosas in gently, 3–4 at a time. Fry slowly for 12–15 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden. The low temperature slowly renders and crisps the pastry all the way through without burning the exterior before the interior heats. Drain on a wire rack, not paper towels — steam must escape from all sides to keep the crust crisp.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Satay Marinade and Peanut Sauce
description: Turmeric-golden skewers of chicken or beef marinated in lemongrass, coriander, and coconut milk, grilled over charcoal until caramel-charred at the tips — served with a peanut-coconut sauce so rich and complex it could be eaten with a spoon. A street-food cornerstone from Penang to Jakarta.

ingredients.text: 1 parts Lemongrass stalk, white part, finely grated or minced
1 parts Palm sugar or light brown sugar
4 parts Roasted peanuts, skins removed, finely ground or crushed
3 parts Coconut milk, additional (for peanut sauce)
1 parts Tamarind water (1 tbsp tamarind paste dissolved in 3 tbsp water)
0.5 parts Fish sauce or soy sauce
0.5 parts Dried chili flakes or sambal oelek

instructions: Combine the turmeric, coriander, cumin, grated lemongrass, and palm sugar in a bowl. Pour in the coconut milk and whisk until the spices are evenly dispersed and the sugar is dissolved. The marinade should be a warm golden-yellow — the turmeric stains everything it touches, so use a non-reactive bowl and be careful of clothing. Taste: it should be fragrant with warm spice, mildly sweet, and richly coconutty. This is used to marinate 500 g of thinly sliced chicken, beef, or tofu for at least 1 hour (overnight in the refrigerator is ideal). Thread onto pre-soaked bamboo skewers before grilling.

Combine the ground peanuts, coconut milk, tamarind water, fish sauce, and chili flakes in a small saucepan. Stir to combine before placing over medium-low heat. Cook, stirring frequently, for 8–10 minutes until the sauce thickens noticeably and the fat begins to separate slightly at the edges of the pan — a ring of golden coconut oil appearing around the peanut sauce is a good sign. The sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon but still pourable. If it seizes up too thick, add a splash of water. Taste: sweet-salty-sour-spicy in balance, with a deep, toasty peanut character. The sauce should be served warm.

Thread the marinated meat onto soaked bamboo skewers, 3–4 thin slices per skewer, keeping the meat flat so it makes good contact with the grill. Grill over high heat (charcoal is traditional and dramatically superior) for 2–3 minutes per side. The exterior should char at the tips and edges — caramel-dark, slightly blackened — while the interior remains just cooked through. Baste with remaining marinade during the first turn. The turmeric in the marinade will darken quickly and smell of toasted spice. Watch carefully: thin satay slices overcook in seconds.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Satay Peanut Sauce
description: A sauce of roasted peanuts dissolved into coconut milk with red curry paste and palm sugar — thick enough to coat a skewer and leave a trembling drop at the tip, with a warmth that builds slowly from the red curry's dried chilies rather than hitting all at once. This is the sauce that makes satay worth the wait.

ingredients.text: 120 g Roasted peanut butter, natural (no added sugar)
30 g Thai red curry paste (store-bought or homemade)
30 g Roasted peanuts, roughly crushed, for topping
2 g Dried chili flakes, for topping (optional)

instructions: Pour the coconut milk into a small saucepan over medium heat. When it begins to steam and show the first signs of simmering at the edges, add the red curry paste. Whisk constantly to break up the paste and disperse it evenly through the coconut milk. Continue to cook over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring regularly. You are not just dissolving the paste — you are cooking out the raw edge of its dried chilies and spices, blooming them in the coconut fat the way you would bloom spices in oil. The mixture will shift from bright orange-red (raw paste) to a deeper, richer terracotta-orange as the paste cooks. The aroma will change from sharp and raw to roasted and complex. This bloom step is what separates a cooked satay sauce from a merely mixed one.

Add the peanut butter to the simmering curry coconut mixture. Whisk vigorously to incorporate — the peanut butter will resist at first, then suddenly combine into a thick, uniform sauce. Add the palm sugar, tamarind paste, fish sauce, and salt. Stir constantly over medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the sugar dissolves and all elements are fully integrated. The sauce will thicken as it heats — adjust consistency with small additions of warm water if it becomes too thick to pour easily. The finished sauce should flow off a spoon in a heavy, slow ribbon. Taste and balance: if too thick and sweet, add a teaspoon more tamarind; if too sharp, add a pinch more palm sugar; if flat, a few more drops of fish sauce. The balance to aim for is rich-sweet-slightly-sour-deeply-savory.

Transfer the warm peanut sauce to a serving bowl or pour it into a small clay pot for table presentation. Scatter the roughly crushed roasted peanuts over the surface — they should be chunky enough to provide texture but not so large they fall off a dipped item. Add a small pinch of dried chili flakes for color and a visual hint of heat. Serve warm alongside grilled chicken or pork satay skewers, fresh cucumber rounds, and the traditional Thai ajad (pickled cucumber relish). The sauce can be made up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated — it will thicken on cooling but returns to the correct consistency when gently reheated with a splash of water or coconut milk.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Satay Sauce
description: Indonesia's magnificent peanut sauce — not the thin, sweet shortcut, but the real thing: dry-roasted peanuts blended into a fragrant lemongrass-galangal-chile paste, simmered with coconut milk, and balanced with palm sugar, tamarind, and fish sauce into something thick, glossy, and savagely complex.

ingredients.text: 2 parts Shallots, peeled and roughly chopped
1 parts Lemongrass stalks (white and pale-green part only), sliced
0.5 parts Galangal (fresh or frozen), peeled and roughly chopped
0.3 parts Kaffir lime leaves, torn (ribs removed)
1 parts Dried red chiles (stemmed and seeded), or 1 tsp sambal oelek
1 parts Palm sugar or packed brown sugar
0.5 parts Tamarind paste (from a block, dissolved in warm water)

instructions: Combine the shallots, garlic, lemongrass, galangal, and dried chiles in a blender or food processor. Add a tablespoon of water and blend until you have a rough paste, scraping down the sides as needed. The lemongrass is fibrous and the galangal is woody — blend for at least 2 minutes at high speed, pausing to scrape the sides, until the paste is as smooth as the blender will allow. Some texture is acceptable and even desirable, but the lemongrass in particular must be finely broken down or it will remain fibrous and unpleasant in the finished sauce. A high-powered blender will give a smoother result; a food processor gives a rougher but excellent paste.

Heat 2 tablespoons of neutral oil or coconut oil in a wok or wide saucepan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the blended aromatics paste and the torn kaffir lime leaves and fry, stirring constantly, until the raw smell of garlic and shallot has cooked out and the paste is fragrant, drier, and deeper in color — 5-8 minutes. Crucially, cook until you can see the oil beginning to separate and collect at the edges of the paste — this is called pecah minyak (oil breaking) in Indonesian and Malay cooking, and it signals that the water in the aromatics has fully evaporated and the paste is truly fried, not merely stewed. This step transforms the raw sharp aromatics into a mellow, complex base.

If using whole roasted peanuts, pulse them in a food processor to a rough, crumbly texture — about the size of coarse breadcrumbs, not a paste. Add the ground peanuts to the fried aromatics paste and stir to coat them in the fragrant oil. Pour in the coconut milk and water, stirring to combine everything into a thick, rough soup. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring frequently, and cook for 10-12 minutes until the sauce is thick, glossy, and the peanuts have absorbed the coconut milk and swelled slightly. The sauce should coat a spoon in a heavy, flowing layer — much thicker than pourable cream.

Add the palm sugar, fish sauce, tamarind paste, and lime juice to the simmering sauce. Stir to dissolve the palm sugar completely and simmer 2-3 minutes more to integrate everything. Now taste carefully and balance the sauce along four axes: savory-salty (fish sauce), sweet (palm sugar), sour-tamarind (tamarind and lime), and heat (chile). The sauce should be rich and deeply savory first, with the sweetness present but not candy-like, the sourness brightening rather than dominating, and the chile an undercurrent of warmth. Adjust each element incrementally — a satay sauce that tastes sweet and peanut-buttery without complexity is incomplete; one that tastes only fishy has the fish sauce ratio wrong.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sauce Robert
description: One of espagnole's oldest children — a brown sauce built on slowly sweated onions, sharpened with reduced white wine, and finished off the heat with a swirl of Dijon. Tangy, mustard-bright, and savory all at once, it is the classic companion to roast pork and grilled meats.
instructions: Melt about a third of the clarified butter in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the mirepoix and cook, stirring occasionally, until deeply browned and sweet-smelling — 12 to 18 minutes. Build a rust-colored fond on the bottom of the pot; that caramelization is the backbone of the espagnole base.

Melt the remaining butter into the cleared part of the pot, sprinkle in the flour, and cook the roux to a deep chestnut brown, stirring almost constantly — 10 to 20 minutes, until it smells nutty and toasty. Stir in the tomato paste and cook it out for 3 to 5 minutes until it darkens to brick-rust and smells sweet rather than sharp. Go low and patient; brown roux scorches in a heartbeat.

Pour in the brown stock a few ladles at a time, whisking out lumps before adding more. Add the bouquet garni, bring to the barest simmer, and hold 2 to 3 hours, skimming the fat and froth from the surface and seasoning lightly with salt near the end. When reduced by about a third and coating a spoon, strain through a fine sieve. This is your base espagnole.

In a separate clean saucepan, melt a little clarified butter over low-medium heat and add the finely diced onion. Sweat it gently, stirring often, until soft, translucent, and just beginning to turn golden at the edges — 8 to 12 minutes. The goal is sweetness and tenderness without hard browning; keep the heat low so the onion melts rather than crisps.

Pour the dry white wine over the sweated onions and raise the heat to bring it to a brisk simmer. Reduce, scraping up any fond, until the wine has cooked down to a syrupy glaze barely covering the onions and the sharp alcohol smell has cooked off — 5 to 8 minutes. This reduction concentrates the wine's acidity into a bright backbone for the sauce.

Pour the strained espagnole into the onion and wine reduction and simmer gently together for 8 to 10 minutes, skimming, until married and smooth. Then pull the pan completely off the heat and let it stop bubbling before whisking in the Dijon mustard. Never let the sauce boil after the mustard goes in — boiling mustard turns harsh and bitter. Taste, adjust the salt, and serve warm.
notes: Espagnole built on sweated onions, white wine, and a finish of mustard — sharp and savory, classic with pork.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sauce Suprême
description: A chicken velouté reduced with cream until it turns lush, ivory, and glossy, then mounted with cold butter for a mirror shine. The supreme of the white sauces — built for poached chicken, supreme of fowl, and anything that wants to taste of pure, silken poultry.
instructions: Melt the butter over medium-low heat until it foams without browning, then whisk in the flour. Cook, stirring, 4 to 6 minutes until the raw-flour smell turns to toasted hazelnut and the paste is pale straw — a blond roux.

Off the heat, whisk the warm white chicken stock into the roux in three or four additions, letting each disappear before the next. Return to medium heat, bring to a gentle boil whisking, then drop to a bare simmer and skim until the surface runs clean.

Pour the heavy cream into the simmering velouté. Reduce gently over medium-low heat, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until the sauce is enriched, ivory, and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. This cream reduction is what turns a plain velouté into a suprême — expect to lose roughly a third of the volume.

Off the heat, whisk in the cold butter a cube at a time, swirling the pan, letting each piece melt into the sauce before adding the next (monter au beurre). This gives the suprême its mirror gloss and a final velvet richness. Season with salt and a touch of white pepper. Keep it warm but never let it boil after mounting, or the butter will split.
notes: A chicken velouté reduced with cream until lush and glossy — the supreme of white sauces, classic over poultry.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sauce Tomate (Classical French)
description: The Escoffier mother sauce — not a quick marinara. Tomatoes melted into rendered pork fat and mirepoix, moistened with white stock, scented with a bouquet garni, simmered slow until jammy, then passed to a smooth, velvety, deeply rounded red sauce.

ingredients.text: 8 parts Ripe tomatoes (or canned San Marzano)

instructions: Dice the salt pork small and set it in a heavy-bottomed pot over low-medium heat (or simply melt the butter). Let it render slowly without browning, drawing the fat out clear and the scraps to a pale gold. You want a film of clean fat coating the pot, not a fry.

Add the finely cut mirepoix and the garlic to the fat. Sweat over low-medium heat, stirring often, until the onion turns translucent and the whole pot softens and goes silent of its raw bite. Do not let it color — this is a foundation, not a fond.

Add the chopped tomatoes (crush canned ones by hand) and the pinch of sugar to correct their acidity. Raise the heat to a lively simmer and cook down, stirring as it thickens, until the watery tomato has collapsed into a thick, jammy base and the bright raw smell turns deep and sweet.

Pour in the white stock, tuck in the bouquet garni, and season lightly with salt (go easy if you used salt pork). Bring to the barest simmer and hold it there, partially covered, for an hour and a half or more, skimming the fat and scum that gather at the surface. The sauce should ripple, never boil.

Discard the bouquet garni and the pork scraps. Pass the sauce through a food mill or push it through a fine sieve with a ladle, working the solids until only dry skins and fibre remain behind. Return it to the heat, taste, and adjust salt and the pinch of sugar to balance the acidity into a smooth, velvety sauce.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Rhineland Sauerbraten
description: Germany's pot roast nobility — beef marinated for three to four days in red wine vinegar, wine, and a raft of aromatics until the tough outside round transforms into something silken, then braised low and slow with crumbled gingersnaps stirred into the sauce for a haunting, sweet-sour richness unique to the Rhineland.

ingredients.text: 1500 g Beef bottom round or top round (about 1.5 kg, tied)
80 g Gingersnap cookies (Lebkuchen or ginger snaps), crumbled

instructions: Do not heat the marinade — a cold marinade is traditional for sauerbraten. Combine the red wine vinegar, red wine, water, onion, celery, carrot, bay leaves, juniper berries, cloves, peppercorns, sugar, and salt in a large non-reactive bowl or pot (glass, ceramic, or stainless steel — never aluminium or cast iron at this stage). Stir until the salt and sugar dissolve. Submerge the beef completely, pressing it down. Cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for 3–4 days, turning the meat once per day so all sides marinate evenly.

Remove the beef from the marinade and pat it completely dry with paper towels — moisture is the enemy of a good sear. Strain and reserve all the marinade liquid. Heat the lard or oil in a heavy Dutch oven or braising pot over high heat until just beginning to smoke. Sear the beef on all sides, including the ends, for 3–4 minutes per side without moving it. You are building deep brown crust for colour and flavour — the Maillard crust will dissolve into the braising liquid and become the backbone of the sauce.

Return the seared beef to the pot. Pour the strained marinade over it — the liquid should come at least halfway up the sides of the meat. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then cover with a tight lid and reduce to the lowest possible heat (or transfer to a 160°C oven). Braise for 2.5–3 hours, turning the beef every 45 minutes. The meat is done when a carving fork slides in and out without resistance, and the fibres are beginning to separate when pressed.

Remove the beef and keep warm under foil. Pour all the braising liquid through a fine strainer into a wide saucepan — discard the spent aromatics. Bring the liquid to a vigorous boil and reduce by one-third, about 10 minutes. Crumble in the gingersnaps and whisk over medium heat until they dissolve completely and the sauce thickens noticeably to a coating consistency. Taste for balance — it should be sweet, sour, warm with spice, and deeply savoury. If it is too tart, add another crumbled gingersnap. Off the heat, stir in the sour cream if using, and reheat gently without boiling.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Traditional Sauerkraut
description: Cabbage, salt, time, and trust — a Bavarian fermentation that transforms a humble head into something tangy, probiotic, and profoundly alive.
instructions: Quarter the cabbage and remove the core. Slice each quarter into thin ribbons, about 3mm wide. Uniformity matters — uneven shreds ferment at different rates, creating pockets of crunch alongside pockets of mush.

Place shredded cabbage in a large bowl. Sprinkle salt and caraway seeds evenly over the top. Massage with both hands, squeezing and kneading the cabbage firmly. The salt will draw water from the cells. Continue for 8-10 minutes until the cabbage has wilted significantly and sits in its own brine.

Transfer the cabbage and all its brine into a clean glass jar or ceramic crock. Push it down in handfuls with your fist, packing as tightly as possible. The brine must rise above the cabbage surface. Place a weight on top — a zip-lock bag filled with brine works well. Cover with a cloth to keep out dust but allow gas to escape.

Leave at room temperature (18-22 C) for 3-14 days, tasting every two days after day three. Press the weight down daily and skim any scum from the surface. Bubbling is a sign of active, healthy fermentation.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Shanghai Scallion Oil Noodles (Cong You Ban Mian)
description: Plain wheat noodles tossed in a dark, slow-rendered scallion oil that takes forty minutes to build from a bundle of green onions and a cup of oil — the scallions caramelize to a dark, sweet, crispy confetti while the oil absorbs their entire life force, becoming something wholly different from any oil you have ever tasted. A dish of four ingredients that insists on quality in each one.

ingredients.text: 200 g Fresh thin Shanghai noodles (or dried lo mein)
150 g Scallions, cut into 5 cm pieces

instructions: Combine the scallion pieces and neutral oil in a cold small saucepan or wok — starting in cold oil is critical. If you add scallions to already-hot oil they will fry hard and fast, browning too quickly before they have time to release their aromatics into the oil. Place over the lowest heat you can manage and cook for 30–40 minutes. The first 15 minutes will see very little activity — the oil will warm slowly and the scallions will begin to soften and wilt. From 15–25 minutes, the scallions will begin to shrink dramatically and you will see the first signs of browning at the green tips. From 25–40 minutes, the scallions will caramelize progressively from the tips down toward the white roots, going from golden to amber to a deep reddish-brown. The goal is that the scallions go almost fully dark — sweet-bitter, crispy shards — while the oil turns a deep golden-amber and smells like nothing else: sweet, savory, deeply caramelized allium. Stir every 5 minutes, more frequently in the last 10. When the scallion pieces are uniformly dark golden-brown and crispy, remove from heat.

In a large mixing bowl that will also serve as your tossing bowl for the noodles, combine the warm scallion oil (about 3 tablespoons per serving), light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, and sugar. Stir together with a spoon or chopsticks until the sugar is fully dissolved. The sauce will be a dark, glossy, highly aromatic liquid — the dark soy provides color and depth, the light soy provides salinity and brightness. Taste it: it should be very salty and intensely sweet-savory, because it will dilute dramatically when tossed with the starchy noodles. The ratio of scallion oil to soy sauce is important: too much oil and the noodles are greasy; too much soy and they are one-dimensionally salty. Adjust to your preference — more dark soy for a deeper color and molasses-sweet flavor, more light soy for a brighter, saltier result.

Cook the noodles in a large pot of vigorously boiling, lightly salted water until just done — fresh Shanghai noodles take 2–3 minutes, dried lo mein 4–5 minutes, thin spaghetti 7–8 minutes. Drain well, shaking the colander hard. Transfer immediately to the bowl of scallion sauce while the noodles are still very hot — the heat helps the sauce coat every strand. Toss vigorously and quickly with chopsticks or tongs, lifting and folding the noodles continuously for 60–90 seconds until every strand is evenly coated in the dark, glossy sauce. The hot noodles will absorb the soy quickly, so work fast. Taste and adjust: more soy for salt, more oil for richness, a few drops of scallion oil for aroma. Transfer to a serving plate or bowl and scatter a generous amount of the reserved crispy scallion pieces over the top. Serve immediately — scallion oil noodles are a dish of the moment, and the texture deteriorates rapidly.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Scallion Oil
description: Shanghai's most versatile condiment — neutral oil slowly infused with ginger and a mountain of scallions until they turn golden and fragrant, leaving behind an oil that elevates everything it touches.

ingredients.text: 250 g Neutral oil (peanut, canola, or grapeseed)
30 g Fresh ginger, peeled and sliced 5 mm thick

instructions: Trim and wash the scallions thoroughly — any trapped moisture will cause the oil to splatter aggressively when they hit the pan. Pat completely dry with paper towels, or better, lay them out for 30 minutes to air-dry. Combine the oil, whole scallions, and ginger slices in a cold wok or medium saucepan. Place over medium-low heat. Starting cold is essential — it gives the scallion and ginger time to slowly release their volatile aromatic compounds into the oil before any browning occurs. As the oil heats, the scallions will begin to wilt, then soften, then bubble. The bubbling is the water content of the scallion cooking off — as long as it is bubbling vigorously, the temperature will stay below browning. Let the oil slowly infuse for 10–12 minutes, turning the scallions occasionally with tongs.

After the initial infusion, increase the heat to medium and allow the oil to continue cooking the scallions until they transition from jade-green to a pale golden-yellow, with the edges beginning to show the first signs of browning. This stage takes 5–8 minutes after the heat is raised. Watch for the moment the vigorous bubbling slows — this means the scallions have lost most of their moisture and are now beginning to actually fry in the oil rather than steam. This is when browning accelerates rapidly. As soon as the scallions are golden-yellow with pale amber tips, remove from heat — they will continue to cook in the residual heat of the oil.

Remove the pan from the heat and immediately stir in the salt — it will dissolve into the hot oil and season it throughout. Let the oil cool slightly for 2–3 minutes (the scallions will continue to cook in the residual heat, deepening slightly from golden to pale amber). Then strain the oil through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean heat-proof jar or container, pressing gently on the solids to extract every drop of flavored oil. Discard the spent scallion and ginger solids — they have given everything to the oil and have nothing left to offer. Let the oil cool to room temperature before sealing. It keeps refrigerated for up to 3 weeks and solidifies slightly when cold; bring to room temperature before using. Drizzle over cold noodles, steamed fish, congee, or use anywhere the gentle, sweet fragrance of scallion should be present without the texture of raw scallion.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Scallion Pancake (Cong You Bing)
description: Shanghai's beloved street flatbread — a spiral of hot-water dough laminated with sesame oil and a blizzard of dark-green scallion, pan-fried until the exterior shatters into a thousand golden layers while the interior stays yielding and fragrant.

ingredients.text: 0.5 cups Boiling water (just off the boil)

instructions: Place flour in a large bowl and make a well in the center. Pour the boiling water directly into the well and immediately stir with chopsticks or a fork in a circular motion from the center outward — the boiling water partially cooks (gelatinizes) the starch, producing a tender, slightly translucent dough. After stirring for 1 minute, add the cold water and continue mixing until a rough ball forms. The combination of hot and cold water produces a dough that is simultaneously soft (from the hot water gelatinization) and elastic (from the cold water activating remaining gluten). The dough will look shaggy at first — this is correct.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 5-7 minutes until the surface becomes very smooth. Hot-water doughs knead faster than cold-water doughs because the heat has already done structural work — do not over-knead or the dough becomes tough. The finished dough should be smooth as a pearl, non-sticky, and extremely pliable — more so than bread dough, closer to fresh pasta. Divide into 4 equal portions, cover with a damp cloth, and rest for 20-30 minutes.

Working one portion at a time on a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a thin rectangle approximately 30 x 20 cm (12 x 8 inches). Brush generously with sesame oil, leaving a 1 cm border. Scatter a quarter of the scallions evenly across the surface and season with salt and five-spice if using. Starting from the long edge closest to you, roll the rectangle tightly into a log — exactly as you'd roll a jelly roll. Then coil the log on itself into a tight spiral, tucking the tail end underneath, and press down gently to seal the coil. Let the coiled discs rest 10 minutes before flattening. Use a rolling pin to flatten each coil to about 6 mm thickness — the layered spiral compresses without losing its laminated structure.

Heat a wide, heavy skillet (cast iron or carbon steel preferred) over medium-high heat until smoking. Add 1 tablespoon of neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place a pancake in the pan and cook for 2-3 minutes until the bottom is deeply golden brown with some darker spots. Flip, add another small splash of oil to the pan, and press the pancake gently but firmly with a wide spatula for 5 seconds to ensure even contact. Cook another 2-3 minutes. Flip again, pressing once more, and cook a final minute if needed. The total cooking time is 5-7 minutes — enough to cook the interior layers through while building a shattering crust. Drain briefly on a rack (not paper towels, which steam and soften the crust).
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Scallion Pancakes (Cong You Bing)
description: A hot water dough is rolled flat, painted with sesame oil and salt, blanketed in scallion, then coiled and re-rolled — the same lamination trick as a croissant, but humble enough to eat on the street. The result is a flaky, chewy, pan-fried flatbread that shatters at the first bite into dozens of separated, fragrant layers.

ingredients.text: 40 g Neutral oil for frying (vegetable or rapeseed)
3 g Flaky sea salt for layering

instructions: Place the flour in a bowl and pour in the boiling water all at once. Immediately stir with a chopstick or wooden spoon in circular motions until the water is absorbed and the mixture looks like a shaggy, steaming mass. The boiling water partially cooks the starch — this gelatinisation is what makes the dough pliable and the pancake chewy rather than biscuity. Once cool enough to handle (about 2 minutes), knead briefly in the bowl until a smooth dough forms — about 3 minutes. It should feel soft and slightly tacky.

Divide the rested dough into 4 equal pieces. On a lightly oiled surface (not floured), roll each piece into a thin rectangle about 3 mm thick. Brush generously with sesame oil to within 5 mm of the edges. Scatter salt and sliced scallion evenly across the surface, pressing lightly so they adhere. Now roll the rectangle into a tight log from the long edge, like a Swiss roll. Then coil the log into a tight snail shape and press it flat with your palm. Re-roll the coiled disc to about 5 mm thick. This double-rolling is the technique that creates the layered structure.

Heat a heavy skillet or cast iron pan over medium heat. Add enough neutral oil to coat the bottom with a 2 mm layer. When the oil shimmers, add one pancake. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes on the first side without moving it — the underside should be golden and crisping. Flip and press lightly with a spatula to encourage even contact with the pan. Cook the second side for 2 minutes. The pancake is done when both sides are deep golden-brown with dark, crispy edges and you can hear it crackling and hissing in the oil.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Seared Scallops with Pea Purée and Pancetta
description: Pan-seared king scallops with a velvety, sweet pea purée and crispy pancetta — a three-part restaurant classic with a brutally simple margin for error on the sear: golden on one side, translucent at the centre.

ingredients.text: 12 whole King scallops, dry-packed, roe removed

instructions: Melt 20 g of the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced shallot and garlic with a pinch of salt and sweat gently for 3–4 minutes until completely soft and translucent — no color at all. Add the frozen peas and double cream, bring to a simmer, and cook for 3 minutes until the peas are just tender and brilliant green. Transfer everything to a blender, add the mint leaves, and blend on high until completely smooth. Pass through a fine sieve if you want restaurant-level silkiness. Season with salt, white pepper, and a small squeeze of lemon. Keep warm.

Place the diced pancetta in a cold dry frying pan and set over medium heat. As the fat renders slowly, the pancetta will crisp evenly without burning. Cook for 5–7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the dice are deeply golden and crispy and the surrounding fat has fully rendered out. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Reserve the rendered fat in the pan — this will be used to sear the scallops.

Pat the scallops completely dry with paper towel — this is the single most important step. Any surface moisture will steam rather than sear. Season both flat faces with salt and white pepper. Add the neutral oil to the pancetta-fat pan and heat over the highest possible heat until the oil just begins to smoke. Place scallops flat-side down in the pan, one by one, and do not touch them for exactly 90 seconds to 2 minutes. The sear must be uninterrupted. They are ready to flip when they release easily from the pan — not when the timer says so.

The moment the scallops are flipped, add the remaining cold butter to the pan in two pieces. It will melt and foam immediately in the residual heat. Tilt the pan and use a spoon to continuously baste the scallops with the foaming butter for 30–45 seconds. Add a tiny squeeze of lemon. Remove scallops the moment the second side shows a pale gold — the center should still feel yielding. Rest on a warm plate for 30 seconds while you arrange the components.

Working quickly, spoon a swoosh of warm pea purée across each plate using the back of a warm spoon. Arrange three scallops per plate on and around the purée, seared-side facing up to display the crust. Scatter the crispy pancetta dice over and around the scallops. Finish with a small cluster of pea shoots or watercress placed in the center, dressed with a tiny drizzle of olive oil. The three elements must arrive together: any one of them cold ruins the dish.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Schiacciata
description: Tuscany's answer to focaccia — thinner, crispier at the edges, and so saturated with good olive oil that the first bite releases a warm, grassy flood — the word 'schiacciata' means crushed, and the flat, dimpled dough delivers exactly that: deliberately pressed-down, maximally crisp.

ingredients.text: 8 parts Extra-virgin olive oil, plus generous amount for pan and top
0.3 parts Flaky sea salt (Maldon or Fiore di Sale)

instructions: Combine the flour, instant yeast, and fine salt in a large bowl, keeping the salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl initially. Pour in the warm water and olive oil. Mix with a dough scraper or your hand until no dry flour remains — the dough will be moderately sticky, softer than a bread dough but not as wet as focaccia. It should pull away from the sides of the bowl. Do not add more flour. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Perform three sets of stretch-and-fold over 60 minutes, one set every 20 minutes. For each set: wet your hand, grab the dough at one side of the bowl, stretch it firmly upward as far as it will reach without tearing, then fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat until you have completed four folds. After three sets, the dough should be noticeably smoother, more cohesive, and beginning to show bubbles beneath the surface. Cover and let bulk ferment at room temperature for another 30 minutes until puffy.

Pour a very generous amount of olive oil onto a half-sheet pan or rimmed baking tray — at least 4-5 tablespoons. Schiacciata is an olive oil bread and should practically float in it. Transfer the dough to the pan and use your fingertips to begin pressing and stretching it toward the edges. If the dough springs back firmly, cover and wait 10-15 minutes, then try again. The dough should eventually be pressed quite flat — roughly 1.5 cm thick throughout. Cover with plastic wrap and proof at room temperature for 30-45 minutes until noticeably puffy and slightly domed.

Using all ten fingers held flat, press the dough firmly and repeatedly across its entire surface, pushing all the way through to the pan. The dough should be pressed quite flat — flatter than focaccia. This is the 'schiacciata' — the crushing. Drizzle another generous pour of olive oil across the entire surface, letting it pool in the dimples. Scatter the flaky salt and rosemary leaves if using. The salt goes on now, not after baking.

Bake at 230 C (450 F) on the lowest rack for 15-20 minutes. Schiacciata bakes hotter and faster than focaccia because it is thinner. Watch carefully after 12 minutes. The edges should be deep brown and very crisp; the center should be golden. Remove from the pan immediately to a wire rack — do not let it cool in the pan or the bottom will steam and soften. Cool for 5 minutes before cutting. Schiacciata is best eaten within 1 hour of baking, while the contrast between the crisp exterior and the moist, oily crumb is still at its peak.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Scotch Egg
description: A soft-boiled egg cocooned in seasoned sausage meat, armored in golden breadcrumbs — shattered open to reveal a coral-centered yolk ringed by a collar of perfectly pink pork.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Eggs (large, for boiling, very fresh)
1 parts Black pepper, white pepper, mace blend

instructions: Lower eggs gently into a pot of vigorously boiling water. Cook exactly 6 minutes 30 seconds for a jammy, coral yolk. Transfer immediately to an ice bath and chill for 10 minutes — this stops the carry-over cook that turns yolks grey. Peel carefully under cold running water, keeping the white intact. Pat dry with paper towels.

Mix sausage meat with salt and spice blend until evenly seasoned. Fry a small patty in a dry pan and taste — the sausage should be boldly seasoned, as the egg and breadcrumbs will dilute its flavor. Adjust. Divide the meat into equal portions — one per egg. Flatten each portion into a thin, even disc on a sheet of cling film.

Dust each boiled egg lightly with flour — this helps the sausage grip. Lay a flattened sausage disc on cling film and center the egg on top. Use the film to lift and wrap the sausage around the egg, sealing it with wet hands and pinching any seams closed. Roll in flour, dip in beaten egg, then coat thoroughly in panko, pressing to adhere. Rest in the fridge for 20 minutes.

Heat oil to 170 C (338 F) in a deep, heavy pot. Lower Scotch eggs in carefully — do not crowd the pot. Fry for 7–8 minutes, turning every 2 minutes for even color, until the crumb is a deep, even mahogany and the sausage reaches 70 C (158 F) internal. Drain on a rack, not paper towels. Rest 5 minutes before cutting.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Scotch Eggs
description: Soft-boiled eggs encased in seasoned pork sausage, breaded and deep-fried to a mahogany crust — the perfect portable British snack with a molten golden yolk at the centre.

ingredients.text: 6 eggs Eggs, for the centres (large, very fresh)
5 parts Good-quality pork sausage meat (or sausages, skinned)
0.5 parts Dijon mustard, fine salt, and black pepper
0.2 parts Fresh sage and thyme, finely chopped together
0.5 parts Eggs, beaten for the coating (2 eggs)
2 parts Panko breadcrumbs (Japanese-style for maximum crunch)

instructions: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Gently lower the eggs on a spoon — do not drop them or the shells will crack. Boil for exactly 6 minutes for a runny-firm yolk that will hold together during frying. Transfer immediately to an ice bath — a bowl of water with as much ice as you can spare — and leave for 5 full minutes. The cold stops the carry-over cooking that would ruin the yolk. Peel carefully under cold running water, starting from the wide air-pocket end. The whites will be very delicate.

Combine the sausage meat, mustard, chopped herbs, nutmeg, and a generous seasoning of salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix with your hands until the seasonings are fully incorporated and the mixture feels slightly tacky and cohesive — no streaks of mustard visible. Fry a small nugget in a hot dry pan and taste it: the sausage should be boldly seasoned, herby, and slightly mustardy. Season more aggressively than seems right — the breaded exterior and the bland egg will absorb a lot of that punch.

Working with one portion of sausage meat at a time, flatten it in your damp palm into a thin, even oval about 3 mm thick. Set a peeled boiled egg in the centre. Bring the edges of the sausage up and around the egg, pressing gently to seal at the top. Work around the egg, ensuring the sausage layer is even all the way around — thin spots will burst open in the fryer. Roll gently between your palms to even out the surface and seal any seams. The finished shape should be a uniform oval with no visible egg beneath.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with flour seasoned with salt and pepper, one with the beaten eggs, one with the panko breadcrumbs. Working one at a time, roll a wrapped egg firmly in the flour, patting off any excess (a thick flour coat creates pastiness). Dip in beaten egg, letting any excess drip for 3 seconds. Roll in panko, pressing the crumbs firmly into every surface — no bare patches. For an extra-crunchy crust, repeat the egg-and-panko dip for a second coat. Set on a rack.

Heat at least 8 cm of oil in a heavy, deep pot to 170°C (340°F) — slightly cooler than standard frying temperature to allow the thick sausage layer to cook through before the crumbs burn. Carefully lower 2 or 3 eggs at a time (never crowd). Fry for 7–8 minutes, turning every 90 seconds for even colour, until the crust is a deep mahogany-brown and the eggs float freely. Transfer to a wire rack (not paper towels) for 2–3 minutes to let residual heat finish cooking the centre. Test by pressing: the crust should feel rigid, not soft.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Scottish Kedgeree
description: A colonial-era dish born from Indian khichdi and Scottish smoked haddock — basmati rice scented with curry and butter, folded with flakes of golden haddock and gently hard-boiled eggs, scattered with crisp parsley and a squeeze of lemon.

ingredients.text: 300 g Basmati rice, rinsed until clear

instructions: Place the haddock skin-side down in a wide pan. Pour over the milk — it should just cover the fish. Bring to the barest simmer over medium-low heat. As soon as the milk begins to shiver and small bubbles appear around the edges (not a full boil), turn off the heat, cover the pan, and let the fish poach in the residual heat for 8–10 minutes. Lift the fish out and reserve the poaching milk. When cool enough to handle, peel off and discard the skin, then flake the flesh into large chunks, checking for pin bones.

Bring a pot of water to a full boil. Lower the eggs in gently and cook for exactly 8 minutes for yolks that are set but still have a faintly creamy center — a true soft-set rather than chalky hard-boiled. Transfer immediately to a bowl of ice water for 2 minutes to stop the cooking and make them easier to peel. Peel and cut into quarters lengthwise.

In a large, wide saucepan, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the diced onion with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, for 8–10 minutes until soft, translucent, and beginning to turn pale gold at the edges. Add the curry powder and stir for 60–90 seconds until the spices bloom and turn fragrant and dark. Add the rinsed rice and stir to coat every grain in the spiced butter — about 1 minute. Measure 450 ml of the reserved haddock poaching milk (top up with water if needed) and pour it over the rice. Season lightly with salt, remembering the fish and milk are already salty. Bring to a boil, reduce to the lowest simmer, cover tightly, and cook 12 minutes. Remove from heat and steam, lid on, for 5 more minutes.

If using cream, pour it over the rice and fold gently with a wide spatula. Add the flaked haddock in large pieces and fold just twice or three times — you want chunks, not paste. Add half the parsley. Fold once more. Taste and adjust salt and lemon juice — the dish wants brightness. Arrange the egg quarters across the top, scatter the remaining parsley, and bring the pan to the table with lemon halves alongside. Kedgeree is traditionally served at breakfast or brunch, warm but not screaming hot.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Pan-Seared Scallops with Beurre Noisette
description: Dry-brined sea scallops seared in a ripping-hot pan until the bottom face is mahogany and caramelized — then basted in hazelnut-brown butter with capers until fragrant and just-set translucent at the center.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Dry-packed sea scallops (U10, adductor muscle removed)
5 parts Neutral oil with high smoke point (grapeseed, avocado)
5 parts Salt-packed capers, rinsed and dried

instructions: This step is the non-negotiable foundation of a well-seared scallop. Lay the scallops on a wire rack set over a baking tray. Season each one lightly on both flat faces with fine sea salt. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 20 minutes, up to 1 hour. The salt draws moisture to the surface through osmosis, which then evaporates in the cold, circulating air of the refrigerator, leaving the scallop surface perfectly dry. A wet scallop surface will steam in the pan rather than sear — the water must flash to steam before any browning can begin, effectively lowering the effective surface temperature below the Maillard threshold. 'Dry-packed' scallops (never treated with sodium tripolyphosphate) are essential — wet-packed scallops have already been soaked in a phosphate solution that prevents browning entirely.

Heat a heavy cast-iron or stainless steel skillet over the highest heat for at least 3 minutes — the pan must be thoroughly preheated, not just warm. Add the neutral oil; it should immediately begin to shimmer and whisper. Place the scallops flat-face down, spacing them at least 3 cm apart. You must hear a loud, aggressive sizzle the moment they contact the pan — if you don't, the pan is not hot enough. Do not touch, shake, or move the scallops for a full 90 seconds. Resist every urge to peek underneath. After 90 seconds, gently try to slide a thin spatula under one scallop: if it releases cleanly, the crust has formed. If it resists, wait another 15 seconds. Flip each scallop. The sear should reveal a uniform, mahogany-brown crust across the entire flat face — not patchy, not pale in the center.

After flipping the scallops, immediately add the cold cubed butter to the pan in one addition. The cold butter hitting the hot pan will erupt with sizzling foam. As soon as the foam subsides and the butter begins to turn golden (this takes about 45–60 seconds), you will see it shift to an amber color and smell a distinctly hazelnut aroma — this is beurre noisette (brown butter): the milk proteins in the butter are caramelizing. Add the rinsed capers. Using a large spoon, immediately begin basting the scallops by tilting the pan slightly toward you and spooning the hot, hazelnut-scented brown butter over each scallop continuously. Baste for 30–45 seconds. Total second-side contact time (including basting): 60–75 seconds. The scallops are done when they still feel slightly soft and yielding at the very center when pressed.

Remove the scallops from the pan and arrange on warm plates, seared-crust side up. Squeeze lemon juice into the remaining brown butter in the pan, swirling to combine — the acid will stop the butter from browning further and lift the pan into a quick pan sauce. Spoon this brown butter-lemon-caper sauce generously over each scallop. Scatter the finely chopped flat-leaf parsley and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt on each scallop's seared face. Serve within 60 seconds — scallops cool rapidly and the window of perfectly cooked, translucent-centered texture is brief.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Semifreddo al Limone
description: Italy's answer to frozen mousse — a pillow of whipped cream and meringue suspended in gentle cold, sliced to reveal a cross-section of pale gold lemon cream that yields instantly on the tongue and vanishes without a trace of ice.

ingredients.text: 2 ea Unwaxed lemons, zest and juice
50 g Candied lemon peel or fresh berries

instructions: Place the egg yolks, caster sugar, lemon zest and lemon juice in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of gently simmering water. Whisk vigorously and continuously for 8–10 minutes until the mixture is very thick, pale and has tripled in volume — it should hold a thick ribbon for several seconds when the whisk is lifted. This is the zabaglione base. Remove from the heat and continue whisking until the bowl feels cool to the touch. The cooking stabilises the yolks so the semifreddo stays aerated when frozen.

In two separate bowls: whip the cold double cream to soft peaks — it should hold a shape but still be silky and flowing, not stiff. In a separate grease-free bowl, whisk the egg whites with a pinch of salt until they hold firm, glossy peaks. Do not overwhip either — both should be airy and light, not stiff and dry. Keep both chilled until needed.

First fold the whipped whites into the cooled zabaglione in two additions, using a large spatula with a cut-and-lift motion. Then fold in the whipped cream in two additions. Be gentle and decisive — the goal is to retain as much air as possible while achieving a fully uniform, streak-free mixture. The finished base should be light, mousse-like and pale yellow. Pour into a loaf tin lined with two layers of clingfilm, with plenty of overhang on all sides.

Fold the clingfilm over the surface to seal completely. Freeze for a minimum of 4 hours, preferably overnight. To serve: unwrap, invert onto a chilled serving plate and peel off the clingfilm. The semifreddo should hold its shape cleanly and be easy to slice with a warm knife. Decorate the top with candied lemon peel or fresh berries. Slice into 2–3 cm portions and serve immediately — it softens quickly at room temperature.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sfogliatelle Ricce
description: Naples' supreme pastry achievement: a layered shell of paper-thin laminated dough, each leaf barely thicker than a page, cradling a filling of ricotta, semolina cream, and candied citrus — the shell shatters into a thousand crisp fragments at the first bite while the interior yields into a dense, fragrant, barely-sweet cream. Every sfogliatella is a feat of patience made edible.

ingredients.text: 150 g Lard (or cold unsalted butter), for laminating
60 g Candied orange peel, finely diced
5 ml Pure vanilla extract or vanilla paste

instructions: Combine semolina flour and salt in a large bowl. Make a well. Add the beaten egg and warm water to the well. Mix by hand until a stiff, cohesive dough forms — this dough should be very firm and smooth, like pasta dough. Knead on the bench for 10–12 minutes until very smooth. The dough will be stiff and fight you — this is correct. A stiff dough extends into very thin sheets without tearing. Wrap tightly in plastic and rest for 30 minutes.

Bring milk to a simmer in a saucepan. Rain in semolina in a thin stream while whisking constantly. Cook over medium-low heat, whisking, for 5–7 minutes until the mixture becomes very thick and pulls away from the sides of the pan. Remove from heat. Beat in sugar, vanilla, and candied orange peel. Spread on a tray, cover with plastic touching the surface, and cool completely in the refrigerator — at least 2 hours.

Beat the cold semolina cream to break it up slightly.
