description: Nice's beloved street pancake: a thin, caramel-spotted disc of chickpea flour batter cooked in a blazing iron pan until the edges shatter and the center stays yielding, then torn apart at the table and eaten with fingers dusted in black pepper.

ingredients.text: 1 parts Chickpea flour (farine de pois chiches)
0.15 parts Extra-virgin olive oil (plus more for the pan)

instructions: Place chickpea flour in a bowl. Slowly pour the cold water over it while whisking — always add water to flour, not flour to water, to prevent lumps. Whisk until completely smooth, then add olive oil and salt. Whisk again. The batter should be thinner than pancake batter — nearly as thin as whole milk. Skim off any foam. Rest uncovered at room temperature for 1 hour minimum. The rest allows the flour to hydrate fully and the batter to develop a creamy, nutty character.

Place a 30–32 cm cast-iron skillet or a round carbon-steel pan under the broiler set to maximum. After 10 minutes, use thick oven gloves to remove the screaming-hot pan. Pour in 2 tbsp olive oil, swirl to coat, then quickly pour in enough batter to cover the surface to 4–5 mm depth. Return immediately to the broiler. Broil 6–8 minutes until the top is blistered and golden-brown in patches and the edges are dark and crisp. Scatter cracked pepper over the top in the last 2 minutes. The center will remain slightly soft — this is correct.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Italian Soffritto
description: The invisible foundation of a thousand Italian dishes — onion, celery, and carrot cooked slowly in olive oil until they surrender into a golden, yielding mirepoix that smells of pure comfort and deep savory sweetness.

ingredients.text: 1 parts Celery stalks with leaves, finely diced
1 parts Carrots, peeled and finely diced

instructions: Cut all vegetables to a uniform, fine dice: approximately 2-3mm cubes for soffritto, no larger than 5mm. Uniformity is key — if pieces vary in size, the smaller ones will burn before the larger ones soften. For onion: halve through the root, make horizontal and vertical cuts keeping the root intact, then slice across to produce a fine dice. For celery: strip off the tough outer strings with a peeler if the stalks are thick, then dice finely. For carrot: square off the rounded sides, cut into planks, then batons, then dice.

Add the olive oil to a wide, heavy-bottomed pan over medium-low heat. When the oil shimmers, add the diced onion and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring every 2-3 minutes, for 8-10 minutes until the onion is translucent and beginning to soften. Add the celery and carrot, stir to combine. Continue cooking for another 15-20 minutes, stirring every 3-4 minutes, maintaining gentle heat. If the pan sounds loud and active, lower the heat — soffritto should sizzle softly, not fry aggressively.

Taste the soffritto and adjust salt. It should taste mellow, sweet, and deeply savory without any single vegetable dominating. If it tastes sharp, it needs more cooking time. If it tastes flat, add a small pinch more salt and cook for 2 more minutes. Remove from heat. Use immediately as the base for Bolognese, minestrone, risotto, or braised meats. Soffritto freezes beautifully in ice cube trays — a cube per portion makes weeknight cooking effortless.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sofrito Català
description: The slow-fried tomato and onion base of Catalan cooking — cooked until it darkens and concentrates into a sweet, jammy reduction that is the foundation of countless Catalan dishes.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Very ripe tomatoes (grated on a box grater, skins discarded)
25 parts Extra-virgin olive oil (fruity, not bitter)

instructions: Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan (preferably cast iron or enameled) over medium-low heat. Add the finely diced onion and salt. Cook slowly, stirring every 3 to 4 minutes, for 20 to 25 minutes. Do not rush with higher heat — the onion must caramelize gently into a sweet, golden mass. It will pass through translucent, then blond, then deep gold.

Add the minced garlic and thyme sprigs to the caramelized onion and cook for 2 minutes over medium heat, stirring frequently, until the garlic is soft and fragrant but not browned. The garlic should melt into the onion rather than stay as distinct pieces.

Add the grated tomato to the pan — it will spit and sizzle energetically. Stir to combine with the onion and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring every few minutes, for 20 to 25 minutes. The tomato will pass through saucy, then thick, then deeply concentrated — it is ready when it has reduced by two-thirds, turned a deep brick-red, and no longer sticks to a spatula dragged across the base.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sofrito
description: The aromatic engine of Spanish and Catalan cooking — onion, tomato, and pepper reduced over patient heat into a sweet, jammy, deeply concentrated paste that carries the flavor of every dish it touches. An hour of low heat transforms a handful of vegetables into something that makes you wonder what food tasted like without it.

ingredients.text: 400 g Yellow or white onion, finely diced
400 g Ripe plum tomatoes, grated or blended
150 g Red bell pepper, finely diced
3 g Fresh thyme or bay leaf

instructions: Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pan — a large skillet or sauté pan that gives the vegetables room to spread and evaporate efficiently. Add the finely diced onion and red bell pepper along with a generous pinch of salt and the thyme or bay leaf. Set the heat to medium-low — not a gentle sizzle, not a full fry, but a slow, patient cook where the oil is barely moving and the vegetables sweat rather than brown. Stir every 3–4 minutes. Cook for 20–25 minutes: the onion will go through distinct stages — white and opaque, then translucent, then softened, then finally beginning to turn pale gold at the edges with a deeply sweet aroma. The pepper will collapse and its skin will soften completely. Do not rush this stage with high heat; the sweetness of sofrito comes entirely from the slow conversion of vegetable starches to sugars. A fast-cooked sofrito tastes raw and sharp; a slow one tastes like something ancient and essential.

Add the minced garlic and cook, stirring, for 90 seconds until it turns golden and fragrant — stop before it browns. Remove the pan from the heat briefly, add the smoked paprika, and stir for 10 seconds. The paprika blooms in the oil off the direct heat, releasing its fat-soluble pigment and aroma without scorching. Return the pan to medium heat and pour in the grated or blended tomato. The tomato will spit and sizzle as it hits the hot oil — stir it in vigorously and raise the heat to medium. Let the tomato reduce: this is the long stage. The water in the tomato must fully evaporate and the tomato solids must cook down and concentrate. Stir every few minutes and adjust heat as needed — you want steady activity, not violent spattering. After 30–40 minutes, the tomato will have darkened from bright red to a deep rust, the oil will separate and pool around the edges of the mass, and the paste will be thick enough to mound on a spoon without flowing. This is done sofrito.

Remove the bay leaf or thyme sprig. Taste the finished sofrito — it should be intensely sweet and savory simultaneously, with a deep tomato richness, the smoke of the paprika, and only a faint residual sharpness from the garlic. Adjust salt if needed. Transfer to a clean container to cool. Sofrito keeps refrigerated for up to 1 week and freezes beautifully in ice-cube trays for up to 3 months — a tray of frozen sofrito cubes is one of the most useful things you can have in a kitchen. Use sofrito as a base for paella, fideuà, all manner of braises, white beans, lentils, rice dishes, and stews. A tablespoon stirred into a soup that seems flat will transform it. The ratio for most applications is approximately 1 tablespoon of sofrito per serving, added at the beginning of cooking.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Ajitsuke Tamago
description: Soft-boiled eggs with a jammy, barely-set yolk, peeled and marinated overnight in a soy-mirin-sake tare until the whites stain amber and the yolks turn into a fudgy, deeply savory gold.
instructions: Bring a pot of water to a vigorous, rolling boil — enough water to cover the eggs by at least 2 cm. Lower the eggs in one at a time using a slotted spoon or spider, straight from the refrigerator (cold eggs into boiling water give more predictable timing). Boil at a steady medium-high simmer — not a furious churn that cracks the shells — for exactly 6 minutes and 30 seconds. Meanwhile, prepare an ice bath in a large bowl. At time, transfer immediately to the ice bath and chill for at least 5 minutes before peeling.

Peel the chilled eggs under a thin stream of cold running water. Crack the shell all over by rolling the egg gently on the counter, then begin peeling from the broad end where the air pocket is, slipping your thumb under the membrane. The cold water helps the membrane separate from the white cleanly. Work slowly — a 6.5-minute egg white is set but more delicate than a hard-boiled one. Pat dry with kitchen paper when done.

Combine the soy sauce, mirin, sake, water, and kombu in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat and cook for 3 minutes to cook off the alcohol from the sake and let the kombu begin releasing its glutamates. Remove the kombu after 4 minutes total (over-steeped kombu turns slimy and bitter). Cool the tare completely to room temperature before adding the eggs — adding warm eggs to warm tare cooks the yolk further. The tare can be prepared hours ahead.

Place the peeled eggs in a zip-lock bag or a snug container just large enough to hold them. Pour the cooled tare over the eggs and seal the bag, pressing out the air so the tare contacts every surface of each egg. Refrigerate for at least 4 hours; overnight (8–12 hours) is ideal. Do not exceed 24 hours — the salt will tighten the white to a rubbery, overly-dense texture and the yolk will lose its fudginess. Turn the bag occasionally so all sides marinate evenly.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Bavarian Soft Pretzel
description: A dense, chewy braid of strong wheat dough dipped in baking-soda lye solution, salted, and baked until mahogany-brown with a shatteringly crisp skin and a soft, salt-flecked center.

ingredients.text: 1.5 % Barley malt syrup or brown sugar
4 % of bath water Baking soda (for bath, 4% solution)

instructions: Combine the flour, yeast, and malt syrup. Add the warm water and butter and mix until a shaggy dough forms. Add the salt and knead by hand for 10–12 minutes or 8 minutes in a stand mixer with the dough hook. Pretzel dough should be stiff — stiffer than pizza dough, drier than sandwich bread dough. The low hydration (58%) and strong flour create the dense, tight crumb and chewy bite characteristic of an authentic pretzel. The dough should clear the sides of the bowl and feel firm to a confident press. Do not add extra water. Cover and bulk-ferment 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

Divide the dough into 8 equal pieces (about 90 g each). On an unfloured surface, roll each piece into a rope 50–60 cm (20–24 inches) long, thicker in the center and tapered at the ends. To form the pretzel knot: hold the rope at both ends, cross the ends over to form a loop, twist the ends once around each other, and fold the twist down to press onto the lower sides of the loop. The pretzel shape should be defined with a visible fat belly and distinct arms. Place shaped pretzels on parchment-lined trays and freeze for 10 minutes — a firm dough takes the lye bath without losing its shape.

Bring 2 liters of water to a boil, then add the baking soda carefully — it will foam dramatically. Reduce to a gentle simmer. Working one or two at a time, lower each shaped pretzel into the soda bath using a slotted spoon or spider for 20–30 seconds per side. The alkaline bath (pH ~12 with baking soda, higher with food-grade lye) denatures the surface proteins into a gel that sets into the characteristic shiny, mahogany crust during baking. Baking soda yields a milder flavor and safer handling than lye; lye gives a deeper mahogany and more pronounced alkaline flavor (Brezel-Geschmack). Remove with the slotted spoon, let the excess drip, and lay back on the parchment. Immediately scatter coarse salt on the fat belly of each pretzel while the surface is wet and sticky.

Bake at 425°F / 220°C for 16–20 minutes, rotating the tray halfway, until the pretzels are a deep, uniform mahogany brown — the color of dark caramel, not light toast. The Maillard reaction proceeds vigorously in the alkaline environment created by the soda bath, which is why pretzels brown faster and darker than regular bread. A pale pretzel is an underdone pretzel. Transfer to a wire rack and eat within 2 hours — soft pretzels are best warm and lose their crust crisping within a few hours of baking.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Bavarian Soft Pretzels
description: A twisted rope of lean dough bathed in lye solution bakes to a mahogany crust with a deep, alkaline tang, a chewy-dense crumb, and a snowfall of coarse salt that cracks between your teeth like edible gravel. This is the bread of Oktoberfest and every Bavarian beer hall worth its Weissbier.

ingredients.text: 3 % Food-grade sodium hydroxide lye (3–4% solution in cold water — use gloves)

instructions: Combine the flour, salt, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer (or a large mixing bowl). In a separate vessel, dissolve the malt syrup in the warm water, then add the softened butter in small pieces. Pour the liquid into the dry ingredients and mix on low speed with a dough hook for 2 minutes until the shaggy mass comes together. The dough should be noticeably stiffer than a bread or focaccia dough — this is intentional. A stiff dough holds the pretzel shape.

Knead on medium speed for 8–10 minutes (or 12–15 minutes by hand) until the dough is smooth, slightly tacky but not sticky, and passes the windowpane test: a small piece stretched between two thumbs and forefingers should stretch to a translucent membrane without tearing. The gluten development is essential — under-developed pretzel dough tears during shaping. Form into a ball, cover with a damp cloth, and let rest at room temperature for 1 hour until doubled.

Divide the rested dough into 8 equal pieces (about 100 g each for standard pretzels). Roll each piece into a rope 60–70 cm long, keeping the center thicker (about 3 cm diameter) and tapering to thin ends (5–7 mm). To form the pretzel: make a U-shape with the rope, cross the two ends twice (a double twist), then fold the twisted ends down and press them firmly onto the fat middle portion at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions. Press firmly — the seal must hold through boiling and baking. Place on parchment-lined baking sheets and refrigerate uncovered for 30 minutes to firm up before dipping.

SAFETY: Wear rubber gloves and eye protection. Prepare a 3–4% lye solution by adding sodium hydroxide to cold water (never the reverse — always add lye to water). Working with cold lye solution, briefly submerge each pretzel for 20–30 seconds per side, then transfer immediately to a lye-safe (non-reactive) surface or directly to parchment-lined baking trays. Alternatively, use baked baking soda solution (boil 1 L water with 60 g baked baking soda) for a safer but less dramatic crust. Score the fat belly with a sharp knife or lame in a single confident cut. Sprinkle with pretzel salt immediately.

Bake at 220 C (425 F) on the middle rack for 16–20 minutes until the belly is deeply mahogany and the twisted section has darkened further to near-black. The crust should sound hollow when tapped. The pretzel salt will have fused slightly into the surface. Remove and cool on a wire rack for at least 5 minutes. Bavarian pretzels are best eaten within 2 hours of baking — the crust softens as they cool and becomes leathery by the next day.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sole Meunière
description: The dish that made Julia Child fall in love with France — a whole Dover sole dredged in flour and laid in foaming butter until its skin crackles gold, then bathed in nutty noisette butter sharpened with a squeeze of lemon and a flurry of parsley. Three simple things done perfectly: flour, butter, fish.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Whole Dover sole (skinned dark side, scaled, trimmed)
1 parts Fine sea salt & white pepper
25 parts Cold unsalted butter (for the noisette)
8 parts Lemon (juice of, plus wedges to serve)

instructions: Pat the sole bone-dry on both sides. Season all over with salt and white pepper. Just before cooking, lay the fish in the flour, press lightly, turn, and coat the second side, then lift and pat off every loose speck — you want the thinnest possible veil, not a crust. Flour too early and it goes pasty; flour at the last second so it stays dry and powdery.

Heat the clarified butter in a wide pan until it foams and just begins to smell nutty. Lay the sole in presentation-side down and fry without moving it, 3-4 minutes, until the underside is crisp and deep gold. Flip once with a long spatula and cook the second side 2-3 minutes more, basting the top with the hot butter. The flesh is done the instant it turns opaque and lifts from the bone.

Wipe the pan and return it to medium heat. Drop in the cold butter and let it melt, foam, and then quietly sizzle as the water cooks off. Swirl constantly as the milk solids fall to the bottom and toast from pale to hazelnut brown, 2-3 minutes — pull it the moment it smells of toasted nuts, because it tips from noisette to burnt in seconds.

Off the heat, squeeze the lemon juice into the brown butter — it will hiss and foam — and stir in most of the parsley. Spoon the foaming lemon-butter generously over the waiting sole, scatter the remaining parsley on top, and serve at once with lemon wedges. The sauce should arrive still bubbling, so the fish hits the table at its crispest.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Green Papaya Salad (Som Tam)
description: A study in controlled violence — green papaya, bird's eye chilies, garlic, lime, fish sauce, and palm sugar pounded in a clay mortar until the papaya weeps its juices into the dressing, creating a salad that is simultaneously crunchy, sour, salty, hot, and subtly sweet. Born in the rice paddies of Isan, eaten everywhere in Thailand.

ingredients.text: 4 parts Green (unripe) papaya, peeled and julienned (about 2 cups)
1 parts Bird's eye chilies (prik kee noo), 2–5 depending on heat preference
1 parts Fish sauce (or soy sauce for vegan version)
1 parts Cherry tomatoes, halved (or 1 Roma tomato, quartered)
0.5 parts Long beans (tua fak yao), cut in 5 cm pieces (optional, traditional)

instructions: Place the bird's eye chilies and garlic in the mortar. Pound with decisive, rhythmic strokes until they are roughly broken — not a paste, but crushed and fragrant. The goal here is not smoothness but bruising: you want the cell walls ruptured so their oils bleed into the dressing. This takes 30–60 seconds of firm pounding. The garlic should be in irregular pieces, the chilies split and releasing seeds. The heat you see here is proportional to the number of chilies — taste a tiny piece before committing.

Add the palm sugar and dried shrimp to the mortar. Continue pounding, this time more gently — you are trying to dissolve the palm sugar into the chili-garlic juices and break the dried shrimp into small pieces, not pulverize everything further. Pound for 30 seconds, then add the lime juice and fish sauce. Stir to combine with the pestle rather than pounding. Taste the raw dressing: it should be aggressively seasoned — very sour, very salty, visibly spicy. It will seem over-seasoned until the papaya absorbs it.

Add the cherry tomatoes and long bean pieces to the mortar. Use the pestle to lightly bruise them — you want the tomatoes to burst and release their juice into the dressing, and the beans to be lightly crushed to absorb flavor, not turned into mush. 3–4 firm presses on each tomato is sufficient. Use a large spoon or spatula to fold the released tomato juices into the dressing. The mortar should now be a fragrant pool of intensely seasoned dressing with tomato, bean, and shrimp pieces.

Add the julienned green papaya to the mortar in batches. Using a combination of the pestle and a large spoon, toss and lightly pound the papaya — you want to bruise it enough to absorb the dressing without turning it limp or breaking the shreds. Add the remaining lime juice and fish sauce, fold to combine. Add more lime juice, fish sauce, or palm sugar to calibrate: the best som tam is loud and assertive on all three axes. Pile onto a plate or serve directly from the mortar. Scatter crushed peanuts over the top immediately before serving. Serve with sticky rice.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Som Tum (Green Papaya Salad)
description: Shredded unripe papaya pounded with garlic, chilies, lime, fish sauce, and palm sugar — a kinetic balance of sour, salty, sweet, and incendiary heat that is simultaneously refreshing and addictive.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Green (unripe) papaya (peeled, shredded or julienned)
4 parts Bird's eye chilies (prik kee noo)
15 parts Long beans or green beans (cut in 3 cm lengths)

instructions: Place the garlic and bird's eye chilies in a large Thai clay mortar (krok din). Pound with the pestle until the garlic and chilies are roughly broken — not a smooth paste. You want visible chunks of garlic and chili, the oils released but the texture still coarse and chunky. Reduce or increase the number of chilies according to heat preference: 2 chilies is mild, 5 is Thai-market standard, 8 is Isaan-grandmother level.

Add the long bean pieces to the mortar and pound gently 4 to 5 times to bruise and split them — they should crack and release juice but not turn to mush. Add the halved cherry tomatoes and pound another 3 to 4 times until the tomatoes burst and release their juice into the mortar. Add the dried shrimp and pound once or twice to incorporate. The goal throughout is bruising, not pureeing — you want the vegetables to break open and release their liquid into the dressing, not dissolve.

Add the palm sugar, fish sauce, and lime juice to the mortar. Use the pestle to stir and lightly bruise to dissolve the palm sugar. Taste the dressing with a spoon — it should be aggressively sour from lime, salty from fish sauce, and sweet from palm sugar, with the heat of the chili building at the finish. Adjust the balance now before adding the papaya. The dressing should be slightly more intense than desired in the finished dish, as the papaya will dilute it.

Add the shredded green papaya to the mortar in several handfuls. Use the pestle to lightly pound and the spoon to simultaneously toss — a two-hand technique that bruises the papaya slightly while coating every strand in dressing. Pound lightly 5 to 6 times while turning with the spoon, then taste and adjust seasoning. Add roasted peanuts and toss once more. Serve immediately in the mortar or transfer to a serving plate. Som tum does not keep — the acid wilts the papaya within 30 minutes.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sauce Soubise
description: Béchamel turned silken and sweet by a purée of onions sweated low and slow until they surrender all their bite. Pale, glossy, faintly perfumed — the classic partner to roast meats, eggs, and anything that wants a soft allium hum.
instructions: Melt the butter over low heat, add the sliced onions and a pinch of salt, and cover with a lid or a cartouche. Sweat them gently for 20-30 minutes, stirring now and then, until completely meltingly soft and translucent. This is sweating, not sautéing — the onions must NOT take on any color, or the finished sauce will turn gray and taste of fried onion instead of sweet.

In a separate pan, melt the butter until foaming but not browning, whisk in the flour, and cook 2-3 minutes over medium-low heat to a pale white roux, stirring constantly. Keep it white to protect the sauce's delicate color.

Stream in the warm milk, whisking constantly, then simmer gently 8-10 minutes to a nappe consistency that coats the back of a spoon. Season with nutmeg and white pepper. Keep it on the thicker side — the watery onions will loosen the final purée.

Stir the sweated onions into the béchamel and simmer together a few minutes to marry. Purée smooth with a blender or immersion blender, then pass through a fine sieve for the silkiest texture — push the purée through with a ladle and discard any fibers left behind. Taste and adjust salt; finish with a knob of butter for gloss if you like.
notes: Béchamel enriched with a silky purée of slow-sweated onions — classic with roast meats and eggs.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Cheese Soufflé
description: A trembling column of Gruyère and Parmesan that rises from its ramekin like a crown — its crust cracks to reveal a molten, eggy interior threaded with nutmeg and sharp cheese.

ingredients.text: 30 g Unsalted butter (plus extra for greasing)
20 g Parmesan (finely grated, plus extra for dusting)
5 g Egg whites (large, at room temperature)

instructions: Preheat oven to 190 C (375 F) with a rack in the lower third. Generously butter four 200 ml ramekins, coating the sides with upward strokes. Dust the interior of each with finely grated Parmesan, tilting and tapping to coat evenly, then knock out any excess. Place on a baking sheet and refrigerate until the base is ready — cold walls help the soufflé grip and climb.

Melt butter in a heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add flour all at once and stir vigorously for 90 seconds until the roux smells of cooked pastry but is still pale. Pull the pan from heat and pour in the warm milk in one steady stream, whisking constantly to prevent lumps. Return to medium heat and whisk until the béchamel thickens to a stiff, glossy paste — it should pull away from the pan walls. Remove from heat. Beat in the egg yolks one at a time, then fold in both cheeses, salt, nutmeg, and cayenne. Cover the surface with plastic wrap and keep warm.

Ensure the bowl and whisk are perfectly clean and grease-free. Add a tiny pinch of salt to the egg whites. Whip on medium speed until foamy, then increase to high and whip until stiff, glossy peaks form. The whites should hold their shape firmly when the whisk is inverted but the very tips may curl ever so slightly — this is perfect. Do not whip to dry, dull peaks.

Stir a large spoonful (about one-quarter) of the stiff whites vigorously into the warm cheese base to lighten it. This sacrificial spoonful opens the texture. Using a wide spatula, gently fold the remaining whites into the base in three additions: cut down through the center, sweep along the bottom, and roll up the sides, rotating the bowl a quarter turn after each stroke. Stop the instant no white streaks remain. Every unnecessary fold costs lift.

Fill each prepared ramekin to within 1 cm of the rim. Run your thumb around the inside lip of each ramekin to create a shallow groove — this guides the soufflé to rise straight up rather than mushrooming to one side. Bake at 190 C (375 F) for 12–14 minutes without opening the oven door. Serve immediately the moment they come out — a soufflé waits for no one.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Soupe à l'Oignon Gratinée
description: Onions slow-cooked until impossibly sweet and jammy, then simmered in beef stock and poured over toasted bread, buried under molten, bubbling Gruyère — the Parisian cure for anything.

ingredients.text: 15 parts Baguette slices (1 cm thick, toasted)
2 parts Fine salt and black pepper

instructions: Melt the butter in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-low heat. Add all the onions with a generous pinch of salt and stir to coat. Cook uncovered, stirring every 5–8 minutes, for 45–60 minutes total. Do not rush this: the onions must pass through transparent, then blond, then golden, then a deep mahogany-brown. They should reduce to roughly one-fifth of their original volume and smell sweet and nutty, never scorched.

Pour in the white wine and scrape vigorously with a wooden spoon to lift all the browned fond from the pot bottom. Add the thyme sprigs. Let the wine reduce until almost completely absorbed, about 3–4 minutes — you should hear an aggressive sizzle that fades to a quiet bubble.

Pour in the beef stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 20 minutes, allowing the onion sweetness and stock depth to meld. Taste and correct seasoning with salt and pepper. Fish out the thyme stems.

Ladle the hot soup into oven-safe crocks placed on a baking sheet. Float one or two toasted baguette slices on each surface. Pile the Gruyère generously over the bread and the rim — the cheese should completely cover the surface and drape over the edge of each crock. Broil on the top rack for 4–6 minutes until the cheese is deeply golden, bubbling, and spotted with brown blisters.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sourdough Boule
description: A high-hydration country loaf born of wild yeast and patience — its crust shatters like porcelain, its crumb opens in dramatic, irregular caves that catch butter and hold jam. This is the Pacific Northwest's daily bread: naturally leavened, deeply flavored, unapologetically sour.
instructions: Combine flour and water in a large bowl. Mix by hand until no dry flour remains — this takes about 2 minutes of rough mixing. The dough will be shaggy and rough, almost reluctant. Cover and rest at room temperature for 30–60 minutes. During this rest, the flour's enzymes begin breaking down proteins and starch, and gluten bonds form without any mechanical effort. When you return to the dough, it will have visibly smoothed and relaxed.

Add the active starter and scatter the salt over the dough surface. Dimple the salt in with your fingers, then perform a series of 4 stretch-and-folds: wet your hand, reach under one side of the dough, stretch it up until you feel resistance, then fold it over the top. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat all the way around. Do this for 4 rounds total, spaced 30 minutes apart. After the last fold, let the dough bulk ferment undisturbed at 75–78°F (24–26°C) for a total of 4–5 hours from when starter was added, until it has grown by 50–75% and is visibly bubbly throughout.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Fold the edges in toward the center, then flip it seam-side down. Using both hands cupped around the dough, drag it toward you across the bench with gentle downward pressure — the friction tightens the surface. Repeat this motion 4–5 times, rotating slightly each pass, until the boule has a taut, smooth top with no tears. Transfer seam-side up into a well-floured banneton (rice flour is ideal) or a flour-dusted bowl lined with a floured tea towel. The boule should hold a round shape and not sag sideways.

Refrigerate the shaped boule, covered, for 10–16 hours (overnight is ideal). The cold retard slows fermentation while allowing the sour flavor to develop and the dough to firm up for cleaner scoring. The dough does not need to look dramatically different after retarding — a slight increase in size is normal. Bake directly from the refrigerator without warming to room temperature; the cold dough will score more cleanly.

Place a Dutch oven in the oven and preheat to 500°F (260°C) for at least 45 minutes. When oven-hot, remove the boule from the refrigerator. Cut a large square of parchment to act as a sling. Flip the cold boule seam-side down onto the parchment. Using a lame or sharp bread knife held at a 30–45° angle, score a single confident arc across the top — the ear — with one continuous stroke. Depth should be about ½ inch (1.2 cm). Additional decorative scores can be added perpendicular, but the main ear is the pressure valve.

Lower the boule on its parchment into the preheated Dutch oven. Cover with the lid and bake at 500°F for 20 minutes (the steam from the dough creates the oven-spring environment). Remove the lid, drop the temperature to 460°F (238°C), and bake a further 20–25 minutes uncovered until the crust is a deep mahogany-brown. Remove from the Dutch oven and cool on a wire rack for at least 1 hour before cutting — the crumb is still setting up inside.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Rustic Sourdough Loaf
description: A hearty open-crumb sourdough with a shattering mahogany crust — built on wild fermentation, cold time, and the living tang of an active starter. The crumb is irregular and custardy; the crust sings as it cools.
instructions: Combine bread flour and cool water in a large bowl. Stir with wet hands or a dough whisk until absolutely no dry flour remains — scrape the bowl bottom. The dough will be rough and shaggy. Cover tightly with a damp towel or plastic wrap and rest for 45 minutes. During this rest, flour proteins absorb water and gluten begins organizing without any kneading effort. Do not add starter or salt yet.

Wet the work surface lightly. Pour the active starter over the autolyse dough; scatter the salt on top. Perform a lamination fold: stretch the dough out into a wide, thin rectangle, fold it into thirds like a letter, then fold into thirds again the other direction. Gather back into the bowl. This weaves the starter and salt into every gluten layer in one pass. Then perform one set of stretch-and-folds to unify the mass.

Cover the bowl and bulk ferment at room temperature (21–23 C / 70–73 F) for 4–5 hours. During the first 2 hours perform four sets of stretch-and-folds, one set every 30 minutes. For each set: wet your hand, grab one side of the dough, pull up as high as it will stretch without tearing, fold over the center. Rotate 90 degrees and repeat four times total. After the last set, leave completely undisturbed for the remainder of the bulk.

Dust a round banneton generously with rice flour. Tip the bulk dough onto a bare, unfloured work surface. Pre-shape: fold the edges in toward the center, flip seam-side down, and drag the ball gently across the table surface to build tension. Cover and rest 20 minutes. Final shape: flip the round, stretch to a loose oval, fold the far third to center, the near third over that, then roll toward you with both hands tucked under to tighten. Place seam-side up in the banneton. Cover with plastic and refrigerate 12–16 hours.

One hour before baking, preheat a Dutch oven with its lid on at 260 C (500 F). Score the cold loaf with a lame or razor blade: a single confident slash at 30–45 degrees to the surface, about 1 cm deep. Lift from the banneton using a parchment sling and lower into the screaming-hot Dutch oven. Bake covered 20 minutes — steam from the cold dough lets the loaf spring and bloom. Remove the lid, lower heat to 230 C (450 F), and bake 22–27 minutes more until deeply caramel-brown.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sourdough Country Loaf
description: A naturally leavened open-crumb loaf built from active starter, high-hydration dough, cold retard overnight, and baked in a Dutch oven until the crust shatters and the interior glistens.
instructions: Combine the bread flour and whole wheat flour in a large bowl. Pour in the water (holding back about 30 g for the salt later) and mix with your hand until no dry flour remains — squeeze and fold until the mass is shaggy and fully hydrated. Cover and rest 30–60 minutes at room temperature. The autolyse lets enzymes begin degrading the starches and the gluten proteins hydrate and loosely align without mechanical work, making subsequent mixing far more efficient and giving the crumb a silkier extensibility.

Dissolve the salt in the reserved water, then pour starter and salt water over the autolysed dough. Use the pinch-and-fold method: pinch the starter through the dough in 10–15 passes until integrated. Then begin the series of stretch-and-folds: every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, grab one edge of the dough, stretch it up until you feel resistance, and fold it to the opposite side. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat four times per set. After four sets, leave the dough covered to finish bulk fermentation — roughly 10–14 hours at 68°F / 20°C, or 4–5 hours at 76°F / 24°C. The dough is ready when it has grown by 50–75%, feels airy and domed, and a flap peeled back shows a network of bubbles just below the surface.

Turn the dough gently onto an unfloured surface. Using a bench scraper and one cupped hand, do a pre-shape: drag the dough toward you while the scraper pushes from behind, rotating to build surface tension into a loose round. Rest uncovered 20–30 minutes (bench rest). Then flour the top of the round generously, flip it, and do the final shape: for a boule, grab the far edge, fold it to the center, then fold left, right, and roll the whole package toward you, using your palms to drag and seal the bottom seam tight against the bench. The surface should be taut like a drum. Drop seam-side-up into a well-floured (rice flour is ideal) banneton or a bowl lined with a floured towel. Pinch the seam closed. Cover and refrigerate 12–16 hours.

Preheat the oven with a Dutch oven (lid on) inside to 500°F / 260°C for at least 45 minutes. Turn the cold loaf out of the banneton onto a piece of parchment. Working fast, score with a lame or sharp razor blade held at a 30–45° angle: a single ear cut down one side of the dome, or a bold cross-hatch. The cut should be decisive and swift — 5–7 cm deep — not a timid scratch. The cold dough (straight from the fridge) is easiest to score cleanly.

Using the parchment as a sling, lower the loaf into the screaming-hot Dutch oven and put the lid on. Bake covered at 500°F / 260°C for 20 minutes — steam from the dough trapped inside the pot creates the glossy, extensible crust needed for maximum oven spring. Remove the lid, drop the temperature to 460°F / 238°C, and bake a further 20–25 minutes until the crust is deep mahogany and an instant-read thermometer at the center reads 205–210°F / 96–99°C. Transfer to a wire rack and resist cutting for at least 1 hour — the interior crumb is still setting via residual heat.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sourdough Discard Pancakes
description: A zero-waste weekend pancake that transforms unfed sourdough discard into tall, fluffy rounds with a subtle tang and a crumb shot through with tiny tunnels from baking soda reacting with the starter's acid.
instructions: In a large bowl, combine the sourdough discard, milk, eggs, melted butter, and maple syrup. Whisk until the discard is fully broken up and the mixture is uniform. The discard should dissolve smoothly into the milk and eggs — if your discard is particularly stiff, whisk it with the milk first until smooth before adding the eggs. The wet mix will smell pleasantly tangy from the discard.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the flour, baking soda, and salt. Pour the dry ingredients into the wet all at once. Fold with a rubber spatula using large, sweeping strokes — just 10–15 folds until the dry ingredients are barely incorporated. The batter will be lumpy. This is correct. Over-mixing activates the gluten and produces tough, chewy pancakes instead of tender, fluffy ones. Stop mixing when you still see a few streaks of flour — they will hydrate during the rest.

Heat a cast-iron or non-stick skillet over medium heat for 3 minutes. Lightly grease with butter or neutral oil, wiping away excess with a paper towel — too much fat causes uneven browning and no crust. Pour a ladleful (about 80 ml) of batter per pancake. Do not spread it — let it pool naturally. Watch the surface: bubbles will appear at the edges first, then march toward the center. Flip when bubbles cover most of the surface AND the edges look set and matte (not shiny). Cook 90 seconds on the second side. Serve immediately — pancakes lose their steam-puffed height within minutes.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sourdough Focaccia
description: A slow-fermented sourdough focaccia — pools of olive oil settling into finger-pressed dimples over an open, webbed crumb, finished with flaky salt and rosemary, the crust crackling and caramelized on the bottom.

ingredients.text: 20 parts Active sourdough starter (100% hydration, fed 8–12 hrs ago)
15 parts Extra-virgin olive oil (for pan and dimpling)

instructions: Verify the starter is active: it should float in water and smell pleasantly sour and yeasty. Combine warm water, starter, and olive oil in a large bowl. Add flour and salt. Mix with a wet hand or a spatula until no dry flour remains — about 3 minutes. Unlike commercial-yeast focaccia, this dough moves more slowly and benefits from patience. Cover and let rest 30 minutes for autolyse.

Perform four sets of coil folds over 2 hours: wet your hand, slide it under the dough, lift the whole mass, and let it fold under itself. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat. Perform one set every 30 minutes for the first two hours. After the fourth set, cover and let bulk ferment at room temperature until the dough is 50–75% larger, visibly bubbly, and airy — typically another 3–5 hours depending on room temperature and starter strength.

Pour a generous pool of olive oil (at least 3 tablespoons) into a half-sheet pan. Tip the dough in and gently stretch it toward the edges. Cover loosely with plastic and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) for a slow, cold final proof. The next day, remove from the refrigerator 2 hours before baking. The dough should have spread to fill most of the pan and look puffy and airy.

Drizzle additional olive oil generously over the surface of the dough. Spread your fingers wide and press them firmly through the dough to the pan bottom, creating deep dimples across the entire surface. Don't be timid — press firmly. Scatter fresh rosemary sprigs and flaky sea salt. The oil will pool in the dimples. Bake immediately at 230 C (450 F).

Bake at 230 C (450 F) on the lower-middle rack for 20–25 minutes until the top is deeply golden with darker blistered spots at the dimple peaks and the bottom is crispy and caramelized. Lift a corner with a spatula to check the bottom. Remove from the pan immediately to a wire rack to preserve the crisp bottom.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sourdough Pizza Dough
description: A naturally leavened variant that swaps commercial yeast for a mature sourdough starter. Longer ferment, deeper flavor, more open crumb. The tang is a feature, not a bug.
instructions: Combine flour and water. Mix until no dry flour remains. Do not add starter yet — let the flour hydrate alone.
Cover and let the dough rest for 45-60 minutes. The flour absorbs water and gluten organizes without work.
Add the starter and salt. Squeeze through the dough to distribute, then perform 4 sets of stretch-and-folds at 30-minute intervals.
Cover. Bulk ferment at room temperature for 6-10 hours (or overnight in the fridge). The dough should grow 50-75%, not double.
Divide into portions. Pre-shape into rounds, rest 15 minutes, then shape into tight balls. Refrigerate for 12-24 hours before using.
notes: Replaced commercial yeast with sourdough starter. Longer ferment, more complex flavor, slightly tangier crumb.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sourdough Sandwich Loaf
description: A soft, Pullman-style American sandwich loaf leavened entirely by an active sourdough starter — tender enough to slice thin for toast yet tangy enough that you taste the ferment on the back of every bite. The crumb is pillowy and close-knit, the crust thin and golden, and the whole kitchen smells like a proper bakery for hours.

ingredients.text: 20 % Active sourdough starter (100% hydration, fed 8h ago)

instructions: Combine the flour, water, active starter, and honey in a large bowl. Stir with a wooden spoon or dough whisk until no dry flour remains. The dough will be rough and sticky — resist the urge to add more flour. Cover with a damp towel and let it rest (autolyse) for 30 minutes. This rest allows the flour to fully hydrate and gluten to begin forming without any kneading, which reduces mixing time significantly and improves the crumb structure. Check that your starter is truly active: it should have doubled since feeding and smell yeasty and pleasantly sour.

Sprinkle the salt over the rested dough and squeeze it through the dough with your fingers until evenly distributed — about 2 minutes of aggressive squeezing. Add the softened butter in small pieces and continue squeezing and folding until fully absorbed. Perform stretch-and-folds: wet your hand, grab the far edge of the dough, stretch it up overhead without tearing, and fold it over the center. Rotate 90 degrees and repeat — 4 folds equals one round. Do 4 rounds total, spaced 30 minutes apart, over 2 hours. By the final round the dough should be smooth, strong, and clearly elastic.

Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled container and bulk-ferment at room temperature (21–24 C) for 8–10 hours, or overnight in the refrigerator (4 C) for 12–14 hours. The cold retard slows fermentation and develops deeper sour flavor — for a tangier loaf, always go cold. The dough is ready when it has grown by 50–75% in volume (not doubled, as sourdough is slower), feels lighter and jiggly, and small bubbles are visible along the sides and bottom of the container. Dimples pressed into the surface spring back slowly and lazily.

Turn the dough onto an unfloured surface. Gently pat it into a rectangle roughly the length of your loaf pan. Fold the long sides in toward the center like a letter, then roll it tightly from the top, sealing the seam with your thumbs as you go. You want surface tension without degassing the crumb — firm but not aggressive rolling. Lower the log seam-side down into a well-greased 9x5 inch (23x13 cm) loaf pan. The dough should fill the pan about 60–65% and sit slightly below the rim.

Cover the pan with oiled plastic wrap and proof at room temperature (21–24 C) for 3–5 hours, or until the dome of the dough crests about 2 cm above the rim of the pan. If you retarded the bulk in the fridge, the final proof will take the longer end of this range. You can also do a cold final proof overnight in the fridge for baking the next morning — pull it directly from the fridge into the oven. Thirty minutes before baking, preheat the oven to 200 C (400 F).

Score a shallow slash down the center of the loaf (optional but gives the crust a controlled split). Bake at 200 C (400 F) for 35–40 minutes, covering the pan loosely with foil for the first 20 minutes to keep the crust from browning too fast before the crumb sets. Remove the foil and continue baking until the internal temperature reads 93–96 C (200–205 F) and the top is a rich golden brown. Let cool in the pan 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Do not slice for at least 1 hour — the crumb continues to set as the bread cools.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Sourdough Starter
description: A living culture built from nothing but flour and water — coaxed over a week from a flat, lifeless slurry into a billowing, sweet-sour leaven that doubles on schedule and smells of ripe yogurt and green apple. Feed it, watch it breathe, and it will raise bread for a lifetime.

ingredients.text: 50 g Whole rye flour (for the first build — high in wild yeast and enzymes)
50 g Unbleached bread or all-purpose flour (for daily feeds)
50 g Mature starter discard (carried forward at each feed)

instructions: In a clean glass jar, stir the whole rye flour and warm water into a thick, lump-free paste — the consistency of pancake batter. Scrape down the sides, mark the level with a rubber band or tape, and cover loosely so gas can escape but the surface stays protected. Rest at warm room temperature, 24–26°C, for 24 hours. Rye carries a dense population of wild yeast and lactic bacteria plus the enzymes that feed them, so it kick-starts a culture faster than white flour ever could.

Begin daily feeds. Discard all but about 50 g of the slurry, then stir in equal weights of fresh flour and warm water — roughly 50 g each. Switch to unbleached bread or all-purpose flour now; it builds the gluten strength you want in a leaven. Re-mark the level, cover loosely, and keep warm. Feed once every 24 hours for days 3 and 4. Discarding keeps the culture young and the acid low enough for the yeast to multiply; without it the mixture turns too sour for the yeast to thrive.

From around day 5, feed twice daily, every 12 hours, discarding to ~50 g each time and refreshing with equal flour and water. The culture should now be reliable: rising and falling on a predictable rhythm. Watch one full cycle from feed to peak — when it consistently doubles within 4–8 hours and smells sweet-sour and ripe, it is mature. Confirm readiness with the float test: drop a spoonful of peaked starter into water. If it floats, it is buoyant with gas and ready to leaven bread.

To keep the starter alive long-term, settle into a maintenance feed: carry forward 50 g of mature starter, discard the rest, and refresh with 50 g flour and 50 g water (a 1:1:1 ratio). If baking often, hold it at room temperature and feed once or twice daily. If baking occasionally, store it in the fridge and feed weekly — let it warm and rise once at room temperature before each bake. A well-kept starter improves for years, deepening in flavor and reliability.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Bobotie
description: A Cape Malay baked dish where curried minced lamb or beef — sweetened with apricot jam, sharpened with lemon, and perfumed with turmeric and cinnamon — is crowned with a quivering, golden egg custard that sets soft as a just-firm crème brûlée.

ingredients.text: 1 parts Curry powder, turmeric, cinnamon, allspice
0.5 parts White wine vinegar or lemon juice
1 parts White bread slices, soaked in milk and squeezed

instructions: Fry the onion in a splash of oil over medium heat until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the spices and fry for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the mince and cook, breaking it up, for 8–10 minutes until browned and cooked through with no pink remaining. Stir in the apricot jam and vinegar. Taste — the filling should be sweet, savory, and warmly spiced with a background sharpness. Season with salt and pepper. The sweetness and acidity are what make this distinctly Cape Malay rather than a standard curry mince.

Squeeze the milk-soaked bread firmly to remove excess liquid, then crumble it into the meat filling and mix well. The bread acts as a binder and moisture reservoir — it keeps the filling from drying out during baking and gives it a slightly soft, yielding texture beneath the custard. Transfer the filling to a buttered oven dish (about 30 x 20 cm), pressing it down into an even layer. Tuck bay leaves on top. Preheat oven to 180 °C.

Whisk the eggs and milk together with a pinch of salt and turmeric until smooth and uniformly yellow. Pour the custard mixture slowly and evenly over the meat layer. The custard should cover the surface completely and be visible around the edges — about 1 cm deep. Bake at 180 °C for 35–40 minutes until the custard is just set throughout and golden on top. The center should barely wobble when the dish is shaken.

Rest the bobotie for 5 minutes out of the oven — this allows the custard to fully set and the filling to firm up so it cuts cleanly. Serve in squares directly from the dish, accompanied by yellow rice (cooked with turmeric and raisins), chutney, and sliced banana. Remove and discard bay leaves before serving. A proper bobotie plate should have sweetness (banana, chutney), warmth (the spiced filling), and the silky custard acting as a gentle, binding crown.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: South Indian Idli Batter
description: Parboiled rice and split black lentils, soaked separately and ground to a silky batter, then left overnight to ferment until airy and slightly sour — the foundation of idli, dosa, and uttapam across South India.

ingredients.text: 1 parts Urad dal (split black gram, husked)
1.5 tsp per cup of batter Non-iodized salt
0.25 tsp per cup of urad Fenugreek seeds (methi)

instructions: Rinse the rice 3-4 times until the water runs clear. Rinse the urad dal and fenugreek seeds together 2-3 times. Soak them in separate bowls of cold water for 6-8 hours (or overnight). Keep the bowls in a cool spot — not refrigerated. The soaking water should cover the grains by at least 5cm as they will swell significantly. The fenugreek seeds soak with the urad dal. After soaking, drain each bowl but reserve the urad dal soaking water separately — it contains wild yeasts and bacteria that help fermentation.

Grind the urad dal and fenugreek seeds first in a wet grinder or high-powered blender with the reserved soaking water (or cold water), adding water tablespoon by tablespoon. Grind for 20-30 minutes in a wet grinder (or 5-10 minutes in a high-speed blender) until the batter is completely smooth, extremely fine, and very fluffy — it should have a whipped, airy quality from the air incorporation during grinding. The traditional wet grinder stone generates minimal heat and grinds ultra-fine. Transfer to a large bowl. Then grind the soaked rice with cold water until smooth but slightly grainy — just a bit of texture is desirable in idli rice batter. Combine both batters and mix well.

Stir the salt into the combined batter thoroughly — salt helps control unwanted bacteria during fermentation. The batter should be of a consistency that falls off a spoon in a thick ribbon. Transfer to a large container (the batter will roughly double in volume during fermentation — the container must be large enough). Cover loosely with a lid or cloth. Leave in a warm place — 28-32°C (82-90°F) is ideal. In Indian summer climates this happens overnight (8-12 hours). In cooler climates it may take 16-24 hours. The oven with only the light on (around 27°C) works well in cool kitchens. Fermentation is complete when the batter has risen significantly, looks fluffy and aerated, has a pleasant sour smell, and tiny bubbles are visible throughout.

Grease the idli molds lightly with oil. Gently stir the batter from the bottom without deflating it too much. Ladle batter into each mold, filling about three-quarters full — they will expand during steaming. Steam over vigorously boiling water for 10-12 minutes. Do not lift the lid during steaming. The idli are done when a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean and the surface is set and slightly dry. Unmold immediately after 2 minutes of cooling by running a wet spoon around each idli. They should pop out cleanly.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spanakopita Filling
description: The savory filling at the heart of every great spanakopita — wilted spinach wrung bone-dry, crumbled feta, egg, scallion, and dill stirred together into a rich, briny mixture that stays moist inside phyllo pastry.

ingredients.text: 100 % Fresh spinach, stems removed (or baby spinach)
50 % Feta cheese, crumbled (not pre-crumbled — buy a block)

instructions: Heat a large, dry skillet over high heat until it is very hot. Add the fresh spinach in large handfuls — it will collapse dramatically, reducing to a fraction of its original volume in about 1–2 minutes per batch. Stir and press the spinach to encourage even wilting. Do not add water or oil at this stage; you want the leaves to steam in their own moisture and give up as much liquid as possible. Once all the spinach has wilted, transfer it to a colander and let it cool enough to handle. Then take handfuls and squeeze them with maximum force over the sink — wring them like a wet cloth. The goal is to extract every possible drop of water. The dry spinach should feel almost gritty in your hand, not damp. Then chop the wrung spinach roughly into 1 cm pieces.

In a small skillet, warm the olive oil over medium heat. Add the sliced scallions and cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they are wilted and sweet-smelling but not browned. The goal is to take the raw edge off the scallion flavor — raw scallion in a baked filling can be sharp and pungent, whereas briefly cooked scallion becomes sweet and integrated. Remove from heat and allow to cool slightly. The scallions will continue to soften in the residual heat. They should look translucent and smell mild and sweet.

In a large bowl, combine the wrung, chopped spinach, cooled sweated scallions, crumbled feta, beaten eggs, chopped dill, black pepper, and freshly grated nutmeg. Mix thoroughly with your hands or a large spoon, breaking the feta into crumbles no larger than a small pea — some very fine feta dust is fine and helps bind the filling. Do not add salt before tasting: the feta carries significant salt and the filling may need none. Taste critically and add salt only if truly needed. The mixture should smell of fresh dill, creamy feta, and cooked spinach — fresh and grassy with a briny background. The texture should be cohesive enough to hold its shape briefly when scooped but not stiff.

Leave the combined filling to rest for 10 minutes at room temperature. During this time, the egg will begin to bind more firmly with the spinach and feta, and the dill and scallion flavors will bloom and integrate. After resting, taste once more — flavors will have mellowed and merged. Make any final adjustments: more dill if the herb flavor is too subtle, a few more grinds of pepper if it tastes flat, a drop of lemon juice if it needs brightness. The filling is now ready to be used with buttered phyllo sheets for triangles, a pan pie, or rolled cigars. It holds refrigerated for 24 hours with minimal quality loss; the flavors actually deepen slightly overnight.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spanakopita (Greek Spinach Pie)
description: Crisp, golden phyllo pastry layered with a filling of wilted spinach, crumbled feta, dill and egg — each shattering, paper-thin sheet giving way to the creamy, herby, salty filling within. The kind of pie that disappears the moment it reaches the table.

ingredients.text: 400 g Phyllo dough (fresh or fully thawed)
1000 g Fresh spinach (or frozen 500g, fully thawed and squeezed)
120 ml Olive oil or melted unsalted butter (for brushing)

instructions: If using fresh spinach, wilt it in a dry pan or with a splash of water over high heat until completely collapsed, then tip into a colander and cool. When cool enough to handle, squeeze the spinach in your fists — hard, relentlessly, handful by handful — until almost no water comes out. This is the most critical step in the recipe: residual spinach water makes the filling wet, turns the phyllo soggy, and ruins the finished pie. A kilogram of raw spinach will reduce to about 200g of dry, dark-green paste. Transfer to a large bowl and coarsely chop. Add the crumbled feta, beaten eggs, spring onions, dill, black pepper and nutmeg. Mix together with a fork until cohesive — the filling should look like a rough, green-flecked, salty mixture, not a smooth paste. Taste (carefully — the feta is already salty) and add more pepper or dill as needed. Set aside.

Preheat the oven to 190°C / 375°F. Brush a 30×22cm (or equivalent) baking pan generously with oil or melted butter. Work with phyllo quickly — it dries and tears within minutes of exposure to air; keep the stack covered with a damp towel between sheets. Lay the first sheet of phyllo in the pan, letting the excess hang over the edges. Brush the entire surface generously with oil or butter, reaching all the way to the edges and corners. Lay another sheet perpendicular to the first, brush again. Repeat this layering and brushing process until you have used roughly half the phyllo sheets (8–10 sheets depending on thickness). The fat between each layer is what creates the shatter-crisp, separated layers of the finished crust — do not skimp.

Spread the filling evenly across the phyllo base using a spatula, pressing it into an even layer and tucking it into the corners. Fold the overhanging phyllo edges inward over the filling — they will form part of the top crust. Now layer the remaining phyllo sheets over the top in the same oiled fashion, sheet by sheet, each one brushed generously. Fold or tuck the overhanging top sheets under the pie to form a neat border. Brush the entire top surface very generously with oil. Score the top layers only with a sharp knife in the portion sizes you want before baking — the classic diamond or square patterns — cutting through only the top 4–5 sheets, not all the way through to the filling. This prevents the crust from shattering uncontrollably when you cut after baking.

Bake at 190°C / 375°F for 45–55 minutes until the top is a deep, even golden-brown across its entire surface. Rotate the pan once at the halfway mark to ensure even browning. The pie is done when the scored lines have opened up and the phyllo between them has puffed and crisped, the edges are a slightly darker amber, and the kitchen smells of buttered pastry and herbs. Rest for at least 10 minutes before cutting along the pre-scored lines — the filling needs a moment to firm from liquid-eggy to sliceable. Serve warm or at room temperature; it is equally magnificent both ways.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spanish Bacalao al Pil-Pil
description: Basque salt cod confited gently in olive oil at a whisper of heat, then coaxed by swirling the pan into a trembling, ivory emulsion from its own collagen — no cream, no flour, nothing but the fish and oil.

ingredients.text: 600 g Dried salt cod (bacalao), skin-on, bone-in
2 whole Dried guindilla or árbol chili
0 g Fine sea salt (for soaking water only)

instructions: Submerge the salt cod in a large bowl of cold water, skin side up. Refrigerate for 24–48 hours, changing the water every 8 hours (at least 3 changes). The fish is ready when a small piece, tasted raw, is pleasantly salty — like a lightly seasoned piece of fish, not aggressively briny. The flesh will have rehydrated and turned from stiff board to supple, with a pearlescent color. Cut into 150g portions. Pat completely dry.

In a wide, heavy skillet or earthenware cazuela, pour all the olive oil. Add the garlic slices and dried chilies. Over very low heat, slowly bring the oil to 60–65°C — use a thermometer; it must never boil or even simmer. Gently lay the cod portions skin-side up in the oil. Confit for 12–15 minutes at this gentle temperature, carefully turning once. The oil should show only the faintest, laziest movement around the fish — almost still. Remove the cod and set aside, reserving the oil.

Remove the garlic and chilies from the oil and set aside for garnish. Return the cazuela with the oil to the very lowest heat. Return the cod to the pan, skin-side down. Begin swirling the pan in a continuous circular motion, or use a flat-mesh spider to agitate the oil in circles around the fish. The gelatin released from the cod's skin will slowly emulsify with the oil over 8–15 minutes of continuous swirling. Do not stop or add any other ingredient. The sauce will gradually turn from translucent golden oil to an opaque, ivory-cream sauce — the pil-pil.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spanish Clams with Chorizo and White Wine
description: Littleneck clams steam open in a broth of smoky chorizo fat, white wine, and garlic — the most effortless dish in the Spanish canon, and the one most likely to make you forget everything else you planned to cook.

ingredients.text: 150 g Spanish chorizo (cured, sliced into coins)
200 ml Dry white wine (Albariño or Verdejo)
3 g Smoked paprika (pimentón de la Vera)

instructions: Soak the clams in cold, lightly salted water (30g salt per liter) for 30 minutes. The clams will expel any sand and grit they are holding. Drain and scrub the shells under cold running water. Discard any clam with a cracked shell or any that does not close when tapped — these are dead and will ruin the dish. Sort through them one by one; a single bad clam can make the entire broth bitter and unpleasant.

Heat the olive oil in a wide, heavy pan with a lid over medium heat. Add the chorizo coins and cook for 2–3 minutes until the fat renders and the oil turns a vivid orange-red from the paprika in the chorizo. Add the sliced garlic and smoked paprika, cooking for 60 seconds until fragrant. Do not let the garlic brown. This rendered chorizo fat is the foundation of the entire dish.

Add the scrubbed clams to the pan and immediately pour in the white wine. Cover tightly and raise the heat to high. Cook for 4–5 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice. Begin checking at 4 minutes — the moment all (or nearly all) the clams are open, they are done. Remove the lid and add the parsley and lemon juice. Toss quickly and serve in deep bowls with crusty bread to mop the broth. Discard any clam that has not opened after 6 minutes — it was dead before cooking.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Churros with Chocolate Dipping Sauce
description: Crisp ridged batons of hot fried choux dough, deeply golden and shattering at the bite, dunked into a thick, dark Spanish-style drinking chocolate.
instructions: Combine water, butter, salt, and sugar in a medium saucepan. Bring to a rolling boil over medium-high heat, stirring to ensure the butter is fully melted. Every granule of sugar and crystal of salt must be dissolved before the flour goes in — the liquid must be at a full boil, not just simmering.

Remove the boiling liquid from heat. Add all the flour at once and stir immediately and vigorously with a wooden spoon. The dough will come together almost instantly into a rough, shaggy ball. Return to low heat and cook, stirring and pressing constantly, for 2-3 minutes until the dough pulls away from the sides cleanly and a dry film forms on the pan bottom. The dough must be dried out slightly — this is what makes churros crisp. Transfer to a piping bag fitted with a large star tip (1.5-2cm).

Heat the frying oil to 180°C (355°F) in a deep pan. Pipe 15-20cm lengths of dough directly into the hot oil, using scissors to cut each churro free from the piping bag. Fry in batches of 4-5 without crowding for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden on all sides. The ridges from the star tip should be the darkest points. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain briefly on paper towels.

Combine the caster sugar and ground cinnamon in a shallow bowl or on a plate. Toss the hot churros in the cinnamon sugar immediately after draining — while still hot, so the sugar adheres to the surface. Roll each churro to coat all sides.

Whisk the cornstarch into 3 tablespoons of the cold milk until smooth. Heat the remaining milk with the sugar in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the chopped dark chocolate and whisk constantly until melted and smooth. Add the cornstarch slurry and continue whisking over medium heat until the sauce thickens to the consistency of a pourable custard — about 3-4 minutes. The sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon heavily and not run off immediately when the spoon is tilted.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spanish Gambas al Ajillo
description: Plump shrimp sizzling in an earthenware cazuela of olive oil so fragrant with garlic and guindilla that the oil itself becomes the sauce you mop up with crusty bread.

ingredients.text: 400 g Large raw shrimp, shell-on or peeled
2 whole Dried guindilla or árbol chili, whole
15 g Fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped

instructions: Pour the olive oil into an earthenware cazuela (or heavy skillet) and place over medium-low heat. Add the sliced garlic and whole dried chilies. Allow the garlic to gently sizzle in the cold oil as it heats, infusing the oil over 3–4 minutes. The garlic should turn golden but not brown — you want aromatic infusion, not fried garlic. The oil should bubble lazily around the garlic slices.

Increase heat to high. Add the shrimp in a single layer and season with salt. They will sizzle dramatically in the hot oil. Add the sherry in a swirl around the pan — it will spatter and steam. Cook without moving for 1 minute until the underside is pink and opaque, then flip each shrimp once. Cook 30–45 seconds more. Total cook time: 2 minutes maximum. Pull from heat the moment all shrimp are pink and just curled.

Off the heat, scatter the roughly torn parsley over the shrimp and oil. The parsley will sizzle in the residual heat and release its chlorophyll fragrance into the oil. Bring the cazuela directly to the table while still sizzling. Serve with lemon wedges and crusty bread to soak up every drop of the fragrant garlic-shrimp oil — the oil is not a by-product, it is the point.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spanish Lentil Stew (Lentejas Estofadas)
description: Earthy green lentils braised low and slow with coins of chorizo, smoked paprika, carrot, and waxy potato — the broth turns brick-red and silky, clinging to each lentil like a glaze.

ingredients.text: 280 parts Water or light chicken stock

instructions: Warm olive oil in a wide, heavy pot (at least 4L) over medium heat. Add chorizo slices and cook until the fat runs and the edges curl, about 3 minutes. Add onion and carrot. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onion is completely translucent and the carrot is beginning to soften, 8–10 minutes. The oil should be stained deep orange from the chorizo.

Add minced garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant. Add smoked paprika and cumin directly to the oil, stirring constantly. Cook for exactly 30–45 seconds — the spices toast in the fat, unlocking oil-soluble compounds. Do not let the paprika burn; it turns acrid instantly.

Add lentils and bay leaves, stir to coat in the spiced fat. Pour in water or stock and bring to a boil over high heat. Skim any foam that rises. Reduce heat to a gentle simmer — small lazy bubbles breaking the surface, not a rolling boil. Simmer uncovered for 25 minutes.

Add potato dice and season with salt. Continue to simmer for 20–25 minutes until potato is completely tender and the broth has thickened to a loose, cohesive stew consistency. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking. Remove bay leaves.

Off the heat, add sherry vinegar and stir through. Taste and adjust salt. The vinegar wakes up the smoked paprika and lifts the whole stew from heavy to vibrant. Let rest 5 minutes before serving — the stew continues to thicken as it cools slightly and is always better the next day.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spatchcocked Herb Chicken with Potatoes
description: A whole chicken opened flat so it roasts evenly and fast, its skin shattering over garlicky herb butter while the potatoes underneath fry in the dripping schmaltz until crisp-edged and seasoned through.

ingredients.text: 1 whole Whole chicken (about 2 kg / 4.5 lb), patted dry
1 whole Lemon (zest into butter, halves roasted in pan)
1300 g Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into 4 cm chunks
0 to taste Black pepper, freshly ground

instructions: Set the chicken breast-side down. With sturdy kitchen shears, cut along both sides of the backbone and remove it (save for stock). Flip the bird, splay the legs out, and press firmly on the breastbone with the heel of your hand until you feel it crack and the bird lies flat. Pat dry, then sprinkle about 16 g of the salt evenly over both sides. Refrigerate uncovered on a rack for at least 1 hour, or up to 24 hours for the crispest skin.

Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) with a rack in the upper-middle position. Mash the softened butter with the garlic, thyme leaves, rosemary, the zest of the lemon, and plenty of black pepper. Slide your fingers under the skin of the breast and thighs to loosen it without tearing, then push most of the butter underneath and massage it out evenly from the outside. Smear the rest over the skin.

Toss the potatoes with the olive oil, the remaining salt, and pepper, and spread them in a single layer in a large rimmed sheet pan (about 33 × 46 cm / 13 × 18 in). Nestle the zested lemon, halved, cut-side down among them. Lay the chicken skin-side up on top of the potatoes, legs pointing toward the back of the oven. Roast 45–55 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part of the thigh (not touching bone) reads 165°F (74°C); the breast should read at least 155–160°F (68–71°C).

Move the chicken to a cutting board and rest 10–15 minutes. Meanwhile, toss the potatoes in the pan juices and return them to the oven for 5 minutes if they need more crunch. Carve the chicken into legs, thighs, wings, and sliced breast, squeeze the roasted lemon over everything, and serve on top of the potatoes.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spiced Apple Butter
description: Granny Smith apples slow-cooked for hours with brown sugar, cinnamon, clove, and nutmeg in apple cider until they collapse and caramelize into a deep, mahogany-brown concentrate — velvety, intensely spiced, and almost impossibly fragrant.

ingredients.text: 100 parts Granny Smith apples, peeled, cored, and roughly chopped
30 parts Fresh apple cider (unfiltered, not apple juice)

instructions: Place the roughly chopped apples and apple cider in a large, wide, heavy-bottomed pot (a Dutch oven or enameled cast-iron braiser is ideal — the wide surface area accelerates evaporation). Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the apples are completely soft and beginning to fall apart — about 25–30 minutes. You are not looking for texture here; the apples must become completely yielding, as they will be blended to a smooth purée. The cider provides both liquid for the initial cooking and a concentrated apple flavor that plain water cannot replicate. As the apples soften, they will release their own juice and the mixture will become more liquid before it begins to reduce.

Add the brown sugar, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, allspice, apple cider vinegar, and salt to the softened apples. Stir to combine. Using an immersion blender directly in the pot, blend until completely smooth with no apple skin or chunk remaining. Alternatively, allow to cool slightly and blend in batches in a countertop blender (fill only halfway — hot liquid can erupt). If you prefer a very smooth, glossy butter, pass the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing firmly. Taste the sweetened applesauce base at this point: it will taste flat and too sweet because the sugar has not yet caramelized and concentrated — this is expected and correct. The transformation happens during the long, slow reduction that follows.

With the pot uncovered, reduce the applesauce over the lowest possible heat for 2 to 3 hours, stirring every 10–15 minutes — particularly important in the final hour when the concentration is high and scorching can occur. As the butter reduces, it will pass through several distinct stages: pale caramel (1 hour), golden amber (1.5 hours), deep mahogany-brown (2 hours), and finally the thick, glossy, spreadable consistency of apple butter (2.5–3 hours). You will know it is done when: a spoonful dropped on a cold plate holds its mound shape and does not run; the surface has a glossy, lacquered sheen; and the color is a deep mahogany-brown. The volume will have reduced by roughly half. Transfer to clean jars immediately while still hot.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Moroccan Slow-Roasted Lamb Shoulder
description: A bone-in lamb shoulder rubbed with a thick paste of ras el hanout, preserved lemon, and garlic, then slow-roasted until the meat yields to the lightest touch and falls from the bone in tender, perfumed shreds.

ingredients.text: 0.5 g Saffron threads, steeped in 2 tbsp warm water
20 g Fresh cilantro and flat-leaf parsley, mixed
30 g Toasted almonds or pine nuts

instructions: Pound or blend the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt. Finely mince the preserved lemon rind. Combine with ras el hanout, olive oil, cilantro, saffron water, honey, and salt to form a thick, aromatic paste. Taste — it should be salty, floral, pungently garlicky, and bright with citrus.

Using a small sharp knife, make 12–16 deep incisions all over the shoulder, 3–4 cm deep. Push a sliver of garlic and a pinch of spice paste into each. Rub the remaining paste all over the exterior, working it into every crevice and around the bone. Tuck rosemary sprigs under the shoulder. Marinate covered in the refrigerator for at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.

Place the shoulder in a large roasting dish. Pour the stock around the base. Cover tightly with two layers of foil, sealing the edges completely. Roast at 160 C (320 F) for 3.5 to 4 hours. The shoulder is done when the meat pulls effortlessly from the bone when probed with a fork.

Remove the foil. Raise oven to 200 C (400 F). Roast uncovered for 20–25 minutes, basting with the pan juices every 8 minutes, until the surface develops a deeply burnished, aromatic crust. The juices in the pan should have reduced to a rich jus.

Rest the shoulder for 15 minutes before serving. Scatter fresh herbs and toasted nuts directly over the shoulder. Serve at the table in the roasting dish, using two large forks to pull the meat apart. Spoon the pan jus over each portion.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Spinach and Ricotta Stuffed Shells
description: Jumbo pasta shells packed with a lemony ricotta-spinach filling, nestled in a quick garlic-basil tomato sauce and baked under a blanket of bubbling, browned mozzarella. Creamy, cheesy, and deeply comforting.

ingredients.text: 280 g Frozen chopped spinach, thawed and squeezed very dry
50 g Parmesan-style hard cheese (vegetarian rennet), grated
0 to taste Kosher salt and black pepper

instructions: Warm the olive oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the garlic and pepper flakes and cook 1–2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold. Add the crushed tomatoes, basil, 1 teaspoon salt, and pepper. Simmer gently 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until slightly thickened. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).

Boil the shells in a large pot of salted water for 2 minutes less than the package time (usually 7–8 minutes). Drain gently, rinse with cool water, and lay them open-side down on an oiled tray so they don't stick together. Cook a few extra — some always tear.

In a bowl, mix the ricotta, squeezed spinach, egg, grated hard cheese, lemon zest, nutmeg, 80 g of the mozzarella, 3/4 teaspoon salt, and pepper until evenly combined. Taste before adding the egg if you want to check seasoning.

Spread two-thirds of the sauce over the bottom of a 23 x 33 cm baking dish. Fill each shell with about 2 tablespoons of filling and nestle them open-side up in a snug single layer. Spoon the remaining sauce over and between the shells.

Scatter the remaining 120 g mozzarella over the top. Cover with foil and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 20 minutes. Uncover and bake 10–15 minutes more until the cheese is bubbling and spotted brown. Rest 10 minutes before serving so the filling sets.
author: ForkRecipe Kitchen

title: Split Pea Soup with Smoked Turkey
description: Green split peas simmered with a smoky turkey leg until they collapse into a thick, earthy, jade-green soup, studded with carrot and pulled smoked meat and brightened by a splash of vinegar.

ingredients.text: 30 g Unsalted butter or olive oil
450 g Green split peas, picked over and rinsed
700 g Smoked turkey leg or wings
0 to taste Kosher salt (add only at the end)
0 to taste Flat-leaf parsley, chopped, and croutons

instructions: Melt butter in a 6 litre pot over medium heat. Add onion, carrot, and celery and cook 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and the onion is translucent. Add garlic and cook 1 minute. Don't salt yet — the smoked turkey will season the pot.

Add split peas, smoked turkey, water, bay, thyme, and pepper. Bring to a boil, skim the foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer.
